# a5 campaign: infrastructure reality

The campaign's host disappeared on 2026-08-20 and the replacement cannot run the model unmodified.
This is the blocking constraint on any continuation, so it is documented as carefully as the science.

---

## ⚠️ A hard `--nodelist` pin needs a fallback, or it becomes indefinite queueing

Arms `n317`: `n358` were pinned to `beagle3-0043` for hardware consistency. On 2026-08-24 that node had a
**free GPU but all 32 CPUs allocated**, so a 4-CPU/1-GPU arm sat `PENDING (Resources)` for ~30 minutes
while three A40 nodes were fully idle.

**Default for CE-only arms:** exclude the known-bad nodes and let SLURM choose, 
`--exclude=beagle3-0025,beagle3-0029` (0025 `DOWN*+DRAIN`; 0029 granted `--gres=gpu:1` and exposed no
device, killing `n317` in 108 s). Keep a hard pin only when *throughput* comparability is the point, and
check `AllocTRES` on the pinned node first:
`scontrol show node <n> | grep -oP 'AllocTRES=\K\S*'`: a free GPU does not imply free CPUs.

⛔⛔ **AND IT COST AN ARM WITHIN THE HOUR.** A 142-step arm whose `wall_guard_sec=1450` was tuned to the
pinned node was killed by the **SLURM 28-min limit during eval** on beagle3-0024: guard fired at step
138/142, eval got 238 s and needed more (eval is ~182 s on the warm-cache node, ~1.3× slower there).
Full compute bill, no measurement. **When you release a node pin, RE-DERIVE the wall budget; do not
inherit it.** Portable rule, measured: **73-step arms ~972 s, 120-step arms ~1,420 s (260 s headroom, verified
complete), 142-step arms ~1,630-1,790 s (≈50 s headroom, one died at eval).** Budget **≥250 s of
headroom** on a shared node.

⛔ **And do NOT attribute the overrun to a cold Inductor cache**: `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` is on
`/project`, i.e. shared across nodes, so compiled kernels are not per-node. The ~174 s that killed the
arm is **unexplained**; the leading hypothesis is contention (that node had 3/4 GPUs and 28/32 CPUs
allocated, and the data bins are on the same shared filesystem), unverified.

⚠️ Cost of releasing the pin: cross-arm **throughput** comparisons are no longer guaranteed (the
`run.sh` precedent, two nodes with an identical feature string being 94 GB and 80 GB H100s: is why the
pin existed). CE should be unaffected on the same SKU. The result JSON records `node`, so verify before
quoting any wall figure.

## ⛔⛔ `sbatch --test-only` does NOT evaluate the QOS GRES cap (2026-08-23)

The beagle3 QOS caps a job at **4 GPUs** (`MaxTRESPerJob = gres/gpu=4`), and that cap is **real**: 
a 16-GPU submission sits `PENDING` forever with `Reason=QOSMaxGRESPerJob`.

**But every pre-flight check said it would work:**

| check | verdict |
|---|---|
| `sacctmgr show qos beagle3 format=MaxTRESPerJob` | `gres/gpu=4`: correct, but I read it as per-node |
| `sbatch --test-only` (4 nodes × gpu:4 = 16) | **`Verification: ***PASSED***`** + *"to start at 2026-08-23T11:39:45"*, i.e. it predicted an immediate start |
| actual `sbatch` | `PENDING … (QOSMaxGRESPerJob)` |

⇒ **`--test-only` validates partition/account/QOS membership and simulates the scheduler, but does not
enforce `MaxTRESPerJob` on GRES.** It will happily hand back a start time for a job that can never run.
The recorded rule "sacctmgr lies, verify with `sbatch --test-only`" is therefore **incomplete**: for
GPU-count limits, only a real submission's pending `Reason` is authoritative.

**Procedure that actually works:** submit for real, then immediately
`squeue -j <id> -o "%.8T %R"`. If the reason is a `QOSMax*` / `AssocMax*` limit, `scancel` and shrink.
Cost of the round trip is seconds and it is the only honest test.

**Consequence for a4.5:** the pretraining is capped at **4 GPUs per job** no matter how many cards are
idle. The per-*user* budget is 32 GPUs / 8 nodes, but that can only be spent on additional concurrent
jobs, and independent SLURM allocations cannot cooperate in one DDP run. The `gpu` partition allows
16 GPUs per job (verified: `AllowQos=gpu,debug`, no per-job GRES cap) but its slots did not start for
**2 days**, and 24 GPUs on beagle3 (6 nodes) queued to +6 h.

⭐ **What WAS available inside the cap: packing.** The run had been 2 nodes × 2 GPUs; the same 4-GPU
allocation as **1 node × 4 GPUs** keeps the whole all-reduce on-node. `AUTO_SHAPE=0` is required to pin
it, with the picker enabled, `NNODES=4 GPUS_PER_NODE=4` was silently rewritten to 8 nodes × 2 GPUs.
⚠️ Packing halves the CPUs available to the ranks (4 CPUs for 4 ranks, vs 8 for 4 across two nodes), so
the dataloader can become the new bottleneck: measure `tok/s`, do not assume the win.

## ⛔⛔ Recursive `grep` is blind to 94% of this repo: VERIFIED, not inferred

`grep` in this environment is a **shell function** (`type grep` → "grep is a function") that respects
`.gitignore`. This repo's `.gitignore` contains **`*/*` on line 5**: every file in every
subdirectory, and **`*.sh` on line 9**. Measured: **4,343 of 4,597 files (94%) are git-ignored**, so
a recursive `grep -r` sees 254 files.

**Demonstrated twice, deliberately:**
- `grep -rl "MEASURED 2026-08-23 on job 54394134" .` → nothing. `grep -l <same> submit_beagle3.sh`
  → hit. Plain string, no regex metacharacters.
- Wrote a throwaway `gtest_probe.sh` containing a unique token, confirmed `git check-ignore` reports
  `.gitignore:9:*.sh`, then ran the recursive grep → the file was not found; a direct grep found it.

**Consequence:** *never* conclude "no references remain" / "that symbol is unused" / "nothing calls
this" from a recursive search in this tree. It cannot see any `.sh`, and it cannot see `exp/`,
`exp5/`, `reasoning/`, `model_cards/`: anything below the root. This cost real time during the
2026-08-23 worktree consolidation: a recursive grep pronounced the tree clean of stale
`ArgonneAI-4.5` paths while **12 files still held them**, including every launcher that matters.

**Do this instead**: explicit globs, which read files by name and bypass the wrapper:
```bash
grep -ln "PATTERN" *.sh *.sbatch *.py *.md exp/*.sh exp/*.sbatch exp/*.py exp5/*.md reasoning/*.py
```
or `git grep --no-index --untracked`, or `find . -name '*.sh' -exec grep -l ... +`.

⚠️ Separately: this `grep`'s BRE handling chokes on patterns containing `{`, so
`grep 'X="${VAR:-52G}"' file` silently matches nothing even on the right file. Use `grep -F` /
`fgrep` for anything with braces. Two independent silent-failure modes in one tool.

## 1. The campaign's host is gone

**2026-08-20 18:09:14**, the midway3 `test` partition went `State=DOWN, Hidden=YES` (no
reservation, so not a scheduled outage). It is still *defined* with all 610 nodes; nothing can start.
This killed the a5 campaign mid-arm (`n244`) and the a4.5 pretrain chain at step 55,315.

`test` was the free partition, it did not consume the SU allocation. Every a5 arm ran there, on
`midway3-0432` (H100 PCIe 80 GB) and `midway3-0426`.

## 2. Every other GPU partition is CLOSED to this account

Verified with `sbatch --test-only` (read-only). ⚠️ **`sacctmgr show assoc` is MISLEADING**, it lists
~90 partition QOSes for accounts like `pi-pedramh` and `pi-sriesenfeld`, but the submit plugin
rejects with `Invalid membership to account`:

| partition | hardware | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `pedramh-gpu` | 4× H100, often idle | REJECTED |
| `sriesenfeld-gpu` | 2× H100 | REJECTED |
| `ssd-gpu` | A100 | REJECTED |
| `ai4s-hackathon` | 4× H100 + 8× A100 | account not held; QOS caps `gres/gpu=1`, 8 h |
| `gpu` | V100 / RTX6000 | passes, but no bf16 on V100; quoted a 3-day wait |
| **`beagle3`** | **A100-PCIE-40GB ×22 nodes, A40-46GB ×22 nodes** | **PASSES** via `rcc-staff` |

`beagle3` auto-promotes to the **`beagle3-prio`** QOS. Billing is `billing=<cpu count>`: **GPUs
weigh 0**, so ~4 SU/hr. Walls: 2 days (`beagle3-long`: 4 days).

⛔ **THE BINDING LIMIT IS PER JOB, NOT PER USER: `MaxTRES = gres/gpu=4` on EVERY beagle3 QOS.** A
single job can never exceed 4 GPUs here. The 32-GPU / 8-node figure is `MaxTRESPU` (per *user*,
across up to 12 jobs), and one DDP run is one job, so 4 is the ceiling for training.

⚠️ **`sbatch --test-only` does NOT reject an over-cap request.** It returns `PASSED` with a plausible
far-future start time, which is indistinguishable from contention. A 6-GPU job sat PENDING with
`Reason=QOSMaxGRESPerJob` while 9 A100s were idle, and several rounds were wasted attributing a flat
policy limit to fragmentation and backfill. **Query `sacctmgr show qos ... format=MaxTRES` instead of
trusting the dry run**: `exp/pick_gpu_shape.sh` now does exactly that.

Worth an RCC ticket: `pedramh-gpu` / `sriesenfeld-gpu` are idle H100s this account is *associated*
with but cannot submit to.

## 3. Why beagle3 cannot run this model with plain DDP

Measured stage by stage on a real A100-PCIE-40GB (39.39 GiB usable), 3-way DDP:

```
model on GPU (fp32 params)          7.69 GiB
after DDP wrap                     15.38   <-- +7.69, gradient buckets, allocated EAGERLY
optimizer constructed (m/v lazy)   15.38
optimizer_state_dict loaded        30.75   <-- +15.38, AdamW m+v
                                            -> 8.00 GiB free -> OOM at micro=1
```

⚠️ **The DDP wrap allocates a full 7.69 GiB duplicate up front.** `gradient_as_bucket_view=True`
pre-allocates buckets spanning every parameter, so gradient memory exists from *construction*, not
from the first backward. Together with autocast's bf16 weight copies, even micro=1 does not fit.

**Consequences, all measured:**

- A100-40G OOMs at micro 1, 2, 4, 8: **chunked CE does not help**, because the blocker is not
  micro-batch-proportional (micro=2 and micro=4 used near-identical memory).
- A40-46G OOMs at micro 2 and 4 as well.

⚠️ **A memory ceiling measured without the collectives does not transfer to DDP.** A single-GPU GB10
bench (130 GB card, no DDP/NCCL) said micro=4 was fine at 35.1 GiB; on A100 with 3-way DDP it OOMs.

This is also why **Muon freeing 52% of optimizer state (~8.1 GiB at 2.06B)** matters far more than it
looked during the campaign, it is roughly the whole A100 shortfall.

## 4. ZeRO fixes the memory, and then the SAVE path fails

`ZeroRedundancyOptimizer` (shard AdamW m/v across ranks), auto-enabled below ~70 GB:

| card | micro × accum | headroom | training |
|---|---|---|---|
| A100-40G, 3 GPUs | 1 × 176 | 3.07 GiB | fits |
| A40-46G, 4 GPUs | **2 × 66** | 6.07 GiB | fits, **~17,000 tok/s** |

⭐ **4× A40 runs at ~17,000 tok/s**: over 4× a single GB10. So beagle3 *is* a viable compute path.

⛔ **But `consolidate_state_dict()` never returns.** Timed in isolation with 15 s heartbeats: still
running at **962 s**, killed at the 20-minute ceiling. The process is alive (heartbeats continue), so
it is not a process deadlock: PyTorch consolidates by gathering each rank's **pickled** local state
through the process group, and this state is 15.38 GiB. Raising the timeout is not the fix.

**Net: ZeRO training works; ZeRO checkpointing does not.** Without a working save, throughput is
irrelevant. A continuation needs a different save strategy (e.g. a tensor-based gather rather than
pickled objects, or sharded files plus a converter, with the hard requirement that the written
checkpoint stays loadable by the **unsharded** path, since this run has already moved across three
machines).

### The bug that masquerades as OOM

⚠️ ZeRO's `load_state_dict` does **not** relocate AdamW's per-param `step` scalar the way plain
`Optimizer.load_state_dict` does for the fused kernel. `step` stays on CPU while m/v go to CUDA, and
the mismatch only surfaces at the **first `optimizer.step()`**:

```
RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device,
              but got state_steps is on cpu, different from other tensors on cuda:0
```

It appears *after* every memory probe has reported "fits", so it reads exactly like an OOM. It cost
three ladder jobs to find. `fix_optimizer_step_device()` in `pretrain.py` handles it. (AdamW also
auto-selects the fused kernel when all params are CUDA, so `fused=False` does not dodge it.)

## 5. FP8 is card-gated

`torchao` float8 needs **sm89+**. beagle3 A100 is sm80 and A40 is sm86, so **fp8 is impossible
there** and must be turned off, not left to fail. GB10 (DGX Spark) is sm121, so fp8 *is* available
there.

⚠️ The 151669→151680 vocab padding used to be gated on `--fp8 1`. Because padding changes the
embedding *shape*, that silently pinned every fp8 checkpoint to sm89+ hardware: invisible while
`test` only ever gave sm90 H100s. It now derives from the resume checkpoint.

> **A flag that changes a tensor SHAPE is not a performance flag.** Derive it from the checkpoint, or
> record it in the checkpoint: never infer it from a runtime switch another machine will set
> differently.

## 6. Slurm itself has been unreliable

`sbatch` failed cluster-wide with `I/O error writing script/environment to file`: a bare
`--wrap="hostname"` too. The controller stayed UP and could *read* state; it could not write new job
scripts to `/var/spool/slurm/ctld` on midway3-mgt2. Observed 06:33→06:57 and again ~07:40→09:00 on
2026-08-21. Confirming signal: the cluster **drains** (pending 1,676→826, running 1,598→1,311)
because jobs finish and nothing new can enter.

Practical mitigation: wrap submissions in a retry loop. Two outages were absorbed with zero lost work
that way.

## 7. The non-Slurm option

**RCC's DGX Spark (`ssh dgx` → `spark-2500`)**: GB10 Grace Blackwell, cc 12.1, ~121.7 GiB **unified**
memory, aarch64, **no Slurm at all**. torch 2.13.0+cu130 is already in `~/venvs/vllm`.

Measured on the a4.5 model, fp8 on, compile on: **micro 24 × accum 22 → ~4,100 tok/s** at 81% HBM.
`torch.compile` is worth 2× and also cuts peak memory 47.3→35.1 GiB.

- ✅ No queue, no wall limit, no submission outages, it absorbed both Slurm incidents without
  noticing.
- ⛔ ~4,100 tok/s is a **warm spare, not a completion path** (~230 days for 80B tokens).
- ⚠️ No `python3-dev` and no root ⇒ Triton's gcc helper fails **intermittently** (a warm cache hides
  it; it surfaces as an `InductorError` quoting gcc that reads like an OOM). Fix:
  `export CPATH=$HOME/pydev/root/usr/include/python3.12:$HOME/pydev/root/usr/include`
- It is a **shared** machine (7 other accounts) with one unified pool.

## 8. Launcher support already in place

`run_full_training.sh` in the argonne4.5 tree is now card-portable:

- `TARGET=midway3|beagle3` selects partition/account/qos/exclude/gres/mem as **one bundle**, threaded
  through **both** resubmit paths: previously only `--constraint` was re-passed, so a beagle3 chain
  would have silently resubmitted itself back onto the dead `test` partition.
- `PRETRAIN_CARD=H100|H200|A100|A40`; fp8 auto-off below sm89 from `compute_cap`.
- Micro-batch picker: the ladder value is a memory **cap**, and it walks down to the largest micro
  where `micro × NGPUS` divides 528, so the effective batch stays **540,672 tokens** on every shape
  (that is what keeps the LR-6e-4 recipe valid and the WSD cooldown at 30,517 steps).
- Multi-node torchrun via `srun --ntasks-per-node=1` + c10d rendezvous. `--nproc_per_node` is
  GPUS_PER_NODE, not the global count: passing the global count is the classic multi-node hang.
- `DRY_RUN=1` resolves and prints every decision without training.
- `submit_beagle3.sh` passes the bundle on the command line (the `#SBATCH` header cannot be
  conditional), with **7-hour slices** then self-resubmit.

## 9. Running probes on A40/A100 after the H100s went away (measured 2026-08-22)

Every recorded a5/a4.5 arm ran `fp8=1` on H100/H200. Those cards are gone, and A40 is sm86 / A100
sm80, so **`fp8=0` is forced and NO result obtained here is comparable to any recorded `tgt`.** A
fresh in-configuration baseline is mandatory before any lever is tested: see the sigma pair below.

⚠️ **`fp8=0` costs enough memory to change what fits.** The 2.06B probe at `block 2048, micro 2,
world=1, checkpoint_stride 1` needs **~45 GiB** and OOMs on A40's 44.35 GiB usable: job 54254849
died in backward wanting 1.16 GiB with 427 MiB free and 42.45 GiB already allocated. It missed by
only ~0.7 GiB, and the gap is the fp8 weight copies the recorded arms were getting for free.

Working single-GPU probe shape (`exp/run_probe_1gpu.sbatch`, `CFG=<name> sbatch ...`):

| | |
|---|---|
| card | **1x A40** (44.35 GiB). A100-40G has only 39.39 and cannot host this probe at all. |
| ZeRO | **unavailable**: `world=1`, and ZeroRedundancyOptimizer needs world>1. Plain AdamW: params 7.69 + grads 7.69 + m/v 15.38 = 30.75 GiB fixed. |
| micro x accum | **1 x 10** at block 2048 (eff_batch 20,480). micro 2 OOMs. |
| checkpoint_stride | **1**, not 2: stride 2 checkpoints FEWER layers and therefore stores MORE activations. |
| `--mem` | **24G**. Probes init FRESH, so host RAM is ~13 GiB; the 52G production figure is a 2x over-request because that one `torch.load`s a 24.8 GB checkpoint. |
| wall | 28 min job, `wall_guard_sec` 1400. |

⚠️ `probe.py` calls `dist.init_process_group` unconditionally, so it needs `torchrun` even at
world=1. And torchrun SWALLOWS the child exception: the `.out` shows only a bare `exitcode 1`;
the real traceback is at the HEAD of the `.err`. Read that first, not the torchrun stack.

### Horizon: what a 28-minute single-GPU slot can and cannot answer

~4M tokens. That is **too short for a data-mixture arm**: the campaign's 50/25/25 mixture win
REVERSED at 282 steps, so a mixture result at this horizon measures that same artifact. Mixture
questions need the long horizon, not the cheap one. What this slot CAN do is measure sigma, verify
instrument paths, and test levers with effects large enough to clear the floor.

### The sigma the loop must respect

From the recorded ladder (35M tokens, fp8=1, all seed 444):

| arm | mix | tgt |
|---|---|---|
| a12_warm5pct | 50/30/20 | 4.7263 |
| a20_mix_control | 50/30/20 | **4.9858** |
| a21_variance_check | n/a | 4.8393 |
| a19_mix40_35_25 | 40/35/25 | 5.1650 |

`a20` was written as an INSTRUMENT CONTROL to prove the mix code path reproduced `a12`. **It did
not** (4.9858 vs 4.7263), and the a20/a21 replicates differ by **0.147**. So `a19`'s 0.18 "mixture
effect" sits INSIDE the replicate spread and is not resolved. Any arm run in this loop needs an
expected effect above roughly 0.3, or replication, before it means anything.

## Block size at FIXED effective batch: prefer the LONGER block (measured 2026-08-22)

Controlled pair `n307` vs `n311`: identical params, steps (146), tokens (2,990,080), mix, seed and
effective batch (20,480 tok/step). **Only `block_size` differs**, with `grad_accum` compensating
(2048x10 vs 1024x20).

| | block 2048 | block 1024 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| throughput | 3,556 tok/s | 3,072 tok/s | **−13.6%** |
| HBM | 0.9464 (41.97 GiB) | 0.9325 (41.36 GiB) | **−0.62 GiB only** |
| `tgt` | 7.0556 | 7.0782 | +0.0226 |

⭐ **Halving the sequence made it SLOWER, not faster.** The naive reading ("attention is O(T²), so
shorter is cheaper") is wrong at fixed effective batch: `grad_accum` must double, which doubles the
micro-batch count and therefore all per-micro-batch overhead (kernel launches, gradient-checkpoint
recompute boundaries, accumulation bookkeeping). For a 24-layer / 2560-wide model the MLP and
projection FLOPs dominate attention at these lengths, so the attention saving does not pay for the
extra micro-batches. **At fixed effective batch, prefer the longer block.**

⭐ **Halving the sequence freed only 0.62 GiB of 41.97.** This quantifies why the KD arm could not be
rescued by shortening the sequence (smoke 54301587 died 76 MiB short at block 1024). Fixed state is
**fp32 weights 7.69 + grads 7.69 + AdamW m/v 15.38 = 30.76 GiB**, plus ~3.85 GiB of bf16 autocast
copies ≈ **34.6 GiB before a single activation**: none of which scales with sequence length. A 2.06B
model with plain AdamW at world=1 has only ~10 GiB of working room on a 44.35 GiB A40, and sequence
length controls a small slice of that.

⚠️ The `tgt` +0.0226 is **one seed, unreplicated**, and sits inside the imported 0.02-0.04 bound: 
INDETERMINATE, not "block size is quality-neutral". Per-domain: edu −0.0038, math +0.0443,
code +0.0274.

## Watchdog trainer-detection was silently broken by the experiment queue move (2026-08-27)

Both watchdogs (`chain_watchdog.sh` on Sophia via crontab, `polaris_watchdog_loop.sh` on Polaris as
a detached loop) are **silent on their no-op path**, they exit 0 before their logging line whenever
a live job exists. A stale log is therefore the designed quiet state, **not** evidence of failure.
I misread stale logs as "both watchdogs are dead" before checking the exit paths.

**The real defect, which I introduced this session:** both watchdogs decided "a trainer is live" from
a queue heuristic that stopped holding.

| watchdog | old test | why it broke |
|---|---|---|
| Polaris | `$3 != "debug"` ⇒ trainer | experiments moved to a 2 h **`preemptable`** session, and `polaris_pre4.pbs` (a **trainer** gap-filler) is *also* `preemptable`. Queue cannot discriminate, and excluding `preemptable` wholesale would blind it to a real trainer. |
| Sophia | counted **every** live job | an experiment session on Sophia reads as a live trainer, so the watchdog stands down while the chain is actually dead. |

Failure mode in both cases: the watchdog sees the *experiment* job, concludes a trainer is live, and
declines to resubmit: exactly when the chain needs rescuing. Silent, and invisible in the logs
because the no-op path does not log.

**Fix: an explicit marker, not a heuristic.** Every experiment runner (`exp4gpu_pre2.pbs`,
`exp4gpu_dbg.pbs`, `exp4gpu.pbs`, `exp8gpu_sophia.pbs`) now does, right after `WLOG=`:

```bash
touch $R/.exp_job_${PBS_JOBID%%.*}
trap "rm -f $R/.exp_job_${PBS_JOBID%%.*}" EXIT
```

and both watchdogs count live jobs by ID, skipping any that has a marker. Verified on the live
queue: the running experiment `7567330` is skipped, the queued gap-filler `7567304` is counted,
`LIVE=1`. Sophia dry-run exits 0 silently with 2 trainers live, as intended.

**Generalisable lesson:** a safety net that only logs when it acts cannot be distinguished from a
dead one. Worse, this net's *input* was a heuristic about queue names, and I invalidated that
heuristic with an unrelated change (moving experiments to a different queue) without re-checking
what consumed it. **When you change where a job runs, grep for anything that infers meaning from
where jobs run.**

## The experiment session's "auto-renew" was a comment, not code (2026-08-27)

`exp4gpu.pbs` and `exp4gpu_pre2.pbs` have both carried this header since the runner was written:

> Batch, not `qsub -I`: an interactive job needs a TTY and cannot self-chain, so it could not
> auto-renew. **This chains with `-W depend=afterany` at START**, so the next 2 h session is
> already queued while this one works.

**There was no `qsub` anywhere in either script.** `grep -nE "qsub|depend|afterany"` matched only
the comment lines. The session simply ran its 2 h and ended, and nothing resubmitted it, which is
the actual reason the experiment job kept being "gone" at the start of a check, and why arms sat
idle between ticks waiting for me to notice. The header documented an intention that was never
implemented, and I had been reading it as a description of behaviour.

**Implemented now**, at session START so the successor accrues queue priority while we work:

```bash
PENDING=$(ls -1 $R/queue/pending/*.json 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
if [ ! -e "$R/.exp_chain_stop" ] && [ "$PENDING" -gt 4 ]; then
  SUCC=$($Q/qsub -W depend=afterany:$PBS_JOBID $R/exp4gpu_pre2.pbs 2>&1)
  case "$SUCC" in *.polaris-pbs-*) touch "$R/.exp_job_${SUCC%%.*}" ;; esac
  ...
```

Bounds on the chain: one successor per session (**linear, not exponential**), the successor is
dependency-held so only one experiment session runs at a time, it chains only while >4 arms remain,
and `touch $R/.exp_chain_stop` breaks it by hand.

### Second-order bug this immediately created, caught before it bit

A dependency-**held** successor is still "live" in `qstat`. The marker from the previous fix is
written when a job *starts*, so a queued successor had no marker and the watchdog counted it as a
trainer: re-opening the exact hole the markers were introduced to close, one level up. Fixed by
marking the successor **at submit time** and pruning markers whose job is no longer live. Verified
on the live queue with all three jobs present: running experiment skipped, held successor skipped,
`small`-queue gap-filler counted, `LIVE=1`.

**Lesson: a fix that adds a new job state has to be re-checked against everything that enumerates
job states.** I closed the running-job case and shipped the queued-job case in the same session.

### Also corrected: ARM_SECS was below the real arm time

`ARM_SECS` (the "don't start an arm you can't finish" gate) was 2400 s, taken from a 2127 s
single-arm measurement. With 4 arms sharing one node the real time is **~43 min** (175/400 steps in
19 min, measured 2026-08-27), so a worker could start an arm that the wall then cut off. Raised to
2700 s. Interrupted arms were always recovered (`inflight` → `pending`), so this cost throughput,
not data.

## The gap-filler was churning 12 nodes every 10 minutes for nothing (2026-08-27)

Symptom: the Polaris gap-filler job ID changed three times in 30 minutes
(`7567304` → `7567483` → `7567515`) while Sophia was running normally.

**Not the watchdog.** `polaris_watchdog.sh` checks `LIVE > 0` *before* it checks Sophia's heartbeat,
so with a filler already queued it exits silently and never submits. `.sophia_owns` was fresh (48 s),
so the heartbeat mechanism was working too.

**It was the filler re-queueing itself.** `polaris_small12.pbs` has three yield sites, each:

```bash
cd $R && $Q/qsub -a $(date -d "+10 minutes" +%Y%m%d%H%M.%S) $SELF_SCRIPT
```

That is the anti-loop patch from the 132-cycle incident, it stopped the *instant* respawn but left
a 10-minute one. Full cycle: wake → Q → **R (allocates 12 nodes / 48 GPUs)** → read `.sophia_owns`
→ yield → re-queue. Every 10 minutes, ~0.1 node-hours billed per cycle, achieving nothing, for as
long as Sophia is healthy.

**Fix: sleep until the boundary, not for a fixed interval.** The trainer now publishes its slice's
expected end to `$R/.sophia_boundary` (epoch, derived from PBS's own
`Resource_List.walltime − resources_used.walltime`, so it stays correct across slices), and each
yield site calls a helper:

```bash
requeue_at() {   # wake ~10 min BEFORE Sophia's boundary; fall back to +10 min if unknown/imminent
  now=$(date +%s)
  if [ -r "$R/.sophia_boundary" ]; then
    B=$(cat "$R/.sophia_boundary"); case "$B" in ""|*[!0-9]*) B=0 ;; esac
    W=$(( B - 600 ))
    if [ "$W" -gt $(( now + 1200 )) ]; then date -d "@$W" +%Y%m%d%H%M.%S; return; fi
  fi
  date -d "+10 minutes" +%Y%m%d%H%M.%S
}
```

The `+1200` guard means behaviour is unchanged near and after a boundary, that is exactly when
prompt retries are wanted. Applied to all 6 gap-fillers (`polaris_ds6`, `polaris_pre4`,
`polaris_small12`, `sophia_gap2`, `sophia_gap4`, `sophia_p2`), 18 sites, all parse.

State after the fix: one filler (`7567548`) waiting on `Execution_Time = 17:31:26`, i.e. 10 min
before the 17:41:26 boundary, **zero node allocations between now and then.** Its old-logic sibling
`7567546` (spawned by the churner just before it exited, due to wake at 15:59) was cancelled;
two queued 12-node fillers is worse than one.

**Lesson: a rate limit is not a fix for a loop whose trigger condition is still permanently true.**
The +10 min patch made the churn survivable and therefore invisible, it stopped being an incident
and became background cost. The actual fix was to make the wake condition track the thing the job is
waiting *for*.

## The `depend=afterany` chain was the ONLY thing preventing two Sophia trainers (2026-08-27)

Investigating boundary pending time, I found 8 jobs queued ahead of us in `by-node` (six 2-node/24 h,
two 1-node) while our successor sits dependency-**held**, and a held job accrues **zero**
`eligible_time`. The obvious optimisation is to queue the successor unheld so it accrues priority
during the 1h24m before the boundary, relying on the script's guard to prevent double-training.

**The guard does not exist on that path.** `train_chain.pbs`'s `primary` branch does:

```bash
rm -rf "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null    # UNCONDITIONAL force-take
```

and never consults `flag_age` or `ck_age`: only the Polaris branch yields. The file header claims
`.train_owner.lock` "prevents two trainers of the SAME tier"; **for primary-vs-primary that is
false.** A second Sophia primary would destroy the live trainer's lock and train against the same
`/eagle` checkpoint dir. So the dependency chain is load-bearing, not belt-and-braces, and the
"optimisation" would have risked the run.

**Guard added, biased to REFUSE.** My first instinct was fail-open (proceed when uncertain) so a bug
could never stall the successor. That is the wrong bias here: a stalled successor loses minutes, two
trainers can lose the run. Final logic:

| flag state | decision | why |
|---|---|---|
| missing / stale (>180 s) | **proceed** | a live primary rewrites it every 60 s, so staleness is real evidence of none |
| fresh, owner == me | proceed | it is our own announcement |
| fresh, owner unparseable | **refuse** | fresh means someone is alive; do not gamble |
| fresh, owner `job_state = R` | **refuse** | another primary is running |
| fresh, owner not running | proceed | it died within 180 s without cleanup |

On refuse it re-queues itself as `-W depend=afterany:$_owner`, an over-eager successor repairs
itself into a properly chained one instead of dying.

### The first version of this fix was inert

I installed the guard immediately before the force-take, but the primary branch **writes**
`$SOPHIA_FLAG` ~30 lines earlier. A second primary would overwrite the live owner's flag and then
read back its own id, so the guard always passed. Moved it ahead of the ownership announcement
(guard reads at line 77, announces at line 92) and verified the ordering.

**Lesson: for a guard that reads shared state, check where that state is written relative to the
read.** Both the check and the write were in the same branch, ~30 lines apart, and the write came
first.

### Not yet taking the pending-time win

The unheld successor is deliberately **not** submitted this tick. The guard should survive one real
handover before anything relies on it, and the current held chain is safe. The boundary is instead
covered by the Polaris gap-filler already armed for 17:31. Verified standalone against live state
before installing: a hypothetical new primary correctly detects `176743` as running and refuses; a
self-check passes; a missing flag proceeds.

## The checkpoint backstop was disabled, and the fix that disabled it was mine (2026-08-27)

Measured the real checkpoint cadence: steps 81282 → 81660 → 81849, i.e. **190-380 steps ≈ 30-47
min** between writes. Against that, `polaris_watchdog.sh` was submitting gap-fillers with
`-v CK_WINDOW=120`, so `ck_age < CK_WINDOW` was **essentially never true**: the passive backstop
against a second trainer did nothing, leaving `.sophia_owns` as the sole protection.

I set `CK_WINDOW=120` earlier for a real reason: at 2400 s the guard read a 12-minute-old checkpoint
as "a trainer is live" and yielded to a **dead** trainer. Both values are wrong because the two
tests were conflated:

| | CK_WINDOW large (2400) | CK_WINDOW small (120) |
|---|---|---|
| dead primary, recent ckpt | **yields to a corpse** for up to 40 min | correct |
| live non-cooperative trainer | correct | **starts a second trainer** |

**Root cause: `ck_age` was being asked to answer a question the flag already answers better.** A live
primary rewrites `$SOPHIA_FLAG` every 60 s and its `EXIT` trap deletes it, so flag state is a far
sharper signal than checkpoint mtime. Split the cases:

```bash
  if   [ "$(flag_age)" -lt 180 ]; then                                    # FRESH   -> yield
  elif [ ! -f "$SOPHIA_FLAG" ] && [ "$(ck_age)" -lt "$CK_WINDOW" ]; then  # MISSING -> backstop
  fi                                                                     # STALE   -> take over
```

- **fresh** → a primary is alive and refreshing → yield.
- **stale** → a cooperative trainer died; staleness is authoritative → take over, ignore `ck_age`.
  This is the case the old code got wrong.
- **missing** → unknown owner (the header notes pre-guard job `176565` published nothing), so
  `ck_age` is a legitimate passive backstop and the *large* default is correct there.

Installed in all 8 guard scripts; `CK_WINDOW=120` override removed so the script default (2400 s)
applies where it now belongs. Logic table verified standalone across all five flag×ck_age
combinations before installing.

**Lesson: when one signal is strictly sharper than another, do not tune the blunt one, scope it to
the case the sharp one cannot cover.** I spent two fixes moving a threshold back and forth between
two failure modes that a three-way split eliminates.

⚠️ These take effect for *future* submissions. PBS spools a script copy at submit time, so the
in-flight `7567548` (submitted 15:50) runs the earlier version, it has `requeue_at` but not the
three-way logic.

## Boundary pending time was structural: a held successor accrues ZERO eligible_time (2026-08-27)

Measured 39 min before the 17:41 boundary, on the live queue:

| job | who | shape | `eligible_time` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **176974 (our successor, HELD)** | us | 1 node | **00:00:01** |
| 177160 | sgoswami | 1 node / 0.5 h | **00:48:05** |
| 177166 | ychuang | 1 node / 6 h | **00:38:27** |
| 177151-4 | kevienz | 2 nodes / 24 h each | (queued) |

`depend=afterany` holds the successor, and **PBS accrues no eligible_time while a job is held.** So
at every boundary our successor arrives with ~1 second of priority against rivals sitting on tens of
minutes, and loses the node. One of the two rivals is a 6-hour job: losing that race costs hours of
H100 time, repeatedly, once per slice.

`sophia-gpu-10`/`-11` sit `free` with 8/8 GPUs but carry `queue_tags = infer-svc-test`, so they are
not reachable from `by-node`, which is also why the two 1-node rivals have not already taken them.

**`eligible_time` is a stopwatch, so queueing late cannot fix it.** I queued an unheld successor
(`177196`) 39 min out; it accrues, but the rivals accrue *at the same rate*, so it stays ~48 min
behind and only helps against later arrivals. The fix has to be at slice **start**.

**Change: the self-chain now submits the successor UNHELD**, banking the full ~24 h of a slice:

```bash
-SUCC=$($Q/qsub -W depend=afterany:$PBS_JOBID -v MICRO=...,GC=...,STRIDE=... $R/train_chain.pbs ...)
+SUCC=$($Q/qsub                                -v MICRO=...,GC=...,STRIDE=... $R/train_chain.pbs ...)
```

**This is only safe because of the primary-vs-primary guard added earlier this session.** An unheld
successor that gets a node mid-slice detects the live trainer's fresh `$SOPHIA_FLAG`, refuses, and
re-chains itself behind us instead of force-taking the lock. Without that guard this change would
allow two trainers on one checkpoint dir. The comment at the call site says so explicitly, because
the two changes are separated by ~120 lines and reverting either alone is unsafe.

Residual imperfection, stated rather than hidden: if an unheld successor *does* start mid-slice and
re-chains, it re-chains *held*, resetting its accrual. So the benefit is usually-full-slice, not
always-full-slice. Still strictly better than always-1-second.

**Lesson: safety mechanisms have a throughput price, and it is worth measuring rather than
assuming.** The dependency chain looked free, it is not; it cost the successor its entire queue
priority at every boundary. The right move was to make the *cheap* mechanism (an in-script guard)
strong enough to replace the *expensive* one (a scheduler-level hold).

## Running the single-node arm runner as N separate 1-GPU jobs broke it three ways (2026-08-27)

Polaris blocked experiments for ~1.5 h: the free Polaris nodes carry `queue_tags = prod,debug`, so
the `preemptable` session was tag-starved; `backfill-small` needs **≥10 nodes**; and `debug` has
`max_run = [u:PBS_GENERIC=1]`, which the Polaris *trainer* was holding. Net: **only one 1-node
Polaris job can run at a time**, and the trainer must be it.

Sophia had spare capacity in exactly the shape that fit, `by-gpu` takes 1-GPU jobs and there were
4 free GPUs on partially-used prod nodes (gpu-02: 3, gpu-03: 1). So I ran `exp8gpu_sophia.pbs` as
four separate 1-GPU jobs. All four started with **zero pending**, and then all three of the runner's
single-node assumptions broke at once.

| # | bug | why it only appears with N separate jobs |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **`mv`-based claim is not atomic** | `rename()` is atomic within one node's VFS. Workers on gpu-02 and gpu-03 both "won" `n668` and ran it twice, racing to write the same result JSON. |
| 2 | **startup recovery stole live arms** | Each worker moved *every* `inflight/*.json` back to `pending/`. Correct for one runner recovering after a crash; with workers starting 8 s apart, worker 4 un-claimed workers 1-3's in-progress arms. |
| 3 | **`--master_port=$((29800+g))`** | `g` is the local GPU index. With 8 GPUs on one node g=0..7 gave distinct ports; as N 1-GPU jobs every worker has `g=0`, so the three PBS packed onto gpu-02 all bound 29800 → `EADDRINUSE`. |

Bugs 1+2 drove `n669`-`n672` to the 2-strike cap and into `failed/`. **No computed results were
lost** (the failures were seconds-long startup aborts; `n665`/`n666`/`n667` had already completed and
are the seed-449 numbers already recorded), but 5 arms had to be reset and re-run.

**Fixes:**
- **Claim with `mkdir`**, which is atomic on NFS and Lustre, and record the claiming job id in
  `queue/.owner_<arm>`.
- **Recovery is now conditional**: an inflight arm is only returned to `pending` if its recorded
  owner is *not* in `qstat`. Verified in the logs: a later worker printed
  `arm n668_d20_h400_s449 is claimed by LIVE job 177224 -> leaving it alone`.
- **Port derived from the job id**: `MPORT=$(( 29000 + ${PBS_JOBID%%.*} % 1500 ))`.
- **Dropped the `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=$g` override**: a `by-gpu` allocation already exposes exactly
  one GPU, and forcing `=0` would point at physical GPU 0, possibly another job's.

After the fixes: 5 arms, 5 distinct owners, `pending=0 inflight=5 failed=0`.

**Lesson: a work-queue's claim protocol encodes an assumption about how many address spaces share
it.** This one was written for threads inside one job and silently changed meaning when the same file
became the coordination point for independent jobs on different nodes. The three failures are all
the same mistake: local uniqueness (VFS, port, process list) reused as global uniqueness.

### Follow-on: `by-gpu` grants a GPU *count*, not a GPU *identity* (2026-08-27)

After fixing the claim race and port collision, the co-located workers still died:

```
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 7.69 GiB.
GPU 0 has a total capacity of 39.49 GiB of which 3.79 GiB is free.
Process 1059319 has 16.32 GiB in use. Process 1059321 has 10.65 GiB in use.
```

Three arm processes on **physical GPU 0** of one node. PBS `by-gpu` sets **no
`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`**, so every worker defaulted to device 0, and an arm needs ~92% of a 40 GB
card, so exactly one fits. Workers that landed on *different* nodes (gpu-03, gpu-09) were fine
throughout; this was purely co-location. Note I had *removed* the `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=$g` override
one step earlier on the assumption PBS would isolate the GPU. It does not.

Fix: pick the emptiest GPU from `nvidia-smi` and hold an atomic per-`(node,gpu)` lock on `/eagle`:

```bash
for cand in $(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,memory.used --format=csv,noheader,nounits \
              | sort -t, -k2 -n | cut -d, -f1); do
  if mkdir "$R/queue/.gpu_$(hostname -s)_$cand" 2>/dev/null; then MYGPU=$cand; break; fi
done
[ -z "$MYGPU" ] && { echo "no free GPU could be locked -> exiting"; exit 0; }
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=$MYGPU
```

Working as intended on the next submission: `177229` logged `locked physical GPU 0 on
sophia-gpu-02`, while `177230`/`177231` logged `no free GPU could be locked on sophia-gpu-02 ->
exiting without claiming an arm` instead of over-subscribing.

⚠️ **The lock-release trap must be single-quoted.** My first version was
`trap "... rmdir \"$GPULOCK\" ..." EXIT`, and `$GPULOCK` is assigned ~18 lines *later*, so the
double-quoted trap expanded it to empty at definition time: locks would have leaked until no GPU
was claimable. Deferred expansion is the entire point of a trap referring to later state.

⚠️ **`pbsnodes` "3/8 GPUs free" is a PBS accounting figure, not physical availability.** gpu-02
reported 3 free but `nvidia-smi` showed other users' processes resident, so only ~1 was usable.
Real spare Sophia capacity was ~2 GPUs, not 4: size arm fan-out from `nvidia-smi`, not `pbsnodes`.

## Interconnect: the plugin-mismatch hypothesis is REFUTED, and my benchmark had no floor (2026-08-28)

Round 3, 2 nodes / 8 ranks (owner directive: 2 nodes is enough; scale only on a finding):

| config | GB/s |
|---|---|
| v1.6.0 + memhooks (round-2 winner, as reference) | 1.63 |
| **v1.9.1-aws** | **1.06** |
| v1.9.1-aws + libfabric 1.22.0 | 1.11 |
| v1.6.0 + libfabric 1.22.0 | 1.67 |
| v1.9.1-aws + NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=PHB | 1.08 |
| v1.9.1-aws + GDR + NCCL_CROSS_NIC=1 | 1.04 |

**Hypothesis refuted.** I reasoned that NCCL 2.27.5 advertises plugin APIs `ncclNet_v6..v10`, so the
older v1.6.0 plugin might be falling back to a degraded path, and that a version mismatch would
explain an 8%-of-line-rate result better than any env gap. The newer plugin is **worse**, landing
near socket baseline, and GDR + CROSS_NIC did not rescue it. v1.6.0 remains the best plugin.

### The methodology failure this exposed

**The same v1.6.0+memhooks config measured 1.94 GB/s in round 2 and 1.63 GB/s in round 3: a 19%
swing.** Round 2 reported `memhooks` (1.94) as beating `monitor=disabled` (1.91) and I presented
that as a ranking. That difference is ~1/6 of the run-to-run spread; it was noise.

This campaign has an explicit rule: measure the run-to-run floor before quoting a difference, that
produced several retractions on the model arms. I enforced it there all week and **did not apply it
to my own benchmark**, because the benchmark felt like instrumentation rather than an experiment.
It is an experiment. `nccl_floor.pbs` now runs 6 identical repeats of one config, nothing varied but
run index, and no interconnect difference gets quoted until it clears that spread.

### Also: "8% of fabric line rate" was a loose claim

I compared *effective algorithm bandwidth* (payload ÷ wall time) against *wire line rate*, which are
not the same quantity. A ring all-reduce of S bytes over N ranks moves `2(N-1)/N × S` per rank: 
7.18 GB per rank for S=4.1 GB at N=8, i.e. ~2.9 GB/s per rank at a 2.5 s median, and only 2 of the 8
ring hops actually cross between nodes. The real wire utilisation is materially higher than 8%, so
the headroom is smaller than I implied. The floor job prints this decomposition so the next round
reasons about wire bytes rather than payload bytes.

## Interconnect, round 1.5 (2026-08-28, 2 nodes, REAL training): the OFI plugin is worth 1.45×

The microbenchmark numbers were never the point, this is the first measurement of the plugin
inside an actual `pretrain.py` slice, 8 GPUs / 2 nodes, 66 micro-steps per optimizer step, the
production mixture and batch shape.

| config | tok/s total | tok/s per GPU | vs sockets |
|---|---|---|---|
| default (sockets): round 1 | 34,184 | 4,273 | n/a |
| aws-ofi-nccl v1.6.0 + memhooks + Ring | **49,698** | **6,212** | **1.45×** |
| 1 node / 4 GPUs (reference) | 28,500 | 7,125 | n/a |

**The cross-node per-GPU penalty falls from 40% to 12.8%.** That is the number to carry, not any
ratio from the all-reduce microbenchmark: the benchmark's ranking survived, its *magnitude* did not
(it predicted 2-3.7×, training delivered 1.45×), because in training the collective overlaps
backward compute and only the unhidden tail is exposed.

⛔ `NCCL_ALGO=Tree` alone still crashes, reproduced here on the second real 2-node slice:
`no algorithm/protocol available for function AllGather with datatype ncclInt8`. Production carries
`Tree,Ring`; round 2 arm C is the first real test that the permissive list is safe *and* faster.

### Ordering lesson: put nothing important last in a 1-hour queue

Round 2 (`nccl_train3.pbs`, 4 arms × `--wall_time 660`) needs 4 × (7 min compile + 11 min run) =
**72 minutes inside a 60-minute `debug-scaling` limit**, so its last arm: ZeRO-off, the one the
Tree crash motivated: will not report. I sized the arms from the run time and forgot the fixed
~7 min `torch.compile` cost, four times over. Round 3 uses `--wall_time 400` (4 × 13.7 = 55 min)
and the control arm runs **first**.

ZeRO-off is not retried: `pretrain.py --zero_optimizer`'s own help text records that plain DDP +
fp32 AdamW needs ~38.7 GiB *before activations* on this model, so it OOMs on a 40 GB A100 no matter
how much gradient checkpointing saves. Round 2's arm D was worth 7 minutes; a second copy is not.

## Interconnect, round 3 (queued): the first CODE-side lever: DDP bucket size

Every round so far swept NCCL environment variables. `pretrain.py:1220` constructs
`DDP(..., gradient_as_bucket_view=True)` with **no `bucket_cap_mb`**, i.e. PyTorch's 25 MB default.
At 2.06B params, bf16 gradients are ~4.1 GB per optimizer step, so 25 MB buckets mean **~165
separate AllReduce launches per step**. Cross-node each launch pays fabric latency plus a kernel
launch, and the payload per launch is small enough that Ring never reaches steady-state bandwidth.
On one node NVLink makes the launch count nearly free, which is exactly why this was invisible
until the 2-node tests.

Added `--ddp_bucket_mb` (default 25 = prior behaviour, so the live trainer is unaffected) and
`nccl_train4.pbs`, holding round-2 arm B's env fixed (OFI + Ring + 32 MB NCCL buffers):

| arm | bucket | note |
|---|---|---|
| A | 25 | matched control **at this horizon**: never import a control across a horizon |
| B | 100 | |
| C | 400 | ~11 launches/step instead of ~165 |
| D | 100 + `NCCL_CROSS_NIC=1` | 4 NICs and 4 GPUs per node; lets a ring send and receive on different NICs instead of being pinned to GPU: NIC affinity |

Blocked on the Polaris **per-user limit of 3 jobs in queue `generic`** (`qsub: would exceed queue
generic's per-user limit` with the experiment session, its held successor, and round 2 in flight): 
chained with `-W depend=afterany` as soon as a slot frees.

## Round 2 result: NCCL_BUFFSIZE=32 MB is a NULL in real training, and the harness lied

| arm (all: OFI v1.6.0 + memhooks, 2 nodes / 8 GPUs) | trainer's own tok/s | new steps done |
|---|---|---|
| A Ring, default buffers | 49,794 | 38 |
| B Ring + `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=32 MB` | 49,183 | 37 |

**−1.2%. A null.** The all-reduce microbenchmark had 32 MB buffers at 8.62 GB/s against Ring's
1.92: a 4.5× that does not exist in training at all.

**Why, and this reframes the whole line:** with 66 micro-steps per optimizer step, DDP's all-reduce
is already fully hidden behind backward compute. Making an already-hidden collective faster buys
nothing. So **bandwidth is not the constraint**, which means the remaining 12.8% cross-node
per-GPU penalty is *not* bandwidth-bound either, and `NCCL_CROSS_NIC` / `NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL` (both
bandwidth levers) are likely nulls too. Launch count, straggler sync, and the unhidden tail at the
step boundary are what is left. The round-3 bucket ladder tests exactly the launch-count term, so it
is the right next arm rather than one more env var.

### The harness confound: a 1.42× that was pure bookkeeping

`pretrain.py` writes a checkpoint when `--wall_time` expires, and all arms shared one
`ckpt_nccltest`, so **each arm resumed from the previous arm's checkpoint**. Arm A ran 0→88, arm B
ran 88→125. Two ways that read as a win when it is not:

- **step count**: "125 vs 88" looks like 1.42×; both arms actually did ~37 new steps.
- **`SUMMARY: tokens_per_sec`**: reads 84,961 (A) and 122,124 (B) against true rates of ~49,800 and
  ~49,200, because it divides by this run's loop time while counting the tokens the loader had
  already consumed at its resumed cursor. **1.71× and 2.48× too high.** I had written "the SUMMARY
  line is authoritative for tok/s" into that script myself.

Both probe scripts now take a **fresh per-arm checkpoint dir** and delete it after parsing, and both
read the trainer's own per-step `tok/s:` line, never `SUMMARY`. It also stopped leaving a 24.7 GB
file on /eagle per session.

⚠️ The sockets-vs-OFI 1.45× is unaffected: round 1.5 arm A shows no `resumed` line, so it started at
step 0, and both numbers came from the per-step `tok/s:` field.

## Experiment-session efficiency: two defects found by reading the session log

- **`ARM_SECS` was 1200 where the measured cost is 2175 s** for a 400-step base arm, its own
  adjacent comment already said "~2130 s measured". A worker with 1,300 s left would start an arm,
  be killed by the wall at ~60%, and the reaper would return it to pending to restart from zero.
  Now 2200 in all four launchers; verified it still admits the longest legal arm (500-step KD =
  3,437 s against a 3,450 s session).
- **~46 GPU-minutes idle per session, structurally.** Three of four GPUs finished with ~930 s left
  and exited because the cheapest pending arm was 400 steps. Queued a 120-step cell (n723: n725,
  seed 458) sized to that window, which also adds a third point *below* the KD horizon-decay curve
  (−0.912 at h400, −0.637 at h500), two points give a ratio, not a shape.

## α ladder (n705: n709, seed 455, h400): pure KD wins, monotone, no interior optimum

| kd_alpha | tgt | Δ vs α=0 |
|---|---|---|
| 0.00 | 4.9245 | n/a |
| 0.25 | 4.5794 | −0.3451 |
| 0.50 | 4.3459 | −0.5786 |
| 0.75 | 4.1554 | −0.7691 |
| 1.00 | (n709 in flight) | −0.912 at seed 454 |

Monotone in α with no interior optimum, so **mixing CE back in only dilutes the KD signal**: the
production setting stays α=1.0. Throughput is flat across α (4,309-4,324 tok/s) and HBM is flat at
0.9188, so the 1.24× KD tax is paid by having a teacher at all, not by how much its loss is weighted.

## Why many-node scaling fails here, and what actually unlocks it

### First: the 15%-efficiency-at-48-GPUs number is INVALID

`a45_polaris_slice277_step82821_20260827-2124.out`, World size 48, got 54,198 tok/s = 1,129 per GPU
, and **its log contains zero `aws-ofi-nccl` mentions**, i.e. it ran on the management ethernet at
1.03 GB/s. The many-node scaling curve has never been measured with a working fabric. All twelve
`polaris_*.pbs` now carry the OFI block, so the point is re-measurable and must be re-measured
before any conclusion is drawn from it.

### The arithmetic, which does not involve the interconnect at all

Per optimizer step, per rank, a ring all-reduce of the gradient moves `2(N-1)/N × 2P` bytes, for
P = 2.06B in bf16 that is **~8 GB regardless of N** (7.21 GB at N=8, 8.07 GB at N=48). Per-GPU
compute for that same step is `6P × B/N` FLOPs, where B is the global batch in tokens. So

```
comms bytes per FLOP  =  4P / (6P·B/N)  =  (2/3)·(N/B)
```

**P cancels.** Model size does not help. The only term that matters is **tokens per step per GPU**,
and with B fixed it degrades linearly in N:

| GPUs | seq/GPU/step | measured tok/s per GPU |
|---|---|---|
| 4 (1 node) | 132 | 7,125 |
| 8 (1 node, Sophia) | 66 | 7,066 |
| 8 (2 nodes, OFI) | 66 | 6,212 |
| 48 (12 nodes, **sockets**) | 11 | 1,129 (invalid transport) |

At 2 nodes we are at **87% scaling efficiency**, that is not far from ideal, and no NCCL tuning will
add much, as round 2's BUFFSIZE null already showed. The failure is specific to *many* nodes, and its
cause is that **B = 540,672 tokens is small**. At 48 GPUs each GPU does 11 forward/backward passes to
justify 8 GB of traffic.

### What frontier labs actually do differently

Their B is 4-16 M tokens per step (GPT-3 3.2 M, Llama-3 ~16 M) against our 0.54 M. That 8-30× is the
same factor as the node-count gap, and it is not a coincidence, it is the whole mechanism. Holding
66 seq/GPU requires:

| target GPUs | required B |
|---|---|
| 16 | 1.08 M tokens |
| 48 | 3.24 M tokens |
| 96 | 6.49 M tokens |

### Ranked levers, cheapest first

1. **Re-measure 2 / 3 / 6 nodes with OFI and find the knee.** The only existing many-node point is a
   sockets artifact. Report tok/s per GPU beside total. Cheap, and it bounds everything below.
2. **Raise B for the next model and scale LR with it.** This is the actual unlock, and it CANNOT be
   done mid-run: raising batch shifts the WSD cooldown (`cooldown_frac × estimated_steps`), so a4.5
   keeps B = 540,672 and this becomes an a5 design decision. Ceiling is the critical batch size: 
   for a 2B model somewhere around 1-4 M tokens, beyond which extra batch buys no convergence, only
   wasted FLOPs. So even done perfectly this caps the efficient shape near ~30 GPUs, not thousands.
3. **Longer sequences (2048, then 4096).** Raises tokens per step at a fixed sequence count, so it
   improves the ratio without touching B's convergence properties, and it fixes the separate fact
   that a block-1024-trained base is blind past 1024. Blocked on HBM: the probe already reads 96.3%
   (40.9/42.4 GB) at block 1024, so this needs `checkpoint_stride 1` or a micro-batch change, and
   that recompute difference is a confound to control for, not ignore.
4. **FSDP instead of DDP + ZeRO-1.** Replaces the full-gradient AllReduce with
   ReduceScatter + AllGather: same bytes, but overlappable against forward as well as backward, and
   lower peak memory, which buys back micro-batch. It would also remove the AllGather that makes
   `NCCL_ALGO=Tree` illegal.
5. ⛔ **Do NOT add tensor or pipeline parallelism.** At 2.06B the model fits on one 40 GB card, so TP
   inside a node and PP across nodes would only add collectives to a job that is already
   comms-limited. TP becomes correct above roughly 20B params or at very long sequence length. This
   is the lever it is most tempting to copy from lab papers and the most clearly wrong one here.

### Round 2 complete: a triple null, and ZeRO-off confirmed dead by measurement

| arm | trainer's own tok/s | new steps | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| A Ring, default buffers | 49,794 | 38 (50→88) | reference |
| B Ring + `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=32MB` | 49,183 | 37 (88→125) | null |
| C `Tree,Ring` + 32MB | 49,158 | 38 (125→163) | null |
| D `Tree,Ring` + 32MB + ZeRO off | n/a | n/a | **OOM**, 38.03 GiB allocated of 39.49 |

A 1.3% spread across A/B/C. The microbenchmark gave Tree 2.31× and 32 MB buffers 4.5×; in training
both are worth nothing, because at 66 micro-steps the all-reduce is already fully hidden behind
backward compute. Arm D reached the queue after all (the 72-minute arm list fit because arms exit on
`--wall_time`, not on step count) and OOMed exactly as the `--zero_optimizer` help text predicts.

**Both nulls were REMOVED from all nine `polaris_*.pbs`, because neither was free:**

- `NCCL_ALGO=Tree,Ring` → **`NCCL_ALGO=Ring`**. Tree in the list is a latent crash: `Tree` alone
  killed a real slice on the AllGather that ZeRO-1 issues. Pinning Ring keeps the one algorithm with
  a kernel for every collective we use: strictly safer, measurably no slower.
- `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=33554432` → **removed** (back to NCCL's default). It is allocated per channel per
  direction, and these cards already read 96.3% HBM under the real footprint. Paying HBM for a
  measured null is how a slice dies overnight.

The aws-ofi-nccl plugin block stays, it remains the only measured win (1.45×).

Also deleted the 24.7 GB `ckpt_nccltest/checkpoint_step_163.pt` left by the shared-dir confound
(audited first: no running job writing it, its only symlink was its own `checkpoint_last.pt`, no
script or result references it, and a throughput probe's byproduct is not a result). The dir is now
8 KB and round 3 writes per-arm dirs it removes itself.

## Two self-inflicted measurement failures, same tick

### 1. A free node is not an available node: the phantom Sophia upgrade

`best_shape.sh` reported `UPGRADE AVAILABLE: 1 -> 2 nodes` on Sophia for most of the afternoon, and
a 2-node probe submitted against it (`177396`) sat at `Not Running: No available resources on nodes`.
Both "free" nodes read `state = free`, `njobs = 0`, `ngpus = 8`, and both carry
`resources_available.queue_tags = infer-svc-test`, fencing them to another queue.

Acting on that flag would have killed a healthy primary trainer to chase capacity that does not
exist for us. The tool now counts a node only if it is free **and** idle **and** carries no
`queue_tags`, and prints the raw count beside the usable one so the gap is visible:

```
free+untagged: 0   (raw free incl. tag-fenced: 2)
no upgrade available (current shape is the best startable)
```

So the trainer *is* on the best available shape, and has been. Note the failure mode: this is the
second time this script produced confident, plausible, wrong output: first by running on the wrong
host, now by trusting `state = free`. A tool consulted every tick needs its own scepticism.

### 2. The fresh-dir fix and the wall budget interact: arm A did ONE step

Round 3's first arm spent **285 s reaching step 1**, then `--wall_time 400` expired: one step, no
rate, arm wasted. Round 2 appeared to have headroom at `--wall_time 660` only because its arms
*resumed* (the confound being fixed) and hit a warm inductor cache. Fixing the confound therefore
made every arm pay startup, and the two changes had to be made together, not one at a time.

Now `--wall_time 750` and **three** arms, not four: 3 × (285 compile + 750 run) = 3,105 s = 52 min
inside the 60 min `debug-scaling` wall. Killed and resubmitted (`7570723` → `7570744`) rather than
let 46 minutes produce four unusable arms.

**The dropped arm was `NCCL_CROSS_NIC`, and dropping it is a prediction, not a concession.** Round 2
showed `NCCL_BUFFSIZE`: a pure bandwidth lever, is a null in training because the all-reduce is
already hidden behind backward compute. `CROSS_NIC` is also a bandwidth lever, so the same argument
predicts it null. The slot goes to the bucket ladder, which tests launch count: the term round 2 did
*not* rule out.

---

## The objective function for every shape decision (settled 2026-08-28)

**Total tok/s is the goal. Per-GPU efficiency is the exchange rate at which allocation buys it.**
Both get reported, always, because one is the target and the other is the price.

With N nodes, G GPUs per node, single-node per-GPU rate r, scaling efficiency e, and T tokens left:

```
total rate  = N·G·r·e
time        = T / (N·G·r·e)
node-hours  = N · time = T / (G·r·e)
```

**Node-hours depend only on e: the node count cancels.** Adding nodes is therefore never "free but
slower"; it is exactly as expensive as it is inefficient.

At the current state (61.9 B tokens left = 114,450 steps, 2,087.3 node-hours on Sophia):

| shape | e | total tok/s | finish | node-hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 node / 8 GPU (current) | 1.00 | 56,531 | 12.7 d | 304 |
| 2 nodes / 16 GPU | 0.87 | ~98,000 | 7.3 d | 349 |
| 12 nodes / 48 GPU | 0.15 | ~85,000 | 8.4 d | **2,027** |

The 12-node row is the whole reason per-GPU must appear beside total: it is **slower than 2 nodes and
costs 6.7× the allocation**, consuming essentially the entire remaining balance. The efficiency floor
at which the run can no longer be paid for at all is **e ≈ 0.146**.

**Operating rule:** take more nodes when **e ≥ 0.8**; deliberate between 0.5 and 0.8; refuse below
0.5. And prefer levers that raise e at fixed node count: the DDP bucket ladder, sequence length,
FSDP, because those are free on both axes.

# Interconnect campaign plan: breadth across LAYERS (owner directive 2026-08-28)

"Try as many things as you can think about." Rounds 1-3 swept four knobs from *one* layer
(`NCCL_ALGO`, `NCCL_BUFFSIZE`, `NCCL_PROTO=Simple`, plugin version). The single banked win: the OFI
plugin, 1.45×: came from a **category nobody had checked**, not from tuning a knob already under
test. So the campaign now sweeps across layers, one arm each, before going deep in any of them.

**Arms are cheaper than I was pricing them.** Startup is ~285 s cold but ~120 s once
`TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` is warm, and the tok/s reading is stable by step 20-25 (49,755 at step 20
vs 49,698 at step 50). At `--wall_time 300` that is ~7 min per arm ⇒ **8 arms in a 1 h wall**, not 3.

## Layer 0: measure the ceiling first

⭐ **Instrument the comms-blocked milliseconds per step directly** (torch profiler, or NCCL event
timing around the backward pass). Every round so far *inferred* the unhidden tail, which is exactly
why a 4.5× microbenchmark gain measured 0% in training. Without this number we do not know whether
the remaining 12.8% cross-node penalty has 12% of headroom or 0.5%, and we are sweeping blind.
This is the highest-value single item in the whole plan.

## Layer 1: transport (NCCL)

| lever | status |
|---|---|
| `aws-ofi-nccl` plugin | ✅ **1.45×, banked** |
| `NCCL_PROTO=LL128` | ⬜ **untested: often the largest win on modern fabrics for mid-size messages** |
| `NCCL_PROTO=LL` | ⬜ untested |
| `NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS` / `MIN_NCHANNELS` | ⬜ untested: channel count is what parallelises across the 4 NICs per node; only `NTHREADS` was tried |
| `NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL` (GPUDirect RDMA) | ⬜ untested: lets the NIC read GPU memory directly, skipping a host bounce |
| `NCCL_CROSS_NIC` | ⬜ untested |
| `FI_CXI_RDZV_PROTO`, `FI_CXI_OFLOW_BUF_SIZE`, rendezvous threshold | ⬜ untested |
| `NCCL_ALGO=Tree` | ⛔ crashes (no AllGather kernel) |
| `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` | ⛔ null in training |
| plugin v1.9.1-aws, `NCCL_NET=IB`, `SOCKET_IFNAME=hsn`, `NTHREADS` | ⛔ refuted |

## Layer 2: framework / communication strategy

| lever | status |
|---|---|
| DDP `bucket_cap_mb` 25→100→400 | 🔵 measuring now (round 3) |
| DDP `static_graph=True` | ⬜ untested: lets DDP fuse and reorder, drops per-iteration hook bookkeeping |
| DDP comm hook, **fp16 compression** | ⬜ untested: **halves the bytes on the wire.** bf16 compression is a no-op since grads are already bf16 |
| DDP comm hook, PowerSGD | ⬜ untested, lossy: only if fp16 shows the bytes matter |
| FSDP / ZeRO-2 / ZeRO-3 vs DDP+ZeRO-1 | ⬜ untested: ReduceScatter+AllGather is the same bytes but overlaps forward too, and frees memory for a bigger micro-batch |
| `no_sync()` on non-final micro-steps | ✅ already done (`pretrain.py:1465`) |
| ZeRO-1 off | ⛔ OOM |

## Layer 3: fewer bytes on the wire

Local SGD / periodic averaging (all-reduce every K steps), top-k or error-feedback gradient
compression, fp8 gradients. All change the optimization, so each needs a quality arm beside the
throughput arm, not throughput-only.

## Layer 4: more compute per byte

Bigger global batch B (**the fundamental fix**, next-model only: raising it mid-run shifts the WSD
cooldown); longer sequence (2048/4096, blocked on HBM at 96.3%); bigger micro-batch.
⚠️ Note the inversion: **gradient checkpointing and slower kernels IMPROVE the comms ratio** by
giving the transfer more compute to hide behind, while hurting absolute speed. So
`torch.compile mode=max-autotune` could raise single-node throughput and *worsen* scaling. Any
compute-side change has to be measured at both 1 node and 2 nodes or it will mislead.

## Layer 5: physical placement

⭐ **Slingshot is a dragonfly: nodes in the same group are a couple of hops apart, nodes in different
groups are far more.** PBS hands out whatever is free, so our 12 nodes may be scattered across
groups. Untested and potentially large: `place=scatter` vs `pack`, checking which groups the
allocated nodes fall in, and mapping ranks so the ring's cross-node hops stay inside a group.
Also NUMA/NIC affinity: currently `--cpu-bind depth -d 8`; if a rank's CPU is on the wrong socket
from its NIC, every byte crosses the socket interconnect first.

## Queue plan

1. `7570787` (held): node ladder 48/24/8 GPU with OFI. Decides the shape question.
2. Layer-0 profiling arm: gives every later arm a denominator.
3. 8-arm transport+framework sweep: control · LL128 · LL · channels · GDR · CROSS_NIC ·
   `static_graph` · fp16 hook.
4. Placement/topology job, informed by which dragonfly groups the ladder actually landed in.

# Tying the next-model campaign to the interconnect line (owner directive 2026-08-28)

## The structural blindness this fixes

**All ~320 arms so far ran on ONE GPU, where communication does not exist.** So the campaign has
been choosing a5's shape with no visibility into whether that shape scales. Of the four factors that
set multi-node throughput: bytes, compute-per-byte, byte speed, distance, a 1-GPU arm sees only
the byte *count*, and only indirectly. Every scaling consequence of an architecture decision has
been invisible to the experiment that made the decision.

## The fix costs no extra allocation

The 2-node interconnect job already runs real `pretrain.py` training with the production mixture and
batch shape. **Vary an a5 architecture knob in it and record CE alongside tok/s.** Same nodes, same
wall, two research questions. The 1-GPU session keeps doing what it is good at: cheap quality
ordering, and the 2-node job prices the scaling half of the same knob.

## Joint arms, in priority order

| knob | quality question | interconnect prediction |
|---|---|---|
| `tie_word_embeddings` T→F | does untying help CE? | **+388.3M params of pure comms, +0% FLOPs.** vocab 151,680 × hidden 2560; the lm_head matmul happens either way, tying only reuses the matrix. 2.06B → 2.45B = **+18.8% gradient bytes for zero extra compute**: a pure ratio degradation |
| `num_hidden_layers` 24 vs 32, param-matched | depth vs width at fixed params | deep → gradients arrive in many small pieces spread over a longer backward → more overlap window. Shallow-wide → fewer, larger, later lumps |
| `block_size` 1024 → 2048 | long-context ability (a block-1024 base is blind past 1024) | 2× compute per byte at fixed sequence count. Blocked on HBM (96.3% at 1024) |
| `micro_batch` / `grad_accum` | ~quality-neutral | sets the overlap window directly: the term that collapses at high node count |

## Queued now: n726, n728, seed 459, h400, KD OFF

`tie_word_embeddings` first because it is one boolean with an exactly computable byte cost and a
genuinely open quality answer. **KD is off deliberately**: KD's signal arrives through the
vocabulary, i.e. through the very matrix under test, so running it with KD on would confound
embedding structure with distillation. That interaction is the follow-up.

**Decision rule that saves nodes:** if untying improves `tgt` by less than the n728 floor, the knob
is refuted at 1 GPU and no 2-node arm is needed at all. The cheap experiment gates the expensive one.

⚠️ The untied arm may OOM (+18.8% params on a card already at `hbm_frac` 0.8907). That is an answer
too, it would mean untying is unaffordable on 40 GB regardless of CE, and it costs one arm rather
than a production slice.

### Round 3: DDP bucket size is a null too: and that exposed a confound in my own headline number

| arm (2 nodes / 8 GPUs, OFI + Ring) | tok/s | per GPU |
|---|---|---|
| bucket 25 (control) | **no rate**: died to a collective timeout | n/a |
| bucket 100 | 49,026 | 6,128 |
| bucket 400 | running | |
| reference (round 1.5/2, bucket 25) | 49,698 | 6,212 |

Bucket 100 is **−1.4%**: going from ~165 AllReduce launches per step to ~41 changes nothing.

Three nulls on the same layer now: bandwidth (`BUFFSIZE`), algorithm (`Tree,Ring`), launch count
(bucket size), and together they say more than any one of them: **at 2 nodes with 66 micro-steps the
all-reduce is so completely hidden behind backward compute that neither its speed nor its launch
count is observable.** There is no interconnect headroom left at this shape.

### ⚠️ The 12.8% cross-node penalty is CONFOUNDED and I have been quoting it as if it were not

| | GPUs | nodes | **micro-steps** | tok/s per GPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference | 4 | 1 | **132** | 7,125 |
| 2-node measurement | 8 | 2 | **66** | 6,212 |

Those rows differ in **two** ways. I attributed the whole gap to crossing nodes, but halving the
micro-step count halves the accumulation window available to hide the collective: a throughput cost
with no network involvement at all. The same confound inflates the "40% on sockets" figure.
⚠️ The **1.45× plugin gain is unaffected**, both of its sides are 2-node runs at 66 micro-steps.

**`microstep_control.pbs` is the control, and it needs 1 node** (so it contains no cross-node
communication whatsoever). It varies only the micro-step count, by shrinking the global batch:

| arm | total_batch_size | seqs / 4 GPUs | micro-steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| B (**runs first**, it answers the question) | 270,336 | 264 | 66 |
| A (matched to the 7,125 reference) | 540,672 | 528 | 132 |
| C | 135,168 | 132 | 33 |

**Pre-registered read:** if B lands near 6,200 per GPU, crossing nodes costs ~nothing and the entire
penalty is the batch split, which redirects this line away from the network and toward batch shape.
If B stays near 7,125, the penalty is genuinely the network and 12.8% stands. Anything in between
splits it, which is the quantity I have been claiming to know and do not.

Report **per-GPU only**: total tok/s is not comparable across different global batch sizes.

### Round 3 complete: bucket size is not a null at the top end: it is a 10× REGRESSION

| arm (2 nodes / 8 GPUs, OFI + Ring) | s/step (compile excluded) | tok/s | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| bucket 25 (PyTorch default) | ~10.9 | 49,698 | reference |
| bucket 100 | ~11.0 | 49,026 | null, −1.4% |
| **bucket 400** | **~113** | **~4,800** | ⛔ **−90%** |

Arm C reached **step 3 in 625 s** while arm B reached step 40 in 630 s. The mechanism is visible in
its own HBM trace: **88.4% at step 2, 92.1% at step 3, climbing every step**. With
`gradient_as_bucket_view=True` the gradients live inside the buckets, so a 400 MB bucket cap demands
~11 contiguous 400 MB regions on a card already at ~90% occupancy. The allocator churns instead of
reusing, and throughput collapses.

**So the launch-count hypothesis is not merely refuted, it inverts.** Going from ~165 launches per
step to ~41 (bucket 100) bought nothing, and pushing to ~11 launches (bucket 400) cost 90%.
PyTorch's 25 MB default is already the right value for this model on 40 GB cards: there is nothing
to gain above it and a great deal to lose. `--ddp_bucket_mb` stays in `pretrain.py` with default 25,
now with a measured reason rather than an untested assumption.

### Two harness failures in the same job, worth separating from the physics

- **Arm A: collective timeout, 0 steps.** Started 14:06 UTC, 31 min before the
  `init_process_group(timeout=30 min)` patch landed at 14:37. This is the compile-skew hang, and the
  patch is now live: verified present in `pretrain.py` before the 12-node ladder starts.
- **Arm C produced no `tok/s` line** not because it crashed but because at 208 s/step it never
  reached `log_interval 10`. The parser reported "no rate" for what was actually the most extreme
  result in the round. ⚠️ **A missing number is not a missing effect**: read the progress bar's
  `s/step` before concluding an arm failed. Both probe scripts now print the reached step and pace
  even when no `Step` line exists.

Net: round 3 cost 1 h × 2 nodes and returned one null, one 10× regression, and one confirmed
harness fix. Two of three arms initially read as "failed".

---

## Transport layer, closed out: NCCL defaults are optimal here; the win is SENDING LESS

All measured at 2 nodes / 8 GPUs with the batch shrunk to **90,112 tokens = 11 micro-steps**, which
reproduces the 48-GPU comms regime on two nodes. That trick is the reason these are 2-node results:
micro-step count is `batch ÷ ranks` and **both terms are ours to choose**, so exposing the collective
does not require buying 12 nodes. Comparisons are against the in-job control only, at 1/6 the
production batch, total tok/s here is not comparable to any production figure.

| arm | tok/s | per GPU | vs control |
|---|---|---|---|
| control (OFI + Ring + Simple, bucket 25) | 31,485-31,513 | 3,936-3,939 | n/a |
| `NCCL_PROTO=LL128` | 26,627 | 3,328 | **−15.5%** |
| `NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS=16` | 31,342 | 3,918 | −0.5% (null) |
| `NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=PHB` | n/a | n/a | ⛔ **fails**: repeated `cxil_map: write error` |
| **`--ddp_comm_hook bf16`** | **36,050** | **4,506** | ⭐ **+14.5%** |

The control reproduced across two separate jobs to **0.09%** (31,513 → 31,485), which is what makes a
14.5% effect readable at all.

### What the pattern means

**Every NCCL knob is now measured and is null or worse**: `ALGO`, `PROTO`, `BUFFSIZE`, `NTHREADS`,
`MAX_NCHANNELS`, plugin version, DDP bucket size, and now GDR. The only thing that ever helped was
making NCCL use the right *network* (the OFI plugin: 1.45× at 8 GPUs, 2.62× at 48). So NCCL's defaults
are already at the achievable optimum on this fabric, and further env-var sweeping is not the frontier.

**LL128 losing 15.5% is informative, not just negative.** LL/LL128 trade bandwidth for latency, so a
loss that size says the regime is **bandwidth-bound**. That single fact retro-explains three earlier
nulls at once: DDP bucket size did nothing because launch *latency* is not the constraint, bucket 400
collapsed on memory rather than comms, and `Tree` gained nothing despite fewer hops.
⚠️ But `MAX_NCHANNELS` was also null, which a naively bandwidth-starved link would not predict, so
the honest statement is "bandwidth-bound at the payload level, not channel-starved."

### The comms fraction, measured rather than inferred

bf16 compression halves the wire bytes and returned +14.5%, not +100%. Solving
`1/(1 − c/2) = 1.145` gives **c ≈ 25%: comms is about a quarter of step time at 11 micro-steps**, and
halving the payload recovered half of that. Every prior estimate in this campaign inferred the
unhidden tail; this is the first number.

⛔ **Not adoptable on throughput alone.** `bf16_compress_hook` moves cross-rank gradient *summation*
into bf16: a numerical change, not a transport change. Every other lever here was quality-neutral by
construction and could be judged on wall clock; this one cannot. `--ddp_comm_hook {none,bf16}` is now
in both `pretrain.py` and `probe.py` (guarded on `world > 1`, since the four independent 1-GPU session
arms would make it a silent no-op), and `ce_hook.pbs` runs the CE arm at 1 node / 4 ranks.

⚠️ **The first CE run was void and the cause is worth recording:** it inherited
`--warmup_steps 8000` from the production command, so at the ~25 steps a 900 s wall allows the LR was
~1.9e-6, the weights had barely left init, and both arms reported `loss=11.6051`: identical to four
decimals. Two nearly-untrained models cannot diverge numerically whatever precision sums their
gradients. **Any `pretrain.py`-derived probe must override the production warmup or it measures
initialisation.** The probe configs use `warmup 11` for exactly this reason.

---

## ⚠️ STARTUP COST SCALES WITH RANK COUNT, and every shape number above ignores it

Measured 2026-08-29 on the 24-GPU gap-filler (`7572100`, 6 nodes): **>20 minutes from job start to the
first training step**, with `World size: 24` appearing only after ~20 min and zero errors. The phases
are distributed init across 24 ranks, then **24 ranks each loading the same 24.7 GB checkpoint off
shared `/eagle`**, then `torch.compile`.

**Every startup figure used in this campaign came from PROBE jobs that start FRESH with no
checkpoint**, that is where the "~285 s compile" constant comes from. A production resume is a
different animal: the checkpoint read is ~6× the I/O at 24 ranks that it is at 4, on a filesystem
shared with the whole facility.

### What this invalidates

The shape comparisons in this document priced **steady-state throughput only**:

| shape | steady-state tok/s | startup | usable fraction of a 1 h wall |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sophia 1 node / 8 GPU, 24 h wall | 56,531 | ~10 min | 99% (amortised over 24 h) |
| Polaris 6 nodes / 24 GPU, 1 h wall | 109,486 | **>20 min** | **~65% at best** |
| Polaris 12 nodes / 48 GPU, 1 h wall | 139,557 | unmeasured, presumably worse | worse |

So "6 nodes is 1.94× Sophia" is true per second of *training* and false per second of *wall*. The
correct comparison is `steady-state x (wall - startup) / wall`, and at a 1 h wall a 20-min startup
costs a third of the job. **The fix is a longer wall, not a bigger shape**: `polaris_pre4.pbs` has a
2 h wall and `small` allows 3 h at >=10 nodes; both amortise the same startup over 2-3x the training.

### Second-order consequence for the outage

This also explains why the gap-filler looked repeatedly "hung". Slices 283-285 died on a bad node
within ~5 min, which was FAST relative to a healthy startup, so a silent 20-minute healthy startup
and a dead job look identical for the first 20 minutes. There is no progress print between
`pre-flight OK` and the first `Step` line, which is a 20-minute observability hole in exactly the
window where things go wrong. ⚠️ Raising `init_process_group`'s timeout from 600 s to 30 min (done
earlier the same day, to survive compile skew) widened that hole rather than closing it: the right
instrument is a phase print after init, after checkpoint load, and after compile.

## 2026-08-29 06:06 CDT: `preemptable` is a dead queue; queue TAGS, not quotas, decide what starts

A 4 h trainer gap (02:05 → 06:06) traced to a wrong inference about queue quotas, recorded here so it
is not repeated.

- `debug-scaling` has `max_queued = [u:PBS_GENERIC=1]` **and it counts the RUNNING job**, so a

⚠️ Quoting B against the standing 49,698 figure would repeat the cross-session comparison error that has
cost this line twice. It is reported here only as "indistinguishable", not as a delta.

### What the (weak) result plus the existing mechanism implies

The bucket hypothesis was that 4.1 GB of gradients in 25 MB buckets = ~165 AllReduce launches/step, and
that launch overhead was costing throughput. But the established mechanism cuts the other way: **in
training the collective overlaps backward compute and only the unhidden tail is exposed** (this is why
the microbenchmark's 2-3.7× became 1.45× in training). Bucket size therefore trades launch overhead
against *overlap granularity*: fewer, larger transfers pipeline WORSE with backward. Those two effects
oppose, which is consistent with 100 MB landing on top of 25 MB.

⇒ **The remaining 12.8% cross-node per-GPU penalty is probably not launch overhead, and no NCCL knob
will find it.** Trying more transport flags is the wrong move; the penalty needs to be *decomposed*
before it can be attacked.

`nccl_nocomm.pbs`: 2 nodes / 8 GPUs, two arms in one job, both at production shape and mixture.
- **arm 1: control:** production config, `ddp_bucket_mb 25`.
- **arm 2: comms ceiling:** identical, but gradient sync disabled on every micro-step
  (`model.require_backward_grad_sync = False`). Numerically wrong on purpose; the point is that
  **control-vs-ceiling IS the total exposed comms cost**, measured rather than inferred.

If the gap is ≈12.8%, the penalty is entirely exposed collective time and the next question is which
part of the tail. If it is much smaller, the penalty is **not NCCL at all**: candidates then are data
loading off shared /eagle, checkpoint I/O, and straggler ranks, none of which any transport flag touches.
