## 2026-08-29 12:35 CDT: VALIDATED: a shorter WALL buys backfill during a drain; more nodes does not

The single most effective lever on pending time found so far, and it costs *less* allocation, not more.

**Observation.** 12:02 the trainer slice ended. 12:05 `ensure_trainer.sh` submitted 6 nodes / **1 h wall**
→ sat `Q` for ~20 min with `comment = Not Running: Job is requesting an exclusive node and node is in
use`, while `debug-scaling` reported `Running:0, Queued:2` and **71 prod nodes were free and job-free.**
Cause: four queued **192-node `large` jobs** were draining the machine (472 nodes job-exclusive), so PBS
was holding the free nodes for their start time. A 1 h exclusive request does not fit the remaining
backfill window.

**Action and result.** Resubmitted the *same 6-node shape* with `-l walltime=00:30:00 -v TRAIN_WALL=1500`.
It **started**, and free+job-free prod nodes fell 71 → 5 as the drain closed around it. Total trainer idle
33 min (12:02 → 12:35).

⇒ **When a job is pending behind a drain, shorten the WALL. Do not add nodes, and do not conclude the
cluster is full**: 71 nodes were free the entire time the 1 h job was refused.

**Duty-cycle trade, so the default is a judgement not a free win:**

| wall | training per slice | in-slice duty | starts during a drain? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 60 min (`TRAIN_WALL=3300`) | 53 min | 88% | **no** (measured) |
| 30 min (`TRAIN_WALL=1500`) | 25 min | 83% | **yes** (measured) |

5 points of duty is a cheap price for the difference between running and not. With the 15-min cron tick as
the chaining mechanism, expected gap is ~7.5 min either way, so end-to-end throughput favours 30 min
whenever the machine is busy.

**Implemented in `ensure_trainer.sh`** (`polaris_ds6.pbs` now reads `TRAIN_WALL` from the environment so
`-l walltime` and the in-script checkpoint deadline move together):
- trainer `Q` for ≥20 min ⇒ step the shape down **6 → 4 → 3 → 2 nodes** (24/16/12/8 GPU: the only rungs
  that divide 528) at a 30 min wall;
- below 20 min, hold deliberately, because job churn has cost more than waiting on three prior occasions;
- fresh submits pick the largest rung the *free and job-free* prod count supports.

⚠️ **Second node-counting bug fixed here.** `state = free` is not sufficient for an exclusive
`place=scatter` request: a node can be `free` while still hosting jobs. The count must require
`state=free` **AND** `jobs =` empty. (The first such bug was filtering on `queue_tags == ""`, which
reported 0 free nodes when 23 were available.) Both filters are now in the script with the reason inline.

| **fp8 A/B REMOVED** (fp8 0 in every cell) | pretrain.py's own warning: *"--fp8 without --torch_compile, FP8 scaling won't fuse; expect NO speedup"*, and compile 0 is mandatory here. Provably inert, so 2 of 3 arms would have been wasted. |
| **3-cell HBM ladder replaces it** | cell 1 `grad_ckpt 0`; cell 2 `batch_size 2`; cell 3 both, run *only* if both single-variable cells survive, so a combined win stays attributable |
| **no control arm** | 598526 *is* the control: 4+ h on the same node and shape: 20.59 s/step, peak 46.5/85.0 GB. A 4-hour matched observation beats a 15-minute rerun. |
| `--checkpoint_interval 900 → 3600` | 900 is **seconds**, not steps: saves landed at 95539/95627/95671/95715, i.e. every ~44 steps, each an ~11 s stall (this is the entire cause of the recurring 31-44 s/step readings). Hourly cuts those stalls 4×. |
| ladder cells write to `ckpt_ab`, `--checkpoint_interval 999999` | an arm can never touch or prune the real checkpoint |
| OOM fallback keeps `grad_ckpt 1 --checkpoint_stride 2`, batch 1 | the fallback must be the *known-good* config, not the one under test |
| `TRAIN_WALL 161000 → 154000` | pays for the ladder's ≤105 min out of the 2-day wall |

Winner rule, pre-registered in the script: lowest s/step among cells whose own `[HBM] peak
reserved` is **≤72 GB** of the 85 GB card (13 GB transient margin); if no cell qualifies it falls
back to the control config. Cell walls are 2100 s because `[HBM]` prints every 100 global steps
and 100 × 20.6 s = 34 min: an OOM cell instead dies in ~2 min, since `block_size` is fixed so
peak memory is reached in the first steps.

**Arithmetic behind the prediction** (recorded so the measurement can confirm or refute it):
fp32 weights 8.25 + fp32 grads 8.25 + ZeRO-1-sharded Adam m,v 2×8.25/4 = 4.13 + bf16 autocast
copies ≈ 4.1 ⇒ ~24.7 GB fixed, so activations+workspace ≈ 46.5 − 24.7 ≈ 21.8 GB with 12 of 24
layers stored. Storing all 24 roughly doubles that term ⇒ **~68 GB predicted peak**. Time: blocks
are ~81% of matmul FLOPs (1.67B of 2.06B params; embed/lm_head 388M is tied and never
recomputed), recomputing half of them adds 0.5 × (1/3) × 0.81 ≈ **13.5%** ⇒ predicted
**20.59 → ~18.1 s/step, −12%**. Both numbers are estimates and the ladder is what decides.

**Three unmeasured things this leaves open**, in priority order: (1) the ladder itself, is the
activation term really linear in stored-layer count; (2) whether `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=
expandable_segments:True` buys enough fragmentation headroom to make a 68 GB config safe (a known
win elsewhere in this project, never tested on mercury); (3) whether `--loss_chunk_size 0`
(compiled chunked CE) is still the right setting with compile OFF, it was chosen on a machine
where inductor worked, and on mercury the compile it depends on is disabled.

## §M+10: the mercury chain was one slice deep; now it is self-sustaining (2026-08-29 23:34 CDT)

**The gap:** the chain ended at `598712`. Its 2-day wall would expire around **Sep 2 ~18:30 CDT**
with nothing queued behind it, and §M+8 established that the moment we release mgpu04 another
user's ~14 pending single-GPU array jobs backfill it. So the run would have stopped silently and
the 4-GPU claim would have been lost, with no error anywhere: the failure mode that produces no
symptoms.

**1. It reads the ladder verdict instead of re-measuring it.** The ladder (§M+8) runs once in
`598712` and writes `$R/.succ_ladder` as `label grad_ckpt stride batch s_step peak_gb`, one line per
cell that *survived*: an OOM'd cell writes nothing. `cont` applies the identical winner rule
(lowest s/step among cells with measured peak ≤72 GB) and falls back to the **control config that
598526 actually ran for 5 h** (20.55 s/step, 46.5/85.0 GB) if the file is missing or every cell
failed. It never guesses a config that has not been observed to work.

**2. It self-chains, guarded.** An unguarded trailing `sbatch` in a handover script already created
a duplicate mercury trainer once, so the chain block fires only when `squeue -u $USER -n
benchmarking -t PENDING` is **empty**, and honours a `$R/.mercury_chain_stop` marker: the same
positive-stop-marker pattern as `.chain_halted` / `.exp_chain_stop` on ALCF. To halt the mercury
line cleanly: `touch /scratch/youzhi/a45/.mercury_chain_stop`.

`TRAIN_WALL=170000` (2-day wall less ~55 min for the final save; `cont` has no ladder to pay for,
unlike `598712`'s 154000). `--torch_compile 0` in both train invocations, verified by count: 2
occurrences of `0`, zero of `1`.

**Aug 31 maintenance needs nothing further:** the ALCF outage (Sophia+Crux 09:00-14:30, Sophia
reservation to 23:30 CDT) falls entirely inside `598526`/`598712`'s mercury window, and the

## §M+11: chunked CE is CLOSED by the code's own record; allocator setting added (2026-08-29 23:50 CDT)

**Open item (3) of §M+8 resolved without a GPU.** The worry was that `--loss_chunk_size 0` had been
chosen on a machine where inductor worked, and mercury runs with compile off. `model.py:1045`
already answers it, in a comment marking a measurement from 2026-08-27:

> ⛔ DO NOT "optimise" this with `_chunked_lm_loss`: MEASURED WORSE … equivalence proven to
> 9.5e-7 … ⇒ the transient was NOT the bottleneck; chunking's recompute overhead is pure loss here.

and `_chunked_lm_loss` carries `@torch.compiler.disable`, i.e. it **always** runs eager, compile or
not. The mechanism that made chunking lose: recompute cost with no memory pressure to pay for it: 
holds *more* strongly on mercury, where HBM sits at 54.7% and there is no pressure at all. So
`loss_chunk_size 0` is right here too, by the same mechanism rather than by transfer.
**Do not re-test chunked CE on mercury.**

**Added to both queued slices, identically: `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`.**
The allocator grows one segment instead of fragmenting fixed pools, so a ~68 GB config on an 85 GB
card is less likely to die on *fragmentation* rather than on true capacity. The failure it prevents
is a **false negative on the highest-value ladder cell**: concluding `grad_ckpt 0` "doesn't fit"
when only the allocator layout was in the way, which is the most expensive kind of measurement
error here. It must be set identically in the ladder job and in the slice that reuses the verdict,
or the measured peaks do not transfer; both now carry it (verified, 1 occurrence each). Pure
allocator behaviour, no numerics change.

Because Slurm **spools an immutable copy of the script at submit time**, patching the files could
not affect the queued jobs, they were cancelled and resubmitted. Both were `Dependency`-held and
therefore ineligible, so no age priority was lost. New chain:
**`598526` (R) → `598803` (ladder) → `598804` (cont, self-chaining)**.

Backup dir is clean: anchor 95055, finalized 95847, and `95891.pt.part` in flight; no stranded
partials accumulating.

**Three unmeasured things, replacing the closed one:** (1) the ladder itself, is activation memory
really linear in stored-layer count; (2) whether `--ddp_bucket_mb` (added for the Polaris
interconnect ladder, PyTorch default 25 MB) does anything at **4 ranks on one node**, where NVLink
replaces the fabric and ~165 AllReduce launches per step may still cost launch overhead;
(3) whether the WSD cooldown fraction is still correctly placed after the handover: `cooldown_frac
0.15` is computed against `estimated_steps`, and the run has now changed rank count (24 → 4) and
`total_batch_size` accounting machines mid-schedule.

## §M+12: completion arithmetic: mercury alone is a 26-day path (2026-08-30 00:20 CDT)

Not previously stated, and it reframes what the ALCF outage actually costs. At step **95,992 of
203,450** the run has done **51.89 B of 110 B tokens (47.2%)**, leaving **58.11 B**. Dividing that
by each machine's *measured* production rate:

| shape | tok/s | tok/s per GPU | days remaining | 2-day slices |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **mercury 4×H100, compile 0 (current)** | 26,246 | 6,562 | **25.6** | 13 |
| Sophia 1 node / 8 GPU | 56,798 | 7,100 | 11.8 | 6 |
| Polaris 2 node / 8 GPU (OFI+Ring) | 49,698 | 6,212 | 13.5 | 7 |
| Polaris 6 node / 24 GPU | ~110,250 | ~4,594 | **6.1** | 4 |

Save stalls are negligible at the new interval (~11 s per save every 3600 s = 0.3%).

**What this means, stated as fact rather than as a recommendation** (mercury is the trainer by owner
directive, specifically so both ALCF machines are free, that decision is not mine to revisit):

1. **The mercury path needs ~13 slice boundaries.** §M+8 established that another user holds ~14
   pending single-GPU jobs on `gpu_h100`, so *every* boundary is a chance to lose the 4-GPU claim.
   The self-chaining `cont` slice (§M+10) is what makes 13 boundaries survivable at all, without
   it the run would have needed 13 manual resubmissions, each one a window for the node to go.
2. **The real cost of the ALCF outage is not the stalled experiment session**, it is that the
   trainer is on the slowest available machine, at 4.2× the wall clock of Polaris 6-node. Two hours
   of no experiments costs 4 arms; two hours on mercury instead of Polaris 6-node costs ~6.3 h of
   equivalent progress.
3. **Sophia is only 8% better per GPU than mercury** (7,100 vs 6,562 tok/s/GPU), its 2.2× total
   advantage is entirely GPU *count*. Conversely Polaris 6-node has the *worst* per-GPU figure
   (~4,594) and still the best wall clock, which is the shape lesson restated: GPU count is not
   throughput, and per-GPU efficiency is not wall clock. Quote both, always.
4. The Aug 31 ALCF maintenance window costs nothing under the current placement, since mercury is
   unaffected: the one situation where being on the slow machine is free.

## §M+14: the ladder would have tripped our own loss alarm (2026-08-30 01:05 CDT)

**A false-positive kill was waiting in the queued ladder.** Its cells write to `$R/ckpt_ab`, which
is empty, so they **start from random init** and their first losses are **~11.9 = ln(151680)**: the
exact number the standing health rule defines as "model effectively random, STOP THE JOB
IMMEDIATELY, do not wait for it to recover". That rule is deliberately written to override
deliberation, which is what makes this dangerous: a tick reading a ladder log at 4am would kill a
perfectly healthy probe, and the honest reading of the directive would say it was right to.

Here the high loss is **correct**: the cells measure s/step and peak HBM, both shape-determined and
independent of the weights, so fresh init is the cheap way to run them without touching the real
checkpoint. Resuming the real one instead was considered and **rejected**: resume reads from
`--checkpoint_dir`, so a resuming cell would have to point at `$R/ckpt` and could then write a
checkpoint there on wall-time exit, at a step and batch shape that do not match the schedule. An
isolated `ckpt_ab` cannot corrupt anything; a shared dir can.

Mechanism fix, not a note: `run_cell` now emits, into the trainer log itself,

    ^ FRESH-INIT PROBE: a loss near 11.9 in <cell log> is EXPECTED, NOT the corruption signature

so the probe declares its own expected anomaly. The structural protection is also worth stating:
cell stdout goes to `$R/logs/ladder_*.log`, **not** the trainer log the tick greps, so the alarm
would only fire if someone widened the grep.

⚠️ **Nested here-docs over ssh mangled the first attempt**: the outer shell ate the quoting and the
Python arrived with its string literals stripped (`old= say LADDER cell: grad_ckpt=...`), then the
remaining lines were executed as shell commands. Nothing was damaged (verified: chain intact, script
unmodified, `bash -n` clean) because the failure was upstream of any mutation. The reliable pattern,
now used: **write the patch script locally, `rsync` it, then run it by path.** Do not nest a
here-doc inside an `ssh '...'` argument.

Chain resubmitted a third time: **`598526` (R) → `598870` (ladder) → `598871` (cont)**. Each
resubmission is free: a `Dependency`-held job is ineligible and accrues no age priority, but the
spooled-copy rule is what forces it: Slurm snapshots the script at submit, so a queued job can
never be patched in place.

## §M+15: the reverse handover path, and a trap in stopping the mercury chain (2026-08-30 01:20 CDT)

`~/bin/a45_push_to_eagle.sh` (new, midway3) implements the documented reverse handover: push the
newest **verified** /project checkpoint to `/eagle/.../ckpt`, md5 both ends, and promote the
`.part` to its final name **only** after the checksums match, writing `.pushed_<step>.md5ok` as the
positive marker: the same "only a passing checksum can create the marker" rule that the forward
direction now uses. Only the /eagle → /project → mercury direction had ever been exercised.

It **refuses to hand over**: it never touches `.trainer_hold` or `.chain_halted`, because mercury is
the trainer by directive and starting an ALCF trainer is an owner decision, not a side effect of
staging a file. It also exits immediately if no ControlMaster is alive, since it cannot create one
(that needs a human passcode). That abort path is the one branch testable right now, and it fires
correctly.

**⚠️ Trap found while writing the closing instructions, and corrected in the script.** My first
draft said "scancel the RUNNING benchmarking job". That is wrong in a way that would silently
continue training: `598870` and `598871` are held by **`afterany`** dependencies, so cancelling only
the runner **satisfies** the dependency and *promotes* the successor. Stopping the mercury line
therefore requires, in this order:

    ssh mercury touch /scratch/youzhi/a45/.mercury_chain_stop   # disarm the self-chain first
    ssh mercury 'scancel -u $USER -n benchmarking'              # runner AND both held slices
    # then verify: squeue -u youzhi -n benchmarking must be EMPTY

This is the same class of error as the Sophia watchdog that resubmitted within a minute of `qdel`: 
a stop that removes the symptom while the mechanism keeps going. The durability built in §M+10 is
exactly what makes it hard to stop, so the stop procedure has to be written down beside it.

Also noted: `rsync.log` carried **no rate line at all** before this change, the invocation had
neither `-v` nor `--stats`, so the copy's own performance has been invisible for the whole night.

## §M+17: one /scratch hiccup would have killed the chain permanently (2026-08-30 02:05 CDT)

**The defect.** Every pre-flight guard in `a45_mercury_cont.sbatch` ended in a bare `exit 1`: the
data-size guard, the no-checkpoint guard, the partial-checkpoint guard, the stalled-copy guard, and
the post-wait recheck. All five return **before** the self-chain block at the end of the script. So
a single transient `/scratch` failure, on a filesystem the standing directive explicitly calls
unstable, currently 89% full: would have exited the slice with **nothing queued behind it**, and
§M+8's ~14 pending single-GPU jobs from another user would have taken mgpu04 within minutes. No
error, no alarm, no trainer. Exactly the failure class that produces no symptoms.

The irony is that §M+10's durability is what made this reachable: the chain is now robust enough
that its *only* remaining single point of failure is its own abort path.

**The fix, and why bounded rather than unlimited.** A `bail()` helper replaces all five exits. It
increments `$R/.mercury_abort_strikes`, then resubmits `cont` unless (a) `.mercury_chain_stop`
exists, (b) three consecutive aborts have accumulated, or (c) a benchmarking job is already pending.
Unbounded retry was rejected: a *permanent* fault, deleted data, a genuinely corrupt checkpoint, 
would spin job submissions forever. Three strikes is the same pattern `polaris_ds6.pbs` already uses
for its no-progress guard, so this is a reused mechanism, not a new invention. Reaching the trainer
invocation clears the counter (`rm -f $STRIKES`), so strikes only accumulate on **back-to-back**
failures: an abort today and another next week do not add up to a stop.

On 3 strikes it says what to do rather than dying silently: *"fix the cause, rm the strike file,
resubmit by hand."*

Patched with the rsync-a-python-script pattern from §M+14 (asserting a unique match for each of the
five substitutions before rewriting, so a silent partial patch is impossible), `bash -n` clean, and
`cont` resubmitted as **`598918`** (`afterany:598870`). Chain: **`598526` (R) → `598870` (ladder) →
`598918` (cont, bounded-retry, self-chaining)**.

⚠️ Note the ladder slice `598870` still has bare `exit 1` guards: deliberately. It runs **once**,
before the long training slices, and if it aborts, `598918` is already queued `afterany` and starts
regardless. It is the tail of the chain that needed protecting, not the head.

## §M+18: contention hypothesis REFUTED; and a correction: the mirror had no md5 (2026-08-30 02:20)

**§M+16's contention hypothesis is refuted by its own measurement.** With `--stats` in place, rsync
reports **72,534,438 bytes/sec = 72.5 MB/s**, i.e. exactly the ~70 MB/s wire cap and only **16% of
`/scratch`'s measured 450 MB/s**. A 16% read load cannot cost 30% of trainer throughput, so the
single 27.30 s/step window was noise, not the backup. **No `--bwlimit` is needed**: the right
outcome for a hypothesis stated as a hypothesis. (24.77 GB ÷ 72.5 MB/s = 341 s, matching the "~5 min
per copy" figure in the standing notes.) Pooled rate now 317 steps / 7202 s = **22.72 s/step**,
unchanged.

**⚠️ CORRECTION to §M+9.** I wrote there that "every backup check so far verified md5 of the
transfer". **That is wrong.** `grep -c md5` over `backup_ckpt.sh`, `backup_finalize.sh` and
`a45_backup_tick.sh` returns **0, 0, 0**. What actually exists:

- **rsync's own end-of-transfer whole-file checksum** (plus `--append-verify` re-checking the
  pre-existing portion before appending): real, checksum-based, but it only covers the **wire**.
- **`backup_finalize.sh`'s promotion gate: a `stat -c %s` size comparison against the live mercury
  source.** Length only: the precise check the standing directive names as having passed on a
  corrupt 23 GB file three times.
- My §M+9 `torch.load` test: the strongest check, but run **once, by hand**.

So the mirror was not unverified, but it was not md5-verified either, and stating otherwise would
have let someone trust a length check. Correcting it matters more than the tidiness of the earlier
section.

**Fix: the load check is now part of promotion, not a one-off.** `~/bin/ckpt_structcheck.py` runs
inside `backup_finalize.sh` immediately after the `.part` is renamed and **before any retention
pruning**. It asserts, via mmap so only touched pages are read (~5 s): the file opens, a state dict
exists, **339 tensors**, `embed_tokens.weight` is **(151680, 2560)**, its norm is finite and in
100-5000, and the stored `loss` is in 1.0-3.0. On failure it prints loudly and **skips retention
entirely**, so a bad promotion can never delete the previous good copy.

A full md5 was considered and **rejected**: it would add a 24.8 GB full-speed read on the *trainer's
own* `/scratch` to every promotion: manufacturing the exact contention I had just refuted, while
testing a weaker property than "does it load".

Verified live against the current mirror: `STRUCT OK step=96243 loss=2.0279 tensors=339
embed=(151680, 2560) |embed|=573.688`. Installed by stage-then-`mv` (a `*/10` crontab shares these
scripts).

## §M+19: the mirror loses a copy when the source is pruned mid-transfer (2026-08-30 02:35 CDT)

**Observed:** `backup.log` shows *"source for step 96287 is gone (pruned); discarding partial"*, the
second such loss tonight (95891 was the first). The copy had reached only **8.38 GB of 24.76 GB in
723 s = 11.6 MB/s**, and the trainer's next save at step 96331 deleted 96287 before it finished.

**The race, quantified.** A copy needs 24.76 GB ÷ 72.5 MB/s = **5.7 min** at full speed. Saves land
every **44 steps × 22.5 s = 16.5 min**. So the margin is ~3×, and it only closes when the transfer
runs slow, which this one did, at 1/6 the normal rate. Verified by byte delta on the *next* copy
(the prompt's rule: measure transfers by byte delta, not by `pgrep`): **14.63 GB → 16.00 GB in 20 s
= 74.0 MB/s**, ETA 1.7 min, comfortably inside the window. `ps -o cmd` confirms exactly **one**
rsync (parent + its receiver child + the ssh), so duplicate transfers are not the cause.

**Cause of the 11.6 MB/s excursion: not established.** One datapoint, and the plausible mechanisms
(a stale `.part` forcing an `--append-verify` re-read, which advances *no* file size while it runs;
or transient network) are not distinguishable after the fact. Stating it as unknown rather than
picking the tidy explanation.

**The mitigation is already queued and needs no new work:** `598870` moves the save interval from
900 s to 3600 s, so saves land every **~175 steps ≈ 66 min** instead of 16.5: the copy window goes
from ~3× to ~11× the transfer time, and a 6× slow excursion would still complete. This is a second,
unplanned payoff from the interval change made for throughput reasons in §M+8.

**Current exposure, which is the number that actually matters:** newest *complete* /project copy is
**96243** while the trainer is at **96349**: 106 steps ≈ **57 M tokens** behind. Two prior
checkpoints (95055 anchor + 96243) are on /project and both pass the structural check, so a total
mercury loss would cost at most those 106 steps, ~40 min of work. Acceptable, and the /project copy
is never the bottleneck for a resume.

⚠️ Also confirmed while checking: the struct check has not fired yet, because **no promotion has
happened since it was installed**: 96287 was discarded and 96331 is still in flight. Absence of a
`STRUCT OK` line is not evidence the wiring is broken; the wiring was verified directly against
96243 in §M+18.

## §M+21: INCIDENT: mercury /scratch purged all 152 GB of training data (2026-08-30 04:42-05:33)

**Timeline (CDT).** 04:42:02, `598526` exits **cleanly** on its own `--wall_time` after 10:12:48
(exit 0:0, checkpoint 96,680 written and already mirrored). 04:43, successor `598870` starts, the
data guard reports **all three flats at 0 bytes**, bails. 04:43:17, `598918` same. 04:43:22, 
`598993` same, third strike, chain stops itself with instructions. 04:48, tick notices
`squeue -n benchmarking` empty. 04:49, restore started from /project. 05:33, 141.75 GiB restored
byte-exact, chain restarted. **Total downtime 51 min; zero training progress lost.**

**Cause.** `edu_flat.bin`, `finemath_flat.bin`, `code_flat.bin` were **gone from the directory**, not
truncated: `ls` no longer lists them and `dd` reads 0 bytes. `/scratch` went 89% → 79% used
(~700 GB freed cluster-wide, of which ours is 152 GB), so this is a **filesystem-wide purge**, not a
targeted deletion. The precise policy is not determinable from the client side; recorded as unknown
rather than guessed. The checkpoint directory was **not** touched.

**Both guards worked, and this is the payoff for building them.**
- The **byte-size data guard** refused to train on missing data. Without it, `pretrain.py` would have
  opened empty/absent .bin files: best case a crash, worst case a corrupted run.
- The **3-strike bounded-retry bail** (§M+17, added 2.5 h earlier) stopped after three consecutive
  aborts and printed what to do, instead of the two failure modes it was designed against: the
  original bare `exit 1` would have killed the chain permanently on strike one, and an unbounded
  retry would have spun job submissions forever.

**What was still missing: the repair was manual.** Detection depended on a human-paced tick noticing
an empty `squeue`. Closed by `~/bin/a45_data_watchdog.sh`, wired into the existing `*/10` crontab: it
compares all three sizes against expected, and if any is short and no restore is already running it
starts `a45_restore_data.sh`. Detection is now bounded to 10 min, repair is automatic, and it survives
this session dying. It deliberately **only restores, never submits**: `a45_verify_and_resubmit.sh`
owns submission and fires only when all three sizes are byte-exact **and** no rsync is still writing
(a length-correct file mid-`--append-verify` is exactly the trap the standing rules warn about).

**⚠️ My own bug cost a job, and `bash -n` could not have caught it.** The restarted ladder `598998`
died in 1 s: `line 118: SL: unbound variable`. The §M+14 "FRESH-INIT PROBE" banner referenced `$SL`
**before** `local SL=` was declared, and under `set -u` that aborts the script. `bash -n` is
syntax-only, so my pre-flight passed a script guaranteed to die on its first cell. The chain absorbed
it correctly: `cont`'s `afterany` dependency started training 15 s later on the control config, but
the lesson is a new pre-flight step, now used: **extract the function and dry-run it under `set -u`
with stubs.** That check confirmed the fix (`rc=0`) where `bash -n` had said nothing.

**Restore economics, for planning:** 141.75 GiB at ~56-60 MB/s = **44 min**. That is the floor on
recovery from a purge, so a repeat costs ~10 min detection + 44 min copy ≈ 55 min of training.

**Two confirmations from the resumed run:**
1. Loss **1.8953** at step 96,700: indistinguishable from the pre-outage level (~1.9), so the resume
   from 96,680 is clean.
2. HBM peak reserved is **44.2/85.0 GB (52.0%)** versus **46.5 GB (54.7%)** before: 2.3 GB less for
   identical work. That is `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` (§M+11) taking effect for
   the first time, since this is the first slice launched with it. Small, but it confirms the setting
   is live and behaving as intended rather than being inert.

Note the save cost itself, **103 s**, is higher than the 55 s implied by 24.76 GB ÷ 450 MB/s. The

## §M+24: the backup promoted on LENGTH alone; added an rsync exit-code gate (2026-08-30 13:05 CDT)

`backup_finalize.sh` promoted `checkpoint_step_N.pt.part` → `.pt` when
`stat -c %s` matched the mercury source, then ran `ckpt_structcheck.py`, then pruned the previous
checkpoint. §M+18 already recorded that no script calls `md5`. What I had not noticed is the sharper
version of the same hole: **`rsync --inplace` grows the `.part` to full length BEFORE it runs its
final whole-file checksum.** So a length-equal `.part` is not evidence of a completed transfer: an
rsync that dies at, or is killed during, that verification leaves a full-size unverified file, and the
size test promoted it and pruned the previous checkpoint behind it. This is the same "absence of a
.tmp is not a positive marker" failure the trainer path was fixed for, still present here.

**Fix: a positive marker only a completed rsync can create.** `backup_ckpt.sh` now wraps rsync so
its exit status lands in `$D/.rsync_rc` as `<step> <rc>`, and clears the file before launching.
`backup_finalize.sh` requires `rc == 0` for that step before promoting, with three outcomes:

| state | action |
|---|---|
| `rc = 0` | promote, structcheck, prune (unchanged) |
| `rc ≠ 0` | refuse; promote nothing, prune nothing |
| no marker, rsync alive | refuse quietly, wait for the next tick |
| no marker, no live rsync | refuse loudly, log `NO-RC`, **keep the `.part`** so the next tick resumes it (`--partial --inplace --append-verify` re-verifies the existing prefix) |

All four verified against an isolated copy with the mercury `stat` and the structcheck stubbed: 
`rc=23` and no-marker both refused and kept the `.part`, `rc=0` promoted. No transition gap: 97,911
was already promoted, so the next transfer is launched by the patched script.

**Still not md5, and deliberately.** rsync's own end-of-transfer checksum covers the wire and now
gates the promotion; a full md5 would add a 24.8 GB read on the trainer's own `/scratch` every ~50
minutes, against the run it is protecting. What the path guarantees is now stated correctly: *the
transfer completed and rsync verified it, the length matches, and the file loads with the right
tensor count, vocab shape, embedding norm and a plausible stored loss.*

## §M+25: the 09-01 slice handover is PRIORITY-SAFE against a 27-deep foreign queue (2026-08-30 13:50 CDT)

Checked explicitly rather than assumed, because a chained trainer that loses its node at the boundary
produces no symptom until the gap has already happened. `gpu_h100` state right now:

| | |
|---|---|
| partition size | **2 nodes**, `mgpu03` + `mgpu04`, 4× H100 each |
| `mgpu03` | `MIXED+PLANNED`: partially allocated **and scheduler-reserved for a pending job**. Not draining. |
| `mgpu04` | `MIXED`: ours, 4 GPUs, job `598999` |
| foreign pending | **27 jobs**: feiyuha0 ×20, haoranzheng ×3, zli27 ×2 |
| our slice | `StartTime=2026-08-30T05:33:18`, `EndTime=2026-09-01T05:33:18` (2-day wall) |

**The concern was `AccrueTime=Unknown`.** Both `599000` and `599001` are `afterany`-held, so they accrue
**no age priority at all** while held, they only start aging when the dependency clears at the
boundary, by which time the foreign jobs have months of age. feiyuha0's oldest are array jobs
submitted **2026-06-29**, pending two months, `AGE=500` (i.e. maxed).

**But they still lose, by 509 points:**

| job | Priority | AGE | FAIRSHARE |
|---|---|---|---|
| our `599000` / `599001` (held) | **2213** | 0 (not accruing) | ~2213 |
| feiyuha0's best pending | 1704 | 500 (maxed) | 1204 |

⇒ `PriorityWeightFairShare=5000` vs `PriorityWeightAge=500` means **age cannot close a fairshare gap
here**: age is worth at most 500 and our fairshare advantage alone is ~1000. Our successor outranks
every foreign pending job *before* it accrues a single point, and gains up to 500 more once eligible.
The handover needs no intervention.

**Consequence for the shape question, which is why I checked.** HBM is 43.2 / 93 GiB = 46% while SM
util reads 98-100%, and `599000` is the chained ladder that measures `grad_ckpt 0` / `batch_size 2` to
fix it. The temptation each tick is to cancel and test the shape now instead of waiting ~40 h for the
boundary. **Don't.** `MaxTRESPerJob node=1` caps us at 4 GPUs (§M+7, shape already closed at the
maximum), so a restart cannot buy a better shape: only the *within-shape* batch question is open, and
that is exactly what the chained ladder tests for free at a boundary we now know we survive. Paying a
checkpoint reload plus a queue re-entry on a 2-node partition to learn it ~40 h earlier is not worth
it. ⚠️ Note the SM-util reading is "fraction of time a kernel was resident", not FLOP efficiency, so
98% util at 46% HBM does **not** prove the card is saturated: the ladder is still worth running.

## §M+26: the "12.8% cross-node penalty" is 2.85 points BATCH SPLITTING and ~10 points network. Measured on ONE GPU. (2026-08-30 17:15 CDT)

§M+25's open item was the confound this line has been carrying since 2026-08-28: the 1-node reference
runs **132** accumulation micro-steps per optimizer step and the 2-node measurement runs **66**, because
a fixed global batch splits across twice as many ranks. I attributed the whole per-GPU gap to crossing
nodes. The control needs **one node**, so it contains no cross-node traffic whatsoever, and therefore
fitted the 1-GPU midway3 allocation at **zero ALCF walltime**.

`exp5/arms_accum/n833`: `n836`. `probe.py` computes `steps = train_tokens // (micro_batch × grad_accum ×
block × world)`, so the token budget is already fixed at 3.0M and only accumulation depth and step
count move. Readout is `tokens_per_sec`; `tgt` is NOT comparable across these arms (eff_batch moves
6.6×) and is not quoted.

| grad_accum | eff_batch | steps | tok/s | vs ga=20 | × sd |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 132 | 135,168 | 22 | **4,395.3** | +15.15% | 132 |
| 66 | 67,584 | 44 | **4,270.0** | +11.86% | 103 |
| 33 | 33,792 | 88 | 4,062.8 | +6.44% | 56 |
| 20 | 20,480 | 146 | 3,817.1 | reference | n/a |

**The throughput floor is 0.12% (n=5 verbatim repeats: 3,816.8 / 3,810.5 / 3,818.9 / 3,822.6 / 3,816.8,
sd 4.4).** That is what makes these readable at 56-132× the noise. Note this is a *tighter* harness than
anything in §M+18's table: 0.12% against the microbenchmark's 12% and the production slice's 12.5%.

⇒ **132 → 66, the exact change going from 1 node to 2, costs 2.85% with no network involved.** So of the
recorded **12.8%**, roughly **2.85 points are batch splitting and ~10 points are the fabric.** The
penalty is real and still the dominant term; it is about 22% smaller than quoted. ⚠️ The 6-node figure
(35.5%) is confounded the same way and worse: 24 ranks split the batch into 22 micro-steps, which on
this curve is between the ga=33 and ga=20 rows, i.e. a batch-splitting cost of roughly 6-9 points
before any network effect. **Restate both figures net of accumulation depth, or do not quote them.**

**The curve is CONVEX, and that is a second finding.** Marginals: **−2.85% (132→66), −4.85% (66→33),
−6.05% (33→20)**. Fixed per-optimizer-step cost (Muon's Newton: Schulz, the optimizer update, per-step
Python) amortises well at depth and badly when shallow. Consequence for scale-out: the same "split the
batch across more ranks" move gets progressively *more* expensive as rank count rises, independent of
any interconnect term. That compounds with the network penalty rather than substituting for it, and it
is a reason to prefer raising the global batch when adding ranks rather than holding it fixed.

**⚠️ Two-point reads are what produced the original error, and I nearly repeated it.** At 2 of 4 arms
the data already supported "2.85%, restate the penalty". I held the write-up until all four landed, and
the third and fourth arms are what revealed the convexity, which changes the 6-node implication
entirely. A two-point read would have given the right number and the wrong model.

**Still open, unchanged by this:** the ~10 residual points are not decomposed. `nccl_nocomm.pbs` (arm 2
disables gradient sync entirely) is the measurement that would bound total exposed comms cost, and it
needs ALCF. Candidates that no transport flag touches remain data loading off shared `/eagle`,
checkpoint I/O, and straggler ranks.

## §M+27: the FREE_GUARD I added on 2026-08-30 was INERT on its own critical branch: it called a function that does not exist

`a45_mercury_cont.sbatch` was patched after the /scratch-full outage with a preflight that refuses to
start a slice below 60 GB free, because a save writes `.tmp` then replaces and so needs ~2x a
checkpoint. Reading the file today, that guard could never have worked:

```
line 55:  say "free space on /scratch: ${FREE_G}G"     # say() is defined at line 79
line 61:  abort "insufficient disk"                    # abort() is defined NOWHERE (it is bail(), line 94)
```

The script runs `set -uo pipefail`: **no `-e`**. So on the low-disk branch bash printed
`abort: command not found`, returned non-zero, and **execution continued straight into training**, 
precisely the outcome the guard exists to prevent. The `say` calls above it were also silently lost.

**What put it there:** I appended the guard at the *top* of the script while the helpers it was
written in terms of live 25 and 40 lines *below* it. Nothing catches this: `bash -n` only checks
syntax, an undefined function is a runtime error, and the branch never executed in testing because
/scratch had space every time the script ran. A guard whose failure path has never been exercised is
an assumption, not a guard.

**Fixed** (verified `bash -n`, backup at `a45_mercury_cont.sbatch.bak2`):
- an early `say(){ echo "=== $* ==="; }` before FREE_GUARD, overridden by the LOG-aware definition later;
- `abort "insufficient disk"` → `exit 1`. Not `bail`: the branch already touches
  `.mercury_chain_stop`, so the correct behaviour is to stop, and `bail` would only increment the
  strike counter and then decline to retry anyway.

⚠️ **This patch does NOT fix job 599878.** Slurm spooled a copy of the script at submit time, so the
pending job still carries the broken guard. It propagates to every *future* slice, because each
successor is `sbatch`'d from the on-disk file at the moment the previous slice ends. 599878 running
with the inert guard is acceptable today only because /scratch now has 1.56 TB free, i.e. the branch
cannot fire. That is luck, not a fix, and it is the reason to state it here rather than call it done.

**The general lesson, which is the reusable part:** a helper used above its own definition is a class
of bug that `bash -n` cannot see and that testing cannot see either, because guard branches are by
construction the paths that do not run. When adding a guard to an existing launcher, either move the
helpers above it or write the branch with builtins only.

## §M+28: 40 h of trainer pending time was a SHAPE problem, not a queue problem. One free H100 was sitting on the other node the whole time.

`599878` (the 4x H100 a4.5 trainer) sat `PENDING Reason=Resources` with
`StartTime=2026-09-01T23:44`, roughly 40 h of dead time, at priority 2249, well above every
competing pending job. The queue was not the constraint. The **shape** was:

```
  mgpu03   CfgTRES gres/gpu=4   AllocTRES gres/gpu=3    <-- ONE H100 free, 24 idle CPUs, ~305G RAM
  mgpu04   CfgTRES gres/gpu=4   AllocTRES gres/gpu=4    <-- full: haoranzheng's four 1-GPU jobs
```

A `gres/gpu:4` request needs four free GPUs **on one node**. Seven of the cluster's eight H100s were
held by 1-GPU jobs, so the only path to four-in-a-row was mgpu04 emptying, and 599878's estimate
lines up exactly with haoranzheng's four jobs hitting their 2-day walls at Sep 1 ~23:40. Meanwhile
mgpu03's fourth GPU was idle and would stay idle, because nothing of ours was shaped to use it.

**Fixed by gap-filling, which is the Polaris-yields-to-Sophia contract applied to one cluster.**
`a45_mercury_gap.sbatch`, job **601068**, RUNNING on mgpu03 since 08:10:38, resuming the same run from
`checkpoint_step_99319.pt`:

- `--nodelist=mgpu03`, **this pin is the entire safety argument.** 599878 will land on mgpu04, so a
  1-GPU job pinned to mgpu03 cannot delay it. Without the pin, taking a GPU on the node that is about
  to free four would be self-sabotage. Do not remove it.
- `--nproc_per_node=1` with `--total_batch_size 540672` unchanged, so grad_accum rises 132 → 528
  micro-steps. 528 is legal (it divides 528). Effective batch, LR schedule and data order are
  identical to the 4-GPU slices: **this is the same run at a quarter of the width, not a new recipe.**
- Two independent anti-overlap mechanisms, because "exactly one trainer ever" cannot rest on an
  estimate: a **yield watchdog** polling 599878's state every 30 s that kills this trainer the instant
  it goes RUNNING, and a **24 h wall** ending Sep 1 08:10, i.e. 15.5 h before 599878's estimate, so a
  dead watchdog still cannot produce two writers.
- The yield kills **without a final save, deliberately**: `torch.save` writes `.tmp` then
  `os.replace`, so the newest complete `.pt` is always intact and the primary resumes from it. Losing
  under one save interval beats two processes in one checkpoint dir. The watchdog then `rm`s any
  orphaned `.tmp`, because the primary's own checkpoint guard *waits* on `ls $R/ckpt/*.tmp` for up to
  40 min and would otherwise stall on a partial write whose owner is already dead.
- **No self-chain, on purpose.** 599878's chain guard counts pending `benchmarking` jobs
  (`"$PEND benchmarking job(s) already pending -- not adding another"`), so a successor submitted here
  would silently suppress the real trainer's chain.

Cost/benefit: ~6,560 tok/s for up to 24 h is roughly **0.55B tokens that would otherwise be zero**, at
no risk to the 4-GPU claim and no extra allocation.

⚠️ **mgpu03's cards report 95,830 MiB, not 80 GB.** The whole HBM story for this trainer was written
against an 85 GB reading (46.5/85.0 = 55%); on a 94 GB card at batch_size 1 it is closer to **49%**.
The gap-filler still runs batch_size 1: the proven config, since an OOM forfeits the gap and 598526
ran 5+ h on it, but this is the clearest case in the campaign of idle HBM that is genuinely idle
rather than one step from the ~95% cliff (§N+31). It belongs to the 4-GPU successor, which already
carries a batch_size 2 attempt with an automatic fallback to 1.

### §M+28b: the gap slice measured, and why I did NOT restart it to fill HBM

Live at step 99325 on mgpu03: **63.19 s/step, loss 1.8114, GPU util 93%, HBM 42,923 / 95,830 MiB
= 44.8%.** Loss reference: the pre-outage slice's last reading was `Step 99450 | Loss: 1.8883`, so a
resume at 1.8114 is below it and the `--torch_compile 0` path is confirmed intact again.

**Per-GPU throughput is 30% HIGHER at world=1 than at world=4:**

```
  4 GPUs (ZeRO-1)   20.55 s/step   26,308 tok/s   6,577 per GPU
  1 GPU  (no comms)  63.19 s/step    8,556 tok/s   8,556 per GPU   = 1.30x per GPU
```

So one card recovers **32% of the four-card rate using 25% of the hardware**, because at world=1 there
is no gradient all-reduce and no optimizer all-gather to hide. That reframes the 4-GPU configuration:
its cross-rank cost is ~23% of per-GPU throughput, which is the same order as the 12.8% cross-*node*
penalty measured on Polaris and had not been separated out on mercury before.

⚠️ **44.8% HBM with 93% util is real headroom, and I still left it alone.** `batch_size 2` would halve
the micro-step count 528 → 264 and plausibly return 15-20%. I did not take it, and the reason is
worth recording because the arithmetic is not close:

- Restarting means `scancel` then `sbatch`, and **~14 pending single-GPU jobs from other users are
  queued on `gpu_h100`.** Any of them can take mgpu03's fourth GPU in the gap between the two
  commands. The downside is not "10 minutes and an OOM fallback", it is losing the GPU claim
  outright and going back to zero tokens until Sep 1.
- The claim is worth ~0.74B tokens. A 20% improvement on it is ~0.15B. Risking the whole thing for
  20% of it is a bad trade at any plausible probability of losing the race.

**So the batch_size question moves to the NEXT gap slice, which is submitted rather than restarted**: 
a `--dependency=afterany:601068` successor can carry `batch_size 2` with the automatic fallback to 1,
and it inherits the claim instead of gambling on re-winning it.

⚠️ And the result does **not** transfer to the 4-GPU slices: at world=1 ZeRO-1 shards nothing, so the
optimizer state sits whole on one card. The 44.8% and the 4-GPU 55% are different memory regimes, and
a batch_size verdict measured here says nothing about mgpu04. The 4-GPU successor keeps its own ladder.

## §M+29: ⛔ the gap-filler's yield watchdog was a DEADLOCK: it waited for a state its own existence forbids. The node pin was necessary and NOT sufficient.

Within an hour of submitting the 1-GPU gap-filler (§M+28), `599878` reported
`Reason=(QOSMaxBillingPerUser)`. Traced to the scheduler's own configuration, not guessed:

```
  scontrol show partition gpu_h100  ->  QoS=qos_gpu
                                        TRESBillingWeights=... gres/gpu=1000, gres/gpu:h100=1000
  sacctmgr show qos qos_gpu         ->  MaxTRESPU billing=4000
  scontrol show job 599878          ->  ReqTRES=...,billing=4000,gres/gpu=4
```

**The primary's request is exactly the entire per-user cap.** One H100 prices at 1000 billing, the cap
is 4000, and the 4-GPU trainer needs all of it. So a 1-GPU gap-filler holding 1000 makes the primary
**arithmetically unschedulable**, not unlikely, impossible.

**And the yield watchdog polled for `[ "$ST" = "RUNNING" ]`.** That is a state the gap-filler itself
prevents: the signal to stand down could never arrive. If mgpu04 had freed early, the primary would
have sat pending behind my own 1-GPU job until its 24 h wall expired, with the watchdog reporting
healthy the whole time. A degraded-but-working job produces no symptoms, this is that failure mode,
built by me, in the same tick as the fix it was supposed to protect.

⚠️ **What put it there: I verified the resource I thought was scarce and never enumerated the others.**
I checked per-node GRES carefully, worked out which node the primary would land on, and pinned to the
other one. Topology was the *only* contention channel I looked for. Billing TRES is a second, entirely
independent one, and on this partition it binds harder than topology: the pin is correct and
irrelevant. The general form: before claiming a gap-fill cannot delay a pending job, enumerate every
TRES the pending job requests and check the per-user cap on each, not just the obvious one.

**No delay was actually incurred**, and that is luck rather than design: the primary's `StartTime`
Sep 1 23:44 is set by haoranzheng's four 1-GPU jobs hitting their 2-day walls at ~23:40, which is
*later* than both gap slices end (601068 at Sep 1 08:10, its successor by 21:10). The backfill
scheduler already priced both in. ⚠️ **This is also why the chain stops at two slices**: a third
would push past 23:40 and would delay the primary for real. Do not add one without recomputing
against the primary's current `StartTime`.

**Fixed in three layers, because the running slice cannot be patched:**

1. **The trigger is now "the primary COULD run", not "the primary IS running":** the watchdog scans
   `gpu_h100` for any node with `CfgTRES gres/gpu - AllocTRES gres/gpu >= 4` and stands down on that,
   keeping the RUNNING test as a belt. No false trigger from our own node: our GPU counts as
   allocated, so mgpu03 can report at most 3 free.
2. **`~/bin/gap_yield_check.sh`, installed in the midway3 crontab at `*/5`.** Slurm spools a copy of
   the script at submit time, so **601068 still carries the deadlocking trigger** and no edit reaches
   it. An external check is the only thing that can cover a job already running. It resolves both job
   ids from `squeue` rather than hardcoding them (a requeue changes the id, and a stale id is exactly
   how a watchdog silently stops watching), scancels the gap job when the primary fits, and clears any
   orphaned `.tmp`. First run logged `hold: ... best node mgpu04 has only 0 free GPU(s)`, correct.
3. **The successor was resubmitted twice** (601074 → 601078 → **601079**) because each cancellation was
   free: a dependency-held job holds no resource, so fixing a pending job's spooled script costs
   nothing, unlike restarting a running one (§M+28b).

### §M+28c: correction: the world=1 grad_ckpt result DOES transfer to world=4, and in the safe direction

§M+28b said the batch/checkpointing verdict measured at world=1 "does not transfer" to the 4-GPU
slices. That understates it in a way that matters for a decision. The regimes differ, but the
direction is knowable:

```
  per-card memory, ZeRO-1
    world=1   params + FULL optimizer state + activations
    world=4   params + optimizer/4         + activations   (same activations: each rank does batch 1)
```

So **world=4 has strictly MORE free room per card than world=1**, which makes world=1 the *harder*
case. A configuration that fits on one card therefore fits on four with room to spare: the
implication runs one way only, and it is the useful way. What does not transfer is the *throughput*
number, because world=4 pays a gradient all-reduce and an optimizer all-gather that world=1 does not
(measured at ~23% of per-GPU throughput, §M+28b).

**Acted on: the empty-ladder default in `a45_mercury_cont.sbatch` is now `--gradient_checkpointing 0`.**
`$R/.succ_ladder` has been 0 bytes since Aug 30 05:33, every ladder cell failed, so nothing was
written, and `[ -s "$AB" ]` then routes to the CONTROL config. That silently spends an entire 2-day
slice on `--gradient_checkpointing 1 --checkpoint_stride 2`: 20.55 s/step at 46.5 GB of a 94 GB card.
The trade it makes is backwards at that fill. With checkpointing the slice stores 24 layer boundaries
(~120 MB); without it, the full activation set, which at batch 1 x seq 1024 x 24 layers is single-digit
GB against ~47 GB free. **Paying ~30% throughput to save ~2 GB on a half-empty card is not a
conservative default, it is an expensive one.**

Defaulting rather than measuring first is safe here for one specific reason: **the OOM fallback already
reverts to exactly this control config**, so a wrong guess costs the minutes it takes to OOM at startup,
not the slice. The same change is also being measured directly at world=1 by gap slice 601079.

⚠️ **This does not reach 599878.** Slurm spooled its copy at submit time, so its first two days still
run the control. The patch applies from the next chained slice onward. The only runtime input that
*could* redirect 599878 is `$R/.succ_ladder`, and I am deliberately not writing to it: that file holds
MEASURED cells (`label grad_ckpt stride batch s_step peak_gb`), and inventing a line would be
fabricating a measurement. Once 601079 reports a real world=1 `peak_gb` (~Sep 1 21:10, about 2.5 h
before 599878 starts), a line may legitimately be written using that peak as a **conservative upper
bound** on world=4 usage, per the argument above, with the provenance stated in the file.

## §M+30: the yield trigger must count OUR OWN GPU as reclaimable: "3 free plus the one we are using"

Owner, 2026-08-31: *"i think we just need 3 available gpus plus the one we are using, so that's 4 if
that's available and we can immediately secure it."* Correct, and the version I had shipped was wrong
on precisely the node we occupy.

Both the external cron and the in-job guards tested for **4 FREE GPUs on one node**. Current state:

```
  mgpu03   3 GPUs held by another user  +  1 held by OUR gap job   = 4
  mgpu04   4 GPUs held by another user                             = 4
```

If mgpu03's three foreign jobs end, the node has **4 usable GPUs for the primary**, but a free-only
count reads 3, decides "not yet", and leaves our own 1-GPU job squatting the fourth. The primary would
then be blocked **by us**, indefinitely, with every guard reporting healthy. That is exactly the
self-sabotage the guard exists to prevent, arriving through the other door.

⚠️ **And this is plausibly the LIKELIER path, not a corner case.** The three jobs on mgpu03 are further
into their 2-day walls than the four on mgpu04 whose expiry sets the primary's `StartTime`. The
scenario I failed to handle is the one most likely to happen first.

**Corrected test, in both places:**

```
  usable(node) = free(node) + (GPUs our gap job holds on that node)
  yield when   usable(best node) >= 4
```

so on mgpu03 three freed GPUs is now enough. Verified live: the cron logs
`best mgpu03 has 1 usable of 4` (0 free + our 1 reclaimable), where the old version reported the
node as simply having 0.

**Also fixed, and this one was fatal:** the in-job startup guard and the watchdog had drifted, the
watchdog was corrected to the COULD-run signal while the startup guard was left testing `RUNNING`
only. They now call **one shared `usable_gpus()`** so they cannot diverge again. And the watchdog's
log line still expanded `$FITS`, a variable removed when the scan moved into the helper; under the
script's `set -u` that expansion **aborts the watchdog subshell at the exact instant it is trying to
yield**, turning the safety mechanism into a no-op precisely when it matters.

**Why the startup guard needs the same test as the watchdog**, spelled out because the ordering is
what makes it subtle:

```
  1. three GPUs free on mgpu03
  2. the */5 cron scancels the running gap slice so the billing cap frees
  3. `afterany` fires the SUCCESSOR -- and at that instant the primary is still PENDING, because
     Slurm has not made a scheduling pass yet
  4. a RUNNING-only guard reads PENDING, concludes "gap still open", starts training, and re-takes
     1000 of the 4000 qos_gpu cap -- re-blocking the primary the yield just made room for
```

**Yield latency and its one real cost.** Detection is ≤5 min (cron) or ≤30 s (in-job, from slice
601121 onward); Slurm then needs one scheduling pass. The kill is deliberate and unclean, so the work
since the last checkpoint is lost: bounded by `--checkpoint_interval 3600`, i.e. up to ~57 steps at
63 s/step. Left at 3600 on purpose: a 24.7 GB save costs ~5 min, so halving the interval would take
save overhead from ~8% to ~17% of wall to cut an expected ~30 min loss that happens at most twice.

### §M+34: 2026-09-01 13:50 CDT: ⛔ the mercury backup cron was DELETING the live offsite backup. Retired.

At 13:12 I md5-verified `checkpoint_step_101388.pt` on /project against /eagle
(`7e29a0bf735d03a9c535975b198ecf72`, identical both ends) and pruned the superseded intermediates.
At 13:20 the `*/10` `a45_backup_tick.sh` cron re-copied MERCURY's step 100654, declared it newest,
and its latest-only retention deleted 101388:
```
13:20:42 OK step 100654 verified 24764476975 bytes + struct
13:20:42 [retention] removed checkpoint_step_101388.pt
  [retention] KEEPING recovery anchor 95055
```
**CAUSE: the cron still treats mercury as the trainer.** Mercury was abandoned by owner directive this
morning and is frozen at 100654, so the cron's "newest" is permanently stale. Every 10 minutes it
re-asserted a 12-hour-old checkpoint as authoritative and pruned whatever the real trainer had
produced. It had been silently undoing the offsite backup all afternoon; I only noticed because a
routine mirror listed `95055 100654` where I had verified `95055 101388` half an hour earlier.
⭐ THE GENERAL LESSON: a retention rule is only safe if its notion of "newest" tracks the CURRENT
trainer. When the trainer moves machine, every backup/retention job pinned to the old machine becomes
a deletion engine pointed at live data. Retiring the mover is not enough -- the PRUNER must be retired
in the same action, and I did not do that when mercury was dropped at ~11:00.
FIX: `a45_backup_tick.sh` (*/10) and `backup_md5_check.sh` (daily 06:20) are commented out of crontab
as `#RETIRED-mercury-abandoned`. The /eagle -> /project mirror is now the only writer, and it resolves
"newest" from /eagle, i.e. from the machine actually training.

⚠️ Mercury's own copy of 100654 still exists on Booth /scratch, so nothing was lost -- but the offsite
copy of the LIVE resume point was gone for ~30 min, which is exactly the exposure the backup exists
to prevent.

## §M+35: ⛔ WHY SOPHIA NEVER RAN: a livelock in my own no-progress guard, not a cluster problem (2026-09-01)

For days the reading was "Sophia cannot place a whole-node 8-GPU request" (§M+33). **That was wrong.**
The jobs placed fine and started fine. `178344.OU` and `178345.OU` both end:

    === PRIMARY (sophia): claimed; waiting up to 5 min for any gap-filler to yield ===
    === handover: checkpoint quiet ===
    === NO PROGRESS since last slice (101235 -> 101235): refusing to train, chain STOPS ===

MECHANISM, end to end:
1. `train_chain.pbs:39-40` reads `STEP_NOW` = newest checkpoint step on /eagle, and `PREV` from
   `$R/.chain_last_step`. Line 174 refused to train if `STEP_NOW <= PREV`.
2. **Checkpoints land every ~900 steps. At 18.83 s/step that is ~4.7 HOURS.** So the guard's
   resolution is 4.7 h, while the claim/retry cadence is minutes.
3. `.chain_last_step` is written ONLY by the sophia-lineage scripts (`train_chain*.pbs`,
   `sophia_*.pbs`); **`polaris_ds6.pbs` never writes it.** It sat at 101235 from 15:57 UTC while the
   run advanced to 101986 underneath it, entirely under Polaris.
4. So every sophia attempt inside that window read `101235 -> 101235` and refused, while training was
   demonstrably healthy on the other tier.
5. It refused with **`exit 1`**, and these jobs are RERUNNABLE, so PBS requeued **the same job id** on
   each refusal. `178348` reached `run_count = 21`, and PBS applied `Hold_Types = s`.
6. `qrls 178348` did nothing; `qrls -h s 178348` returned **`Unauthorized Request`**: a system hold is
   admin-only. The job was unrecoverable, so I qdel'd it.

COST: the PRIMARY trainer (8 GPUs, 56,798 tok/s) was unavailable and the 4-GPU gap-filler
(28,500 tok/s) carried the run: **a ~2x throughput loss that produced no symptom anywhere**, because
every individual component was behaving "correctly". Worse, each sophia attempt made the mutex fire, so
Polaris yielded and stopped training before sophia then refused: the retries were actively harmful.

⚠️ THE LESSON, which is the one that keeps recurring: **a guard whose sampling interval is coarser than
the event it guards against will fire on healthy states.** The no-progress guard sampled a 4.7 h
counter to judge a decision made every few minutes. Same shape as judging trainer health by `cput`
(PBS counts only the mother superior) and by `job_state = R`.

FIXED in all five scripts carrying the guard (`train_chain.pbs`, `train_chain_g4.pbs`, `sophia_gap2.pbs`,
`sophia_gap4.pbs`, `sophia_p2.pbs`; `.bak-noprogress` alongside each), both halves:
1. **Only refuse if NOTHING is training.** Added `FRESH_LOG=$(find $R/report -maxdepth 1 -name
   "a45_*slice*.out" -newermt "-900 seconds")`; the refusal now needs `STEP_NOW <= PREV` **and** no log
   advanced in 15 min. A genuinely crash-looping chain leaves every log stale, so the protection the
   guard was written for is preserved exactly. When the step is unchanged but a log IS fresh it now logs
   `another tier is training, proceeding` instead of dying.
2. **Refuse with `exit 0`.** Choosing not to train is an intentional, successful outcome. `exit 1` is
   what converted a soft skip into 21 requeues and a permanent hold.
Also refreshed the stale marker: `.chain_last_step` 101235 -> 102000.

Sophia 8-GPU primary resubmitted as **178502** (`by-node`, `select=1:ngpus=8:ncpus=64`).

## §M+36: `blockers.sh` reported "NO trainer running" for a healthy trainer, every tick (2026-09-01)

At 18:05 it printed `NEEDS ATTENTION: NO trainer running on polaris` while job 7583452 was advancing at
18.83 s/step. Cause: the test was `awk '$6>=2 && $10=="R"'`, field 6 is NDS, so **only a >=2-NODE
running job counted as a trainer.** Every trainer since the Polaris single-node move is 1 node, so the
check had been structurally blind, not intermittently wrong. A blocker line that cries wolf trains me to
skim blocker lines, which is the actual damage.

Node count cannot identify a trainer, and neither can the job name (ALCF policy forces both the trainer
and the experiment session to be `benchmarking`). So it now keys on the thing actually being asserted: 
**training is advancing**, via the newest slice log's mtime, with the RUNNING count kept as a separate
signal so "more than one trainer" stays detectable. Three outcomes now: ADVANCING (log < 600 s),
NO trainer (0 running), or `N running but the slice log is Xs stale -- training may be wedged`, which is
the state the old check could never report and the one that matters most.
Verified: now prints `polaris trainer ADVANCING (slice log 9s old, newest /eagle ckpt step 101986, 1 job(s) running)`.

## §M+37: the a4.5 loss LEVEL is flat, the per-reading spread is ~0.18, and a 3.00 reading has already happened harmlessly (2026-09-01)

Triggered by slice 306 resuming at 2.3816 -- the highest of the 43 readings then in view, and the first
reading after a resume, which is the signature the tick rule says to check against the checkpoint's own
stored loss. Checked properly instead of eyeballed, and the conclusion is that nothing is wrong.

**Stored checkpoint losses:** `checkpoint_step_95055.pt` -> **1.6228**, `checkpoint_step_102153.pt` ->
**2.0927** (read with `torch.load(..., mmap=True)`, which touches only the scalar and not the 24 GB of
weights -- the cheap way to run this check on a local mirror copy). A naive reading of those two numbers
says the loss ROSE 0.47 over 7,098 steps, which would be a serious problem.

**It did not.** 567 `Step N | Loss` readings from 40 slice logs, steps 82,500-102,175:

| step bucket | n | mean | min | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 85,000 | 40 | 2.0021 | 1.8034 | 2.3224 |
| 89,000 | 40 | 1.9043 | 1.4873 | 2.3313 |
| 93,000 | 40 | 2.0695 | 1.7054 | **2.9999** |
| 94,000 | 40 | 1.9257 | 1.4087 | 2.3864 |
| 101,000 | 40 | 1.9305 | 1.7154 | 2.0919 |
| 102,000 | 8 | 2.0705 | 1.8882 | 2.3816 |

**OLS slope: −0.001001 loss per 1000 steps over 567 readings, flat to slightly improving.**

Three things follow, and they are the reusable part:
1. **A checkpoint's `loss` field is ONE step's value, not an average.** Bucket minima reach 1.4087, so
   1.6228 at 95055 was simply a low draw and 2.0927 a typical one. Never infer a trend from two stored
   scalars 7k steps apart; the field is a single sample from a distribution with ~0.18 sd.
2. **The true per-reading spread is ~0.15-0.2, not the 0.085 that a short window reports.** Consecutive
   readings inside a few slices are correlated (the mixture draws one source per micro-batch and code CE
   sits well above edu), so a narrow window understates sd and inflates every z-score. `loss_check.py`
   was reading 8 slices and scored the benign 2.3816 at **z=+4.9**; widened to 20 slices (n=207,
   mean 1.9756, sd 0.1793) the same reading is **z=+2.3**. A monitor whose own noise estimate is too
   tight manufactures alarms, which is the failure mode that makes people stop reading monitors.
3. ⚠️ **A reading of 2.9999 already occurred at ~step 93,000 and the run was healthy.** So the standing
   band's 2.5 ceiling WILL fire occasionally on normal training. It is kept as-is (it is the owner's
   threshold and it only says "investigate", not "stop"), but this precedent is recorded so a future tick
   spends one grep on it rather than an incident. The genuine stop signatures remain ~7-9 (re-learning
   from random) and >=11 (random, ln(151680)=11.93) -- those are 25-60 sd away, not 3.

## §M+38: the trainer's HBM is 96.8% and it is NOT costing throughput (2026-09-01)

First HBM reading ever visible in a slice log, from the line added this evening:
`HBM: 38.2/39.5GiB (96.8%) peak_alloc 36.5GiB` at step 102,175.

96.8% is far above the ~90% target and past the >93% point where [[chunked-ce-is-the-throughput-lever]]
measured fills to be SLOWER. **But s/step is 18.92 against the recorded 18.9 for this shape, so there is
no measurable penalty here** -- the earlier finding was about activation-driven fills under chunked CE,
and this fill is not that. `peak_alloc 36.5` vs `reserved 38.2` leaves only 1.7 GiB of allocator slack,
so the memory is genuinely in use rather than fragmented, and with `micro_batch` already at 1 the fill is
parameter + optimizer state, which is not a tunable at this shape. Recorded so the number stops being an
open question: high fill here is expected, and the thing to watch is s/step, not the percentage.

## §M+39: interconnect round 3 produced ONE usable arm, and the cause was `--wall_time` vs torch.compile, not the job wall (2026-09-01 21:20)

The DDP bucket ladder (`nccl_train4.pbs`, 2 nodes / 8 ranks) had already run: twice, before I looked at
it, and both attempts came back mostly empty. What survived:

| arm | tok/s | steps | s/step |
|---|---|---|---|
| A bucket 25 (control) | n/a | n/a | 285.32 |
| B bucket 100 | **49,026** | 40 | **15.76** |
| C bucket 400 | n/a | n/a | 208.64 |

285 and 208 s/step are not slow arms. They are arms that completed **1-2 steps** before their per-arm
`--wall_time 750` expired, so the "rate" is a cold-start average dominated by compile. This script's own
line 91 already warns about exactly this: *"`--wall_time 400` expired, ONE step, no rate, arm wasted"*, 
and 750 s minus a cold-cache `torch.compile` of ~420-600 s leaves too little to measure. Arm **B only has
data because arm A warmed the compile cache for it.**

⚠️ **So the surviving 49,026 tok/s is uninterpretable on its own.** It is a treatment arm with no
same-session control, and the recorded 49,698 tok/s baseline is a DIFFERENT DAY'S CELL. Importing a
control across cells is the error this campaign has already paid for twice (the `grad_clip` 73-vs-120-step
reversal, and the doc_mask floor). A lone arm is not a measurement.

ROUND 4 = `nccl_train5.pbs`, job **7584652** (2 nodes, debug-scaling, 1 h): arms **A (25) + B (100)** only,
`--wall_time` raised **750 → 1200** so both clear compile with room to measure. 2 × 1200 s = 40 min inside
a 1 h wall. This SHORTENS THE WORK rather than growing the allocation, per the standing rule. Bucket 400
is deferred rather than dropped, it earns a slot only if 100 beats 25.

## §M+40: `capacity` is the only Polaris queue that takes 1-4 nodes past a 1 h wall, and it is currently unusable (2026-09-01)

Surveying every enabled/started queue for a shape the trainer actually uses:

| queue | wall_max | nodect |
|---|---|---|
| debug / debug-scaling / demand | 01:00:00 | 1..2 / 1..10 / 1..56 |
| **capacity** | **168:00:00** | **1..4** |
| small / medium / large / prod | 03:00:00 / 06:00:00 / 24:00:00 / 24:00:00 | 10..24 / 25..99 / 100..496 / 10..496 |
| preemptable / route_preempt | 72:00:00 | 1..10 |

**`capacity` is the only queue where a 1-node trainer or a 2-node interconnect job can get a wall longer
than an hour** (`small` and above all have `resources_min.nodect >= 10`, so a 1-node request is rejected
by the router, and `preemptable`'s tag never matches: [[polaris-preemptable-is-a-dead-queue]]). No ACL,
Priority 150, `max_run = [p:PBS_GENERIC=1]`, `max_queued = 2`.

That mattered because **~20% of every Polaris node-hour was going to slice restarts**: slice 305 advanced
102,000 → 102,153 = 153 steps in a 1 h wall, and 153 steps at 18.8 s/step is 47.9 min, so ~12 min per hour
was `torch.compile` plus a 24 GB checkpoint load, 24 times a day. Same SU burn, ~20% fewer tokens.

⛔ **BUT capacity carries `max_run_res.nodect = [o:PBS_ALL=32]`, a cap across ALL USERS, not just us, and
it has been saturated all evening.** Both 7584200 (1 node, 24 h) and 7584582 (2 nodes, 3 h) sat Q on
`would exceed overall limit on resource nodect in queue capacity`, the second for 14 min before I retired
it. So capacity is worth *trying* when a long wall would help, but it must never be the only plan: submit
it alongside a debug-scaling fallback, and do not let a parked capacity job masquerade as coverage.
⚠️ That masquerade is a real failure mode, not a hypothetical: see [[§M+38]]-adjacent note: the
`*/5` `polaris_chain_keeper.sh` counted ANY `benchmarking` job in ANY state, so the queued capacity job
made the keeper stand down while training was actually stopped. Fixed to count RUNNING jobs anywhere plus
QUEUED jobs only in debug-scaling.

Round 4 (`nccl_train5.pbs`, job 7584843, 2 nodes / 8 ranks, `--wall_time 1200`) finally ran both arms to
80 steps each: the first complete same-session pair this axis has produced.

| arm | tok/s | steps |
|---|---|---|
| A `--ddp_bucket_mb 25` (control, PyTorch default) | 49,117 | 80 |
| B `--ddp_bucket_mb 100` | 49,406 | 80 |
| same-session delta | **+289 = +0.59%** | |

**And that is inside the noise.** Two independent readings now exist per configuration:

| config | readings | spread |
|---|---|---|
| bucket 25 | 49,017 / 49,117 | 100 tok/s = **0.20%** |
| bucket 100 | 49,026 / 49,406 | 380 tok/s = **0.78%** |

The **same-config, cross-session spread for bucket 100 (0.78%) EXCEEDS the within-session A-vs-B
difference (0.59%).** So the ladder cannot distinguish bucket 100 from bucket 25, and one pair does not
get to claim +0.59% when re-running the *identical* config moves the number further than that.

⛔ **`ddp_bucket_mb` stays at the incumbent 25. The axis is CLOSED.** Compare the bar the one adopted
throughput lever had to clear: `checkpoint_stride` 3 was taken at **+0.932%, 4/4 seeds, 7.8× the floor**.
This is +0.59% at 1 pair against a 0.78% floor, it fails on effect size AND on replication.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES *NOT* SAY: launch count is not proven irrelevant. ~165 AllReduce launches per step for
4.1 GB of bf16 grads is still ~165 launches; the measurement says the cost of those launches is below what
this rig can resolve at 2 nodes, which is a statement about the rig and the shape as much as about NCCL.
At 12 nodes the launch count is unchanged but the collective is far more exposed, so the term could
matter there and be invisible here. Recorded as "null at 2 nodes", not "null".

⭐ THE REUSABLE POINT, and it is the one this campaign keeps paying for: **measure the same config twice
before believing a difference between two configs.** Round 3 left a lone bucket-100 arm at 49,026 and no
control; had I compared that to the recorded 49,698 from another day I would have "found" a −1.4%
regression, and had I compared round 4's pair alone I would have "found" a +0.59% win. Both are artifacts
of a 0.78% floor that only appears once you repeat a configuration.

NEXT: round 5 (`nccl_train6.pbs`, job **7584982**), decompose the 12.8% cross-node penalty by holding
micro-steps at 132 (2 nodes x 2 GPU = 4 ranks) against a same-session 1-node/4-GPU reference, so the
network term is separated from the reduced-overlap term. Bucket stays at 25 in both arms.

## §M+42: ⭐ THE 12.8% "CROSS-NODE PENALTY" DECOMPOSED: only ~5.8% is the network. ~7% is reduced overlap (2026-09-01 23:43)

Round 5 (`nccl_train6.pbs`, job 7584982, debug-scaling, 2 nodes). Both arms 4 ranks, **132 micro-steps**,
bucket 25, 40 steps each, so rank count, micro-step count and batch shape are all held fixed and the
ONLY difference is whether the collective crosses the wire.

| arm | shape | tok/s | per GPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| F | 1 node × 4 GPU (same-session reference) | 27,918 | **6,980** |
| E | 2 nodes × 2 GPU (cross-node) | 26,309 | **6,577** |
| | **isolated network term** | | **−5.76%** |

Against the recorded combined penalty (1-node/4-GPU 7,125 → 2-node/8-GPU 6,212 per GPU = **−12.81%**):

- **network ≈ 5.8%**
- **remainder ≈ 7.0%**: the micro-step halving (528/4 = 132 → 528/8 = 66), i.e. less backward compute
  to hide the collective behind.

**So MOST of what this campaign has been calling a "cross-node penalty" is not the wire.** It is the
batch shape: at 8 ranks the same 528 sequences split into half as many micro-steps, and the standing note
already predicted this mechanism for why the microbenchmark's ordering transferred but its magnitude did
not ("only the unhidden tail is exposed"). Round 5 measures that split instead of assuming it.

CALIBRATION: arm F reads 6,980 per GPU against the recorded 1-node/4-GPU reference of 7,125 = −2.04%.
Close enough to trust the cell, and a reminder that even the reference is only good to ~2%.

⚠️ THE PRE-REGISTERED CAVEAT HOLDS AND MATTERS: Polaris has 4 NICs and 4 GPUs per node, so at 2 GPUs/node
each rank commands ~2× the NIC bandwidth it would in the production 4-GPU/node shape. **5.8% is therefore
a LOWER BOUND on the production network term**, not an estimate of it. What the cell establishes is the
*split*, not the production number.

⭐ **THIS BOUNDS THE ENTIRE REMAINING INTERCONNECT LINE.** Every NCCL knob still open: 
`NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL`, `NCCL_CROSS_NIC`, a 64 MB `NCCL_BUFFSIZE`: acts only on the network term. That
term is ~5.8% at this shape, so **no NCCL tuning can recover more than ~5.8%**, and the bucket ladder
already showed the resolvable floor here is ~0.8%. The ~7% overlap term is not an NCCL problem at all: it
is addressable only by changing the batch shape (more micro-steps per optimizer step at the same rank
count, i.e. a larger `--total_batch_size`), which is a QUALITY lever and cannot be spent freely.

⛔ **AND THE STRATEGIC POINT: production currently runs on SOPHIA, 1 node × 8 GPU, at 56,742 tok/s and
7,093 per GPU, with ZERO cross-node traffic.** The interconnect line only pays off if the run scales past
one Sophia node. At the current shape its value is zero, so it drops behind anything that helps the
single-node case. Recorded here rather than discovered later by spending more 2-node jobs on a term that
production does not currently incur.
