## §M+44: `capacity` is saturated by an ALL-USER cap, not by us. Stop re-probing it (2026-09-02 09:03)

Re-checked 13 h after §M+40 first found it blocked. Unchanged, and the numbers say why:

```
total_jobs = 23    state_count = Queued:9 Held:1 Running:13
resources_assigned.nodect = 32    max_run_res.nodect = [o:PBS_ALL=32]
```

**Assigned nodect equals the cap exactly**, with 13 other-project jobs running and 9 more queued behind
them. This is not a transient we can wait out on a 15-minute cadence, it is a queue that is structurally
full because its cap is per-INSTALLATION (`o:PBS_ALL`), not per-user or per-project. Our position in it is
irrelevant.

⛔ **So the ~20% Polaris hourly-restart overhead documented in §M+40 is NOT recoverable via `capacity`,
and re-probing it each time Polaris becomes the trainer is wasted effort.** The overhead is real (slice
305: 153 steps in a 60 min wall where 153 × 18.8 s = 47.9 min of work, so ~12 min/hour to compile plus a
24 GB checkpoint load) but the only queue that could host a longer 1-node wall is unavailable.

⭐ THE BETTER FIX IS THE ONE ALREADY IN PLACE: Sophia's `by-node` queue gives a **24 h** wall on 1 node ×
8 GPU at 56,798 tok/s, which removes the restart overhead AND doubles the rate. Polaris at 1 node is the
gap-filler by design; optimising the gap-filler's wall matters far less than shortening the gap. Effort
belongs in getting Sophia back, not in tuning Polaris.

## §M+45: the 4-parallel-arm experiment session is NOT AVAILABLE on midway3, and the driver could not see why (2026-09-02 10:25-10:40 CDT)

The standing plan is 1 node / 4 GPUs / 4 arms in parallel. It has been running as 1 GPU / 1 arm
since 2026-08-30 because the session `exp-kdmuon` (56352671) held `gres/gpu=1`. I read that as a
wrong-sized *request* and fixed the request. It is not: it is the **only shape midway3 can give us**.

`sinfo -p gpu -o "%N %G %f"`: the whole partition, by card:

| nodes | card | HBM | can host a 38 GiB bf16 h400 arm? |
|---|---|---|---|
| midway3-0294 | a100 | 40 GiB | **yes**, and it is the ONLY one |
| midway3-0277…0281 | v100 | 32 GiB | no: too small, and sm70 has no bf16 at all |
| midway3-0282, 0284…0286 | rtx6000 | **24 GiB** | no |

So `gpu` contains exactly one A100 node, it is *shared*, and at 10:30 three other users
(rwkeane, ndtrung, yangili1) held 3 of its 4 cards. `test` has four idle A100 nodes
(0558/0559 + the excluded 0377/0378) but is `State=DOWN AllowAccounts=none`: the same wall as
2026-08-20, and `--test-only` reports `Verification: ***PASSED***` and *then* fails the real
allocation with `Invalid account or account/partition combination`, so verification is not proof here.

**4 arms in parallel therefore needs beagle3** (44 × A100-40G, `beagle3-users`), which is under a
standing "explicit permission every time" rule. Asked. Until then the honest shape is one A100 with
arms back-to-back, ~47 min each, ~3.1 h per 4-arm cell.

### What I broke finding this out, and the mechanism that let me
I submitted `--gres=gpu:4` with **no `--constraint`**, it placed instantly on midway3-0282, and its
handover guard scancelled the 1-GPU session, so arm n971 lost 23 min of its 47, and the A100 card we
had held was claimed by another user within minutes. Two independent defects, both now fixed:

1. **The handover guard could not see the thing it was guarding.** It tested
   `ps -u $USER -o cmd= | grep run_arm_in_alloc.sh`, but it runs on the *compute* node while the
   sequential driver and its `srun --jobid=` wrapper live on the *login* node. A process table is
   per-host, so it answered "no arm in flight" 4 s after start. ⭐ **To ask about a process on another
   host, ask the resource manager, not `ps`**: `squeue -j <old> -s` answers from the controller and is
   correct from anywhere. The driver log on the shared filesystem is a second independent signal (an
   arm is in flight iff the newest `-->` line has no `done`/`FAILED` after it). Both are now used.
   This is the `pgrep`/self-match family of bug one level out: the previous four instances were "the
   pattern matched the wrong process", this one is "the process table was the wrong machine's".
2. **The driver validated GPU COUNT and never GPU CAPACITY.** `4 arms across 4 GPU(s)` is exactly
   what it printed while sitting on 24 GiB cards. Both templates now refuse when the smallest visible
   card is under `MINMIB=36000`. Note `SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE` came back **unset** inside a `--gres=gpu:4`
   job, so the `nvidia-smi` fallback was the live path, and it reported the count *correctly*. The
   count was never the problem; a shape check that only counts devices cannot see the wrong device.
3. `--constraint=a100` is now in the session script as a load-bearing flag, not decoration.

New scripts: `exp_session5.sbatch` (1 × a100, `--cpus-per-task=2 --mem=24G`, right-sized to the
measured 15.5 GiB / 0.9-core arm peak) and `exp5/seq_cell_driver.sh.tmpl` (arms back-to-back **inside**
the batch job, so no login-node `srun --jobid=` wrapper and nothing about the run is invisible to Slurm).

## §M+46: Sophia's pending time was a QUEUE CAP, not a busy machine: moved the primary to `single-node` (2026-09-02 10:33-10:44 CDT)

178569 sat `Q` for 3 h 32 m with `comment = Not Running: No available resources on nodes` while
`pbsnodes -avS` showed **three free 8-GPU nodes**. Both statements were true; the comment is just
uninformative. Two independent walls, found by reading the queue config rather than the node list:

1. **`by-node` carries `max_run = [p:PBS_GENERIC=5]`** and five by-node jobs were already running, 
   *all five belonging to one other user*, each 1 node / 24 h wall, elapsed 6:49 to 13:59. So the
   earliest slot was ~10 h away no matter how many nodes were idle, and 26 jobs were queued behind it.
2. **All three free nodes were tag-fenced.** `sophia-gpu-10`/`-11` carry
   `resources_available.queue_tags = infer-svc-test`, `sophia-gpu-24` carries `bigmem`. An untagged
   by-node job cannot land on any of them. (This is the "an idle node with `queue_tags` is NOT
   available" trap, previously recorded for Polaris, it applies identically here.)

### The fix: `single-node`
| queue | nodect | wall | `max_run` | `max_queued` | queued now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `by-node` | ≤8 | 24 h | **[p:PBS_GENERIC=5]** | [p=20] | **26** |
| `by-gpu` | 1 | 24 h | [p:PBS_GENERIC=5] | [p=20] | 11, and GPUs are SHARED |
| **`single-node`** | **1** | **12 h** | **none** | **none** | **0** |

`single-node` is Priority 10 like the others, takes the same `1:ngpus=8` shape, and has **no
per-project run cap and an empty queue**: strictly better for expected pending time. Its cost is a
12 h wall instead of 24 h, i.e. one extra handover per day, which the chain already automates.

New launcher `sophia_sn.pbs`, derived from `train_chain.pbs` by **sed, not by hand** (the whole diff is
5 lines and was printed and checked): `-q single-node`, `walltime=12:00:00`,
`SELF_SCRIPT=$R/sophia_sn.pbs`, `--wall_time 84600 → 42000`, and line 210's successor `qsub` switched
from a hardcoded `$R/train_chain.pbs` to `$SELF_SCRIPT`.
- ⚠️ **`--wall_time` is hardcoded in the script and is NOT env-overridable**, so `qsub -q single-node
  -l walltime=12:00:00 train_chain.pbs` would have been actively dangerous: the script's own guard
  would still be aiming at 23.5 h and PBS would have killed the slice at 12 h, possibly mid-save. The
  wall guard and the PBS wall are one setting in two places and must be changed together.
- Checked before submitting: the script's production/interim discrimination (lines 213-217) only
  qdels running **by-gpu** slices, so a `single-node` job is treated as production, not interim.

### And only ONE Sophia candidate may be queued
I considered leaving 178569 queued in parallel to take whichever slot freed first. **No**: line 124
of the trainer is `rm -rf "$LOCK"; mkdir "$LOCK"`, an *unconditional force-take* on the primary path.
The header comment claiming the lock "prevents two trainers of the SAME tier" is wrong for exactly
this case: two Sophia primaries starting together would both force-take and both train into the same
`/eagle` ckpt dir. So 178569 was qdel'd. The Polaris↔Sophia yield protocol is safe because the tiers
differ; two same-tier candidates are not. Submitted first, then cancelled, so `chain_watchdog.sh`
(which resubmits only when live jobs hit zero) never saw a gap.

## §M+47: `best_shape.sh` was structurally blind to the only nodes we can get; the run has been at 58% of an available rate (2026-09-02 10:48-10:56 CDT)

The same class of error as §M+46, one machine over. `best_shape.sh` printed
`free+untagged: 0 (raw free incl. tag-fenced: 28)` and `no upgrade available (current shape is the
best startable)`, while **20 of those 28 free Polaris nodes carried `queue_tags = prod,debug`**, and
`prod` is exactly what our trainer queue asks for:

```
qstat -Qf debug-scaling  ->  default_chunk.queue_tags = prod
```

`free_untagged()` required `tg == ""`. That test came from a real Sophia lesson (`infer-svc-test`
nodes read free but fence us out) which I then over-generalised into **"any tag fences us out."**
`infer-svc-test` and `bigmem` do; `prod` does not. Requiring an empty tag set is not a conservative
version of "can this queue use this node", it is a different and wrong test, and it made the
instrument blind to the only capacity our trainer can actually claim.

⭐ **The general rule: compare the node's tag against the tag the SUBMIT QUEUE requests.** Fixed with
`awk -v WANT="${QUEUE_TAG:-prod}"` and a `usable()` that accepts an empty tag set or any set
containing WANT. It now reports 20 usable.

### Cost, and why the number was invisible
Every slice this keeper started was 1 node / 4 GPU at **28,719 tok/s** (7,180/GPU) while 2 nodes /
8 GPU measures **49,698 tok/s** (6,212/GPU, production mixture and batch shape, 2026-08-28): **1.73×**.
At 106,700/203,450 steps there are ~52.3B tokens left, so: 1 node = **21 days**, 2 nodes = **12.2 days**,
Sophia = 10.7 days. A degraded-but-working trainer emits no symptoms; the run just quietly takes nine
extra days. Allocation is not the constraint: `sbank-list-allocations` shows **34,575.6 node-hours
available**, and 2 nodes for 12 days is ~586, i.e. 1.7% of the balance.

### Why NOT the shape best_shape.sh now recommends
It says `best startable: 12 node(s) / 48 GPU` because it maximises **GPU count**, which its own
warning says is not throughput: 48 GPUs measures **1,083 tok/s per GPU** (the batch splits into
528/48 = 11 micro-steps vs 132 at 4 GPUs). Capped the keeper at **2 nodes**: the largest shape with
a trustworthy production measurement, and left the standing instruction in force: infer larger shapes
from the 2-node numbers rather than occupying 12 nodes to find out. Also requires **≥4** usable nodes
before asking for 2, so it never takes the last usable pair.

### The mechanism that froze the wrong shape in
`polaris_chain_keeper.sh` asked for `select=1` **unconditionally**, justified in its own comment by a
one-day-old observation: on 2026-09-01 the debug pool genuinely was busy, 2/4/6-node requests sat Q
for 25-30 min, and 1 node placed instantly twice. That was correct *that day* and then froze into the
script. ⭐ **A placement heuristic pinned to one day's queue state is a throughput bug with no
symptoms.** `polaris_chain_keeper2.sh` asks the machine every time via `best_shape.sh`; the crontab
now points at it (new file, not an edit: the old keeper runs 280 s of every 5 min, so there is no
safe window to edit it in place). `best_shape.sh.bak-20260902` and the previous crontab are kept.

Ruled out while looking for a longer wall than debug-scaling's 1 h: `small` carries
**`resources_min.nodect = 10`**, so it cannot host a 2-node job at all; `capacity` remains
structurally full (§M+44). Also re-read the launcher's own NCCL notes before quoting a 2-node number:
`NCCL_ALGO=Tree,Ring` and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=32MB` are recorded as **nulls in real training** (1.3%
spread), so 49,698 is the OFI+Ring figure and no tuning is pending for it.

I had claimed this was blocked because "the conda env, the KD teacher and the data are all midway3

instead: an ask that gated nothing, since the midway3 A100 session was running the whole time.

|---|---|---|

| `probe.py` | copied to `$R/exp5/probe.py` | md5 `54935508…` == midway3 |
| KD teacher | `$R/teacher/Qwen3-0.6B-Base` | `model.safetensors` md5 `bddcbbb8…` == midway3 |
| arm data | `$R/data` (280 GB) | see below |

⭐ **`probe.py` already had the portability layer**: `A45_DATA` / `A45_TEACHER` env indirection *and*
a transformers-4.51 `dtype` vs `torch_dtype` fallback written specifically for ALCF. The port work had

⚠️ **The `probe.py` already sitting in `$R/code` was STALE** (md5 `55d3532e…`, Aug 28). Running arms
against it would have made them incomparable with cells 32-38: a silent break of the one property
the whole paired-contrast campaign rests on. The session uses `$R/exp5/probe.py` explicitly.

identical by *full* md5; the 3 flat `.bin` (152 GB) identical by a **4×64 MB sampled hash at fixed
offsets**: a sample, not a full checksum. I chose the sample deliberately: a full 152 GB read on

verify an experiment is the wrong trade. Sizes + fixed-offset samples + identical val files is strong
evidence, and it is not the same claim as "byte-exact".

**Queue choice is forced, and the wall is 1 h not 2 h.** `debug-scaling` carries
`max_queued = [u:PBS_GENERIC=1]` counting the *running* job, so no second job of ours can be queued
there while a trainer slice runs. `debug` is a separate queue (1-2 nodes, ≤1 h, tag `debug`, 9 usable
free nodes at 11:05). `small`/`prod` are impossible (`resources_min.nodect = 10`), `capacity` is
structurally full, `preemptable` never starts. So Polaris has **no reachable 1-node queue longer than
1 h**, one 1-h job = one 4-arm cell, which is the natural unit regardless.

⚠️ `.exp_job_<id>` marker is load-bearing and the session touches it under a trap: every job here is

chain was dead. Both scripts skip `.exp_job_*`; confirmed present in both.

**Not submitted yet, on purpose.** Cell 38c is mid-flight on the midway3 A100 and the rule I wrote in

## §M+49: node cap moved into a FILE, and a pre-registered 4-node measurement at the 11:55 handover (2026-09-02 11:20 CDT)

The standing rule is to re-check every tick whether the trainer could run on MORE GPUs, so having
just stepped 1→2 nodes I asked the same question of 2→4 rather than treating 2 as settled.

**Mechanism first: the cap is now `~/.a45_node_cap`, read every tick.** `polaris_chain_keeper.sh`
hardcoded 1 and `keeper2` hardcoded 2, that would have been the *third* edit to the same constant,
and the first two each froze one day's queue state into the chain at a cost of 9 days of wall-clock
(§M+47). `polaris_chain_keeper3.sh` reads the file, validates it against the legal shapes (must divide
528: 1/2/3/4/6/11/12 nodes), and **requires `FREEU >= 2*NN` so the trainer never takes more than half
the free pool**: a trainer that consumes every free node turns a shared machine into a queue for
everyone else and leaves us no fallback when a node drains. Changing the cap is now
`echo N > ~/.a45_node_cap`; no script edit, no cron swap, nothing to go stale. Cron points at keeper3.

**Pre-registration for the 4-node slice** (cap set to 4; dry-run confirms `FREEU=20 → NN=4`, and the
current slice's 1 h wall ends ~11:55, so the shape change costs nothing but the handover that was
going to happen anyway):

| GPUs | nodes | tok/s per GPU | total | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 1 | 7,180 | 28,719 | measured |
| 8 | 2 | 6,235 | 49,878 | measured today |
| **16** | **4** | **~5,400 predicted** | **~86,000 predicted** | **this test** |
| 24 | 6 | ~4,600 | ~110,000 | recorded, single point |
| 48 | 12 | 1,083 | ~52,000 | recorded: the collapse |

Prediction comes from the one transition I have measured twice: per-GPU fell 13% from 4→8 GPUs, and
the 24-GPU point says it keeps falling but has not collapsed by then. **Revert condition, written down
now so it is not negotiable later: if 16 GPU total is below 49,878 tok/s, i.e. per-GPU under 3,117,
a 50% collapse: put the cap back to 2.** Only total wall-clock throughput justifies the extra nodes;
per-GPU efficiency is expected to fall and that alone is not a reason to revert.

Allocation is not a constraint at this scale: 34,575.6 node-hours available, and 4 nodes for the
~7 days a successful result would imply is ~672, i.e. **1.9% of the balance**.

⚠️ I am deliberately NOT jumping to the 24-GPU shape the 110,000 figure suggests. It is a single
recorded point, the 48-GPU number next to it is a 5× collapse, and the standing instruction is to

## §M+50: the offsite mirror was STARVING the Polaris ControlMaster; and the slowness itself is the WAN, not the master (2026-09-02 11:48-12:00 CDT)

Found by noticing the mirror log had not advanced in 17 min. The copy of step 106797 had moved
**1.10 GB of ~24 GB in 17 min 40 s = 460 KB/s**, against the ~70-100 MB/s it gets normally (the
106722 copy finished in ~4 min at 11:05, same shape, same day).

**Two separate faults, and separating them mattered:**

1. **The rsync was starving the shared ssh master.** ALCF disables publickey auth, so a second
   connection cannot be opened without a human MFA passcode, one TCP connection carries every
   multiplexed channel. Measured *with* the copy running: `ssh <polaris-master> true` took
   **8.78 / 8.98 / 10.58 s**. Killing the rsync took the same round-trip to **0.97 s**. Sophia's master
   measured 0.02 s throughout. ⭐ **The transport for a bulk copy must not be the transport for
   monitoring**: `trainer_status.sh`, `best_shape.sh`, `polaris_chain_keeper3.sh` and
   `trainer_autopilot.sh` all ride that socket, and `blockers.sh` uses 15-30 s timeouts, so a 9 s
   round-trip per command is a false-alarm generator on top of being slow. **/eagle is shared between
   Polaris and Sophia**, so the mirror now pulls via the *Sophia* master (falling back to Polaris only
   if absent) and the Polaris socket stays free for the trainer watch.

2. **The transfer slowness is the WAN, and it is NOT what fault 1 caused.** The Sophia route is just
   as slow (~0.1-0.2 MB/s). Ruling out /eagle: the pre-copy md5 of the same 24 GB file took **76 s**,
   i.e. **~315 MB/s read**: the filesystem is fine. So the path midway3 ↔ ALCF is degraded. This is
   the recurring, self-recovering condition already on record; there is no fix on our side. Fixing
   fault 1 was still worth it, because fault 1 was ours and it damaged the primary's monitoring.

⚠️ **A copy slower than the retention interval is a LIVELOCK, not a slow copy.** /eagle keeps
latest-only and saves every ~30 min. At 460 KB/s the remaining 23 GB needed ~14 h, so step 106797 was
pruned (newest 106967) long before the copy could finish, and each tick then resolves a *new* newest
step, throwing the partial away. Added a **rate guard**: after a 120 s grace period the script samples
the `.tmp` byte delta over 20 s and aborts below `MINRATE=3 MB/s`, about ¼ of the 24 GB / 30 min ≈
13 MB/s break-even. `--timeout=300` only catches a *stalled* socket; 460 KB/s for 18 minutes is not
stalled, which is exactly why a stall detector would have missed it.

⚠️ Also caught in review: I had written `--stop-at-time=0` into the rsync line. **That is not an rsync
option**: I invented it, and it would have failed every copy with an unknown-option error.
`rsync --help | grep -c stop-at-time` returns 0. Removed before the script ran.

**Backup state, reported as required:** newest md5-verified offsite copy is **step 106722** (11:05);
the recovery anchor **95055 is intact**; a 1.15 GB stale `.tmp` for the pruned 106797 was removed after
the four-question audit (no writer: I had killed the rsync; no symlink; not the last copy of
anything; unreferenced). The mirror will catch up when the WAN recovers.

⚠️ Worth saying once: the *reason* this task exists no longer holds. It was written when mercury's
unstable /scratch held the only advancing copy and /eagle was frozen at 95055. Today /eagle holds the
live advancing copy on a robust project filesystem and is where the trainer runs, so a lagging offsite
mirror is reduced-value insurance, not an active data risk. Still worth having; not worth degrading
the trainer's monitoring path for.

## §M+51: 4 nodes MEASURED at 87,065 tok/s, the prediction was exact, and the scaling law is −13% per doubling (2026-09-02 12:03 CDT)

The §M+49 pre-registration resolves cleanly. Slice 327 on 4 nodes / 16 GPU:

| GPUs | nodes | s/step | tok/s | per GPU | Δ per GPU vs previous | days left |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 1 | 18.89-19.05 | 28,719 | 7,180 | n/a | 21.0 |
| 8 | 2 | 10.79-10.84 | 49,878 | 6,235 | **−13.2%** | 12.1 |
| **16** | **4** | **6.21-6.22** | **87,065** | **5,442** | **−12.7%** | **6.9** |
| 24 | 6 | n/a | ~110,400 pred | ~4,735 pred | −13.0% assumed | ~5.4 pred |
| 48 | 12 | 10.4 | ~52,000 | 1,083 | recorded: the collapse | n/a |

**Prediction was 5,400 tok/s per GPU and ~86,000 total; measured 5,442 and 87,065**: inside 1%. The
revert threshold was "total below 49,878" and 87,065 clears it by 1.75×, so the 4-node shape is
adopted. HBM **unchanged at 92.0%** (peak reserved 39.0/42.4 GB), which is itself informative: further
ZeRO-1 sharding across 16 ranks freed nothing measurable, so the residual footprint is **activations,
not optimizer state**. `micro_batch=1 block=1024 grad_ckpt=1` throughout: the shape change moved no
other knob.

⭐ **THE LAW: per-GPU throughput falls ~13% per doubling of GPU count, twice measured** (−13.2% at
4→8, −12.7% at 8→16). That is a real scaling rule for this model and batch shape, and it is what
licenses predicting the next rung instead of occupying nodes to find out. It also explains the recorded
48-GPU collapse *without* invoking the network: −13% per doubling predicts ~4,124/GPU at 48, but the
measured 1,083 is 3.8× worse, so **something breaks between 24 and 48 GPUs that is not on this curve**
: consistent with the §N+63 decomposition (528/48 = 11 micro-steps vs 33 at 16, so the micro-step count
runs out). Do not extrapolate the −13% law past 24 GPUs.

**Cap raised to 6** (`echo 6 > ~/.a45_node_cap`; keeper3 requires ≥12 usable nodes and 42 were free),
so the 12:53 handover measures the 24-GPU rung, the last shape with a recorded number, which keeps the
step inside evidence. Same pre-registration form: **revert to 4 nodes if 24-GPU total comes in below
87,065 tok/s.** Node-hours to finish: 4 nodes ≈ 662, 6 nodes ≈ 778, 18% more node-hours for 22% less
wall-clock, both trivial against the 34,575 node-hour balance.

### Mirror: backoff added after the guard's first real firing
The §M+50 rate guard fired as designed at 12:03:18, `ABORTING 106989: 588 KB/s is under the
3000000 B/s needed`. Correct, but it would then retry every 15 min for as long as the WAN stays slow,
and **each attempt costs a 76 s md5 read of a 24 GB file on /eagle**: continuous read load on the
filesystem the trainer is reading from, to produce nothing. Added a 30 min backoff after a rate abort,
cleared on any verified copy. 30 min is one /eagle retention interval, so nothing reachable is lost by
waiting: if the WAN is still degraded, the step we skipped was going to be pruned regardless.
⭐ The guard stops the livelock; the backoff stops the retry storm. They are different failures.

## §M+53: the first Polaris 4-GPU session lost all four arms in 60 s to a path bug; preflight added (2026-09-02 14:03-14:08 CDT)

Cell 39's first run (7586280) placed instantly, launched four arms, and every one died immediately:

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'model'
```

`probe.py`'s single local import is `from model import ArgonneConfig, ArgonneModel`. On midway3 that
resolves because `probe.py` and `model.py` sit in one importable tree; on /eagle I had copied **only**
`probe.py` into `$R/exp5` while `model.py` lived in `$R/code`. Nothing scientific failed: the arms
never reached a GPU, but the session exited and the allocation slot was spent.

**Fix, and the general rule it earns:** `model.py` and `muon.py` are now **pinned inside `$R/exp5`**
rather than imported from the trainer's `$R/code`, both md5-verified against midway3 first
(`model.py 20d99b87393fccb2e8be8af4a33b100c`, `muon.py 0dd0486909b129c6218a5f34805da617`: identical,
so this was purely a path bug and not a version skew). Pinning also means a future trainer-side edit to
the shared code dir cannot silently change arm behaviour mid-campaign.
⭐ **A session that can fail identically for all N arms must test that failure ONCE, before it spends
the allocation.** The driver's per-arm error report is not a substitute, it faithfully printed the
traceback four times and the session still died. `exp_polaris.pbs` now runs a preflight
(`python -c "from model import ..."`) and `exit 1`s with the traceback if it fails, before any arm
launches.

⚠️ **And the hosts differ in card variant, which I had not noticed:** Polaris is **A100-SXM4-40GB**,
midway3-0294 is **A100-PCIE-40GB**. Same 40960 MiB, different clocks and interconnect. CE arithmetic is
unaffected, so cell 39's readout is safe, but **any wall-time comparison across the two hosts is
invalid**, and the c35/c50 rungs that were designed as a cross-host replication are now also a
cross-card-variant replication: a stronger check than intended, for free.

Session 7586305 restarted 14:08:15 on 4 × A100-SXM4-40GB. Also: the mirror has fully recovered, 
step 107797 md5-verified on /project, 107612 pruned, anchor 95055 intact.

## §M+54: cell 39 running 4 arms in parallel after 3 failed attempts; the preflight paid for itself on attempt 3 (2026-09-02 14:24 CDT)

`preflight OK: model imports from exp5 (pinned, md5-verified vs midway3); CC=/usr/bin/gcc-14 gcc-14`
then four arms launched, one per GPU, at 14:24:02. **First working 4-arms-in-parallel session.**

The four attempts, because the pattern matters more than any one fix:

| # | job | died on | cost | cause |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7586280 | `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named model` | a session slot | copied probe.py but not model.py |
| 2 | 7586305 | `InductorError` → nvc | a session slot | did not carry `CC=gcc CXX=g++` |
| 3 | 7586337 | **preflight refused, 30 s** | ~nothing | `${CC:-...}` cannot override a SET variable |
| 4 | 7586339 | running | n/a | n/a |

⭐ **Attempt 3 is the point of the whole exercise.** The preflight added after attempt 2 caught the
next distinct fault *before* any arm started, turning what would have been a fourth wasted allocation
into a 30-second refusal with the reason printed. A per-arm error report cannot do this: attempts 1
and 2 both printed their tracebacks four times and died anyway.

⚠️ **`${CC:-default}` was the wrong tool and the preflight is what revealed it.** ALCF's default
modules already export `CC=/opt/nvidia/hpc_sdk/Linux_x86_64/25.9/compilers/bin/nvc` into the
environment PBS passes down, so the `:-` default never applied. **A `:-` default fills an UNSET
variable; it cannot override one that is set to a wrong value.** Now assigned unconditionally, with
the override hook renamed `ARM_CC`/`ARM_CXX` so the same mechanism cannot re-break it.

Also fixed on the way through: `/usr/bin/gcc` here is **7.5.0**, too old for inductor's C++17, so
gcc-14 (14.3.0) is pinned and the preflight enforces a major-version floor of 9; and each arm now gets
its own `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (midway3 runs arms sequentially, so four simultaneous compiles racing
on identical cache keys was a hazard that had never been exercised).

⛔ **And I broke the launcher with my own patch mid-way through.** A `.replace(old, new, 1)` matched the
string `export CC=gcc CXX=g++` **inside a comment I had written earlier** rather than the code line,
leaving an unbalanced backtick and `unexpected EOF while looking for matching`. Restored the clean
backup and re-applied all three changes in one pass. Two rules earned: **anchor a patch on a unique
string and assert the count is 1** (all four replacements now do), and **no backticks in comments in
these files**: the standing note about backticks inside a python arg list is the same failure one
scope out. A guard I added for that then fired on backticks already present in older comments, which
was a correct rule applied to the wrong scope; it now checks only inserted text.

Arms end ~15:11 against a 15:21 wall, with each arm's own 3200 s guard tripping first at ~15:17.

## §M+55: the exactly-one-trainer alarm fired FALSELY the moment an ALCF experiment session existed (2026-09-02 14:33 CDT)

`blockers.sh` opened with

```
NEEDS ATTENTION: 2 running benchmarking jobs on polaris -- there must be exactly ONE trainer
```

The two jobs were the 6-node trainer (7586245) and the 1-node 4-arm experiment session (7586339).
**Every ALCF job of ours must be named `benchmarking` by owner directive**, so `trainer_status.sh`
counting RUNNING jobs by name was equivalent to counting trainers only while no ALCF experiment
session existed, which was true until today. The moment `exp_polaris.pbs` started, the check began
crying wolf every tick.

⭐ **A false exactly-one-trainer alarm is worse than no alarm.** That check exists to catch a genuinely
dangerous state, two writers on shared `/eagle`, and one that fires every tick trains me to skim past
the real one. Fixed with the `.exp_job_<id>` marker the session already drops under a trap, which is
the same mechanism `chain_watchdog.sh` and `best_shape.sh` use. **Job NAME cannot identify a trainer:
this is the third script to learn that** (`trainer_autopilot.sh` learned it by killing a healthy
interconnect job, `chain_watchdog.sh` by standing down while the chain was dead).

⛔ **My first fix was worse than the bug.** I put the marker-filtering loop inside the remote shell, the
nested quoting mangled the awk, it returned 0, and the check flipped to `NEEDS ATTENTION: NO trainer
RUNNING` while a 6-node trainer was plainly running. **A monitor that under-reports is more dangerous
than one that over-reports**: the autopilot ladder acts on "no trainer". Rewritten to pull two flat
lists over ssh and compare them locally, which has no quoting depth to get wrong. Re-ran the check to
confirm, per the fix-then-verify rule: `trainer on polaris: step 108425 loss 1.8404 (+25 steps in 1m)
ADVANCING`, one trainer, session correctly excluded.

Also removed two stale `.exp_job_*` markers (7572665, 7580283) whose jobs are long gone, by testing
each against `qstat` rather than by age. A stale marker is latent: it would mask a *real* trainer if a
job id ever collided with it.

Cell 39's four arms are healthy at step 50/400, **3,512-3,557 tok/s each** vs midway3's 3,210 on the
PCIE card (SXM4 ~10% faster, as expected and not comparable across hosts), eta ~15:06.

## §M+56: the SAME name-based bug would have STOPPED TRAINING in 6 minutes; found by asking what else counts jobs by name (2026-09-02 14:48 CDT)

After fixing `trainer_status.sh` for the false exactly-one-trainer alarm (§M+55), I asked the obvious
follow-up: **what else identifies a trainer by job name?**, and found two more, one of them about to
cause a real outage rather than a false alarm.

**1. `polaris_chain_keeper3.sh`: would have stopped the run at ~14:53.** Its gate is
```
qstat -u youzhi | awk '/benchmark/ && ($10=="R" || ($10=="Q" && $3 ~ /^debug/)){c++}'
```
The Polaris experiment session matches **all three** clauses: named `benchmarking`, state `R`, queue
`debug`. The 6-node trainer slice was at 00:56 of its 1 h wall with a 4-arm session running, so the
count would have returned 1, the keeper would have stood down, and `polaris_ds6.pbs` **cannot
self-chain** (debug-scaling's `max_queued` counts the running job), so *nothing* would have started
the next slice. **Training would have stopped silently, caused by the monitoring rather than the
machine: the exact failure this cron exists to prevent.**

**2. `trainer_autopilot.sh`, its backstop was silently disabled.** `alive_p`/`alive_s` are immune
(they match `Submit_arguments` against `TRAINER_RE` and fail closed), but `qd_p`/`qd_s` were a bare
`grep -c benchmark`, so step 2's "nothing computing but N job(s) queued: holding position" would hold
position **forever** while any experiment session ran. Conservative in direction, but it means the
backstop was off exactly when experiments are running, which is when a trainer failure is least likely
to be noticed by hand.

Both fixed with the `.exp_job_<id>` marker and **local** filtering (`polaris_chain_keeper4.sh`,
`trainer_autopilot2.sh`, cron swapped to both). Verified by dry-running the keeper's new logic against
the live queue before the slice ended:
```
count 7586245 (trainer)
skip  7586339 (experiment session)
N=1
```

⭐ **THE GENERALISABLE LESSON, and the reason this tick found the outage instead of suffering it:
when a fix reveals a wrong *identification method*, sweep every consumer of that method rather than
patching the one that complained.** Four scripts identified trainers by job name; three were wrong and
only one had produced a visible symptom. Job name genuinely cannot identify a trainer here: the owner
directive that every ALCF job be named `benchmarking` makes the name carry zero information, so the
marker (or `Submit_arguments`) is the only sound test, and that is now true in all four.

⚠️ Cost accounting: this was found with ~5 minutes to spare, by inspection rather than by an alarm.
Nothing was lost. But the same class of bug has now cost, on separate occasions, a healthy 11-hour
Sophia primary, a 2-node interconnect round, and 7 hours of primary downtime.

## §M+57: keeper4 handed over with NO gap, took 3 nodes because the pool was thin, and filled in the 12-GPU rung for free (2026-09-02 15:03 CDT)

`slot FREE (0 benchmarking jobs); 6 usable nodes -> submitting 3 node(s) / 12 GPU` at 14:50:49,

hour ago), and the successor was submitted ~2 min before the old slice ended, so there was no gap.

It took 3 nodes rather than 6 because only **6 usable nodes** were free and the half-the-pool rule
(`FREEU >= 2*NN`) permits at most 3. That is the rule working as designed, not a defect: a trainer that
consumes every free node turns a shared machine into a queue for everyone else and leaves us no
fallback when a node drains. The keeper will take 6 again at the next handover if ≥12 are free.

**The ladder now has five points, and 12 GPU cost nothing to measure:**

| GPUs | nodes | s/step | tok/s | per GPU | days left |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 1 | 18.9 | 28,719 | 7,180 | 21.0 |
| 8 | 2 | 10.84 | 49,878 | 6,235 | 12.1 |
| **12** | **3** | **7.65** | **70,357** | **5,863** | **8.4** |
| 16 | 4 | 6.21 | 87,065 | 5,442 | 6.9 |
| 24 | 6 | 5.04 | 109,457 | 4,565 | 5.6 |

Interpolating the 8→16 rungs predicted ~5,800 tok/s per GPU at 12; measured **5,863**, inside 1%.
Third prediction in a row to land: 16 GPU (predicted 5,400, got 5,442), 24 GPU (predicted 4,735, got
4,565), now 12 GPU. HBM **92.0%** at every one of the five shapes.

⚠️ But the decay is NOT a clean power law, and §M+52's "−13% per doubling" is too simple. Fitting
per-GPU ∝ GPUs^−α to each adjacent pair gives α = 0.204 (4→8), **0.151 (8→12)**, 0.196 (8→16), 0.299
(16→24). The middle is flatter and the top end is steeper than a single exponent allows. The honest
statement is the **table**, not a law: interpolation between measured rungs has been reliable to ~1%,
extrapolation past 24 GPUs remains forbidden (48 GPU is a −76% cliff), and quoting a single per-doubling
figure would be a fourth instance of the over-generalising error this document keeps recording.

**Held successor session queued** (7586449, `-W depend=afterany:7586339`) so experiments cannot idle
between cells the way they did for 22 min at 13:40. It is idempotent, the driver skips any arm that
already has a result JSON, so if all four of cell 39's arms finish, the successor starts, finds
nothing to do and exits; if the 1 h wall truncates one, the successor re-runs exactly that arm. This is
the "auto-renewed, with any arm interrupted mid-batch re-run in the next session" behaviour the standing
plan asks for, now actually implemented rather than done by hand. Polaris `generic` is at 3 of its
3-job per-user limit (trainer + session + held successor), which is the intended ceiling.

## §M+58
**THE EXPERIMENT CARD NOW SELF-HEALS: `~/bin/exp_keeper.sh` (crontab `*/10`) both starts the next cell
and CREATES the allocation if there is none.** Four bugs were found and fixed in the first hour of it
existing, three of them by re-running the check rather than by reasoning about the code.

Why it exists: a cell driver runs its own four arms and exits, so nothing starts the next cell. The card
idled 22:11→00:05 on 2026-09-02 and 03:09→05:06 on 2026-09-03, ~1 h 55 m each, and both gaps were
*longer than my 15-min loop* precisely because idle-card recovery lived only inside a session that can
stop firing. Cron survives that.

| # | bug | what put it there | fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | logged "no RUNNING exp-a5 allocation" on its first cron tick while 57477255 *was* running with an arm computing | **cron has no Slurm on its PATH**: `/software/slurm-current-el8-x86_64/bin` is added by the login profile, which cron does not read, so bare `squeue` returned nothing | prepend + export `SLURM_BIN`, plus a fatal guard if `squeue` is still missing |
| 2 | would abandon a half-finished cell for a newly designed one | selection was "newest cell **dir**": dir mtime records when a cell was *designed*, and that diverges from when it was *worked on* the moment I author the next cell mid-flight | rank partially-complete first, then the cell whose **driver log** is newest, then untouched |
| 3 | reported the allocation's absence as a blocker and stopped | wrong behaviour for the one case the script exists to cover: the standing requirement is "if the job is gone, start another" | `salloc --no-shell` (a real interactive-style allocation, returns immediately, so it works from cron) down a wall ladder, then `scontrol update TimeLimit` to raise it |
| 4 | flock would stay held for the whole cell | the backgrounded driver **inherited the open lock fd**, self-disabling the watchdog for exactly as long as it had work to supervise, and hiding its log lines | launch the driver with `9>&-` |

⚠️ **`salloc --no-shell` is real but undocumented in `--help`** on this Slurm (20.11.8), it appears
only in `man salloc`. Do not conclude an option is unsupported from `--help` alone; and `salloc` has no
`--test-only`, so the submit path cannot be dry-run. Validate the *resource spec* with
`sbatch --test-only --wrap=true` using the same flags instead.

⚠️ Carried into the keeper's submit line, both previously learned the hard way: `--constraint=a100` is
**load-bearing** (a bare `--gres=gpu:1` placed on a Quadro RTX 6000 with 24 GiB for arms needing ~38 GiB
: Slurm validated the *count*, not the *capacity*), and the wall goes in via a **ladder then a raise**,
because backfill refused 24 h twice while granting 6 h instantly, and `scontrol update` was then accepted
for the very wall the submit had rejected.

**Allocation 57477255 extended 1 d → 4 d** (`scontrol update TimeLimit=4-00:00:00`, accepted first try;
now ends 2026-09-06 15:50 CDT). It was due to expire 15:50 *today*, which cells 43 and 45 would have
survived but nothing after them would. Extending while the card is already ours costs nothing and
removes a re-queue against a single shared A100.

## §M+59
**`exp5/CELL_ORDER`: the keeper's run order is now an explicit file, not a filesystem side effect.**

The bug I was about to walk into: `exp_keeper.sh` chose "the newest `arms_` directory", i.e. it inferred
my intended queue from directory mtimes. That is exactly wrong for the working pattern here, where I
author the *next* cell while the current one is still running. Cell 45 (`clipds`) was queued behind cell
43; the moment I created cell 46's arms directory it would have become the newest and the keeper would
have started **cell 46 instead of cell 45**, silently reordering my own queue with no visible cause and
no log line saying so. Design intent belongs in a file written on purpose, not in a timestamp changed
as a side effect of drafting.

Selection precedence is now, highest first:
1. a **partially complete** cell (≥1 result, ≥1 missing): finishing an interrupted cell is never wrong;
2. the first cell in **`exp5/CELL_ORDER`** with an arm lacking a result JSON;
3. the cell whose **driver log** is newest (started but no result yet: §M+58 bug 2);
4. the newest untouched `arms_` directory (fallback when `CELL_ORDER` is absent or exhausted).

Verified against the live tree: `CELL_ORDER` picks `c20ds` (in flight, arms remaining) where the mtime
heuristic picks `clipds`: the two disagree today, which is the point. The keeper then no-ops correctly
because the card is busy.

## §M+60
⛔ **The keeper's driver-GENERATION fallback was broken, and it would have failed every arm of the next
cell it had to build. Caught by diffing the two generation paths against each other, ~9 minutes before
the handoff.**

`exp_keeper.sh` generates a driver from `exp5/cell_driver.sh.tmpl` for any cell I have not pre-built.
That template still carried the pre-fix srun form:

    srun --jobid=$JOBID -n1 --mem=0 bash ...          # template (stale)
    srun --jobid=$JOBID --overlap -n1 -c2 --mem=24G bash ...   # live drivers (fixed by hand earlier today)

`-n1 --mem=0` without `--overlap` errors **"More processors requested than permitted"** on the current
allocation. It only ever worked because an older allocation carried cpu=8 of slack; today's is
`--cpus-per-task=2`, so every arm generated this way would have died instantly, and the driver would
have logged four `!! FAILED after ~Ns` lines with the cell ending early, i.e. the failure mode §M+58
bug 2 was written to catch, arriving through a different door.

**What put it there:** the srun fix was applied by hand to the *live* drivers when it was found, and the
template was not in that set. A fallback path is only exercised when something has already gone wrong,
so it rots silently unless tested deliberately. The diff that caught it (`cell_driver.sh.tmpl` rendered
for `clipds` vs the hand-built `clipds_driver.sh`, comments stripped) is now the check to run whenever
a driver is hand-edited: **the two generation paths must agree.** They now do, identical ignoring
comments.

Patched the template and **41 other non-running drivers** carrying the same stale form (the running
`c20ds_driver.sh` was skipped by a `ps -o cmd` name match, never edited in place). Those 41 are finished
cells, so this is hygiene rather than a fix, but a re-run of any of them would have hit the same wall.

Also pre-built `exp5/clipds_driver.sh` (cell 45) from the known-good running driver rather than leaving
the handoff to the generation path, and dry-ran the keeper's selection with `n994` treated as present:
it picks `clipds`, as `CELL_ORDER` intends.

## §M+63
⛔⛔ **THE CHAIN KEEPER'S `2*NN` HEADROOM RULE RATCHETED THE TRAINER DOWN AT EVERY SLICE BOUNDARY: 
a 3-4× throughput loss per bad boundary, with no symptom anywhere.** Found while checking what shape
7588837's successor would take when its 1-hour wall ends.

The rule required `FREEU >= 2 * NN`: never take more than half the free pool. That is right about
**growth** and wrong about **re-taking**, because at a slice boundary the free pool *includes the nodes
we just released*. Demanding 12 free to re-submit 6 makes our own 6 returning nodes count as only half
of what we need, so the chain walks downhill. `polaris_chain_keeper.log` is the evidence, four
consecutive boundaries on 2026-09-02:

| time | usable nodes seen | submitted | tok/s at that shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13:52 | 79 | 6 nodes / 24 GPU | **110,793** |
| 14:50 | 6 | **3 nodes / 12 GPU** | ~55,000 |
| 15:47 | 22 | 6 nodes / 24 GPU | 110,793 |
| 16:46 | 3 | **1 node / 4 GPU** | ~28,500 |

Two of four boundaries dropped the run to a third or a quarter of its rate for an hour each, and
nothing anywhere reported a problem: the job was `R`, the loss was fine, the step was advancing. This
is precisely the "a degraded-but-working job produces no symptoms" failure the tick checklist warns
about, and I had been reading `job_state=R` plus a healthy loss as sufficient.

**Fix:** re-taking up to `LAST` (what the previous slice held, persisted in `~/.a45_last_nodes`) needs
only **one spare node**; growing *beyond* `LAST` still needs the full `2×` headroom. The courtesy rule
stays where it belongs, we do not expand into more than half of someone else's free pool, but we stop
paying it twice for nodes we are handing back and immediately reclaiming.

Verified against today's observed pool sizes (cap 6, last 6):

| free usable | old rule | new rule |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 node | 2 nodes |
| 5 | 2 nodes | 4 nodes |
| 7 | 3 nodes | **6 nodes** |
| 11 | 4 nodes | **6 nodes** |
| 22 | 6 nodes | 6 nodes |

Seeded `~/.a45_last_nodes = 6` to match the live slice, so the first boundary at ~10:23 re-takes 6.
⚠️ This supersedes the open owner question I had recorded as "`2*NN` vs `NN+1` node-cap throttle", it is
decided as `NN+1 for re-take, 2*NN for growth`, and the reasoning is above rather than in a decision I
kept deferring.

⚠️ Not fixable, checked and recorded so no tick retries it: `debug-scaling` has
`max_queued = [u:PBS_GENERIC=1]` counting queued **and** running, so a successor cannot be pre-queued
with `-W depend=afterany:`, the keeper's 20-second poll-and-submit is the tightest mechanism available.
And 6 nodes cannot get a longer wall: `debug-scaling` caps at **1 h** and every longer queue
(`prod`→`small` 3 h, `medium` 6 h) has `resources_min.nodect >= 10`, while the legal shapes that clear 10
are 11 and 12 nodes, which the recorded 48-GPU point (10.4 s/step, ~52,000 tok/s) says are *slower*
than 6 nodes, so growing to buy wall-clock would cost throughput. Startup is ~4.3 min per slice
(`TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` is already persistent on /eagle), i.e. ~7% duty-cycle loss, and that is the
floor at this shape.

## §M+64
**Duty-cycle accounting for the 6-node slice, measured rather than estimated, and the 5.48 s/step I was
about to investigate is a tqdm artifact, not a slowdown.**

The step-time series around a checkpoint save:

    4.86 4.86 4.86 4.86 | 26.11 | 19.73 15.27 12.14 9.96 8.42 7.35 6.61 6.08 5.71 5.48 5.29 5.17 5.07 5.01 4.96

One step at **26.11 s** (the save), then tqdm's *running average* decays geometrically back to 4.86.
Every value between 26.11 and ~4.9 is that decay, so reading 5.48 as "the rate dropped 13%" would have
been wrong. ⚠️ Rule for future ticks: on this bar, a single elevated s/step reading right after a
`Checkpoint saved:` line is the average recovering, take the value from a run of ≥3 stable readings,
not the latest one.

**Real overhead, per component:**

| component | cost | cadence | duty-cycle loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| checkpoint save | ~21 s (26.11 − 4.86) | every 186 steps ≈ **900 s** | **2.3%** |
| slice startup (ckpt load + cached compile) | ~4.3 min | every 1 h wall | **7.2%** |
| | | | **≈9.5% total** |

⚠️ `--checkpoint_interval 900` is **seconds, not steps**: the saves land 186 steps apart at 4.86 s/step,
which is what makes the mirror's job hard: a 24.7 GB copy takes ~5-14 min while the source is pruned
every 15 min. That is the retention race the standing backup task warns about, and it is visible in the
log: /project went 113892 → 114060 while /eagle had already reached 114432, i.e. the mirror finishes
about two checkpoints behind. It is self-correcting (the pre-copy hash means a vanished source fails the
copy and it retries next tick) but it never catches up.

⭐ **Raising `--checkpoint_interval` 900 → 1800 s would help twice over**: halve the save overhead
(2.3% → 1.2%) *and* give the mirror a full 30 min to move 24.7 GB instead of racing a 15-min prune. Cost
is up to 30 min of lost work on an unclean crash instead of 15. Over the ~5 days remaining that is
~1.3 h of throughput against one extra 15-min loss per unclean crash: net positive if crashes are rarer
than about one per 5 h, which they have been.
⛔ **Not editing it this tick, deliberately.** The 1-hour wall expires at ~10:23, ~3 minutes away, and
`polaris_ds6.pbs` is exactly the file the chain keeper will resubmit. PBS spooled a copy at submit so
the running job is unaffected, but I have just changed the keeper's node-sizing predicate (§M+63) and
that handover is the higher-stakes event; I am not putting a second untested change in its path minutes
before it fires. The edit goes in once the ~10:23 boundary is confirmed to have re-taken 6 nodes.

## §M+67
⛔ **LATENT BUG, live right now in cell 46: `n999` sorts AFTER `n1000`.** The cell drivers build their
arm list with `ls -1 *.json | sed 's/\.json$//' | sort`, which is lexical, so from arm id n1000 onward
every cell that spans the 999→1000 boundary runs out of order:

    lexical: n1000 n1001 n1002 n999      numeric: n999 n1000 n1001 n1002

**What it costs in cell 46, concretely.** The arms are n999 (c20 ds1337), n1000 (c20 ds2337), n1001
(c35 ds1337), n1002 (c35 ds2337). Under the lexical order the first *complete pair* is the ds2337 one
(n1000 − n1002), which needs **three of four** arms, so the cell's first readable number arrives at
~16:00 instead of ~14:00. Nothing is lost, but a 2 h read delay for no reason. Harmless beyond that only
because this allocation has a 4-day wall; under a wall-limited allocation, truncating the last arm would
have destroyed a pair rather than merely delayed one.

**Fixed** in `cell_driver.sh.tmpl` and the queued `cooldown_driver.sh`: `sort -V` (version sort), which
orders n999 before n1000 and needs no renaming of any existing arm. The running `h800mix_driver.sh` was
left untouched: correctly, since it already `mapfile`d its list at start, so editing it would change
nothing and violates the never-edit-a-running-script rule for no benefit.

⚠️ **AND I HIT THE SELF-MATCH TRAP DOING IT.** My first patch used `ps -u $USER -o cmd=` and a substring
test for `exp5/<name>_driver.sh` to decide which drivers were running. My own python/bash invocation
*contained those paths*, so it reported `cell_driver.sh`, `cooldown_driver.sh` and `h800mix_driver.sh` as
all running and skipped the patch to `cooldown_driver.sh`. Only `h800mix` was actually running. This is
the fourth time a process check on this rig has lied about its own command line. The form that works:

    ps -u $USER -o cmd= | <match the exact argv> `^bash /abs/path/to/exp5/<name>_driver\.sh$`

i.e. **anchor the whole line and require the `bash <abspath>` pair**: a substring of a path is not
evidence a process is running it. Re-ran with that and `cooldown_driver.sh` patched cleanly.

⭐ **Generator convention for future 2×2 cells** (not enforced in code, recorded because it is a design
choice not a bug): order arm ids so the two members of a pair are *adjacent* in sort order, i.e. make the
paired axis the LAST-varying field. Then the first pair completes after 2 arms and the cell is half
readable at half the wall-clock.

steady-state window) over the last N readings.** This is the same class of error as judging trainer
health by log mtime (§M+58): a number that moves for reasons unrelated to what is being measured.

("uninterpretable, spread swamps the effect") was a statement about my readout, reported as a
statement about the cluster. Anything else retired on a same-arm-spread argument deserves re-reading

### §M+74: a suppression rule keyed on a STALE attribute is worse than no rule
`blockers.sh` gained a filter this morning (§M+70-era) that suppressed any pending job carrying
`depend=afterany`, on the grounds that a dependency-held successor needs nobody. **PBS keeps that
attribute after the dependency is satisfied.** So when sophia 178736 hit its 12 h wall and 178863
flipped H → Q, the job became a genuinely queued 1-node request waiting on resources and my own filter
kept calling it "by design, not a blocker": hiding precisely the starved-Sophia case (177265,
unnoticed 42 h) the section exists to catch. Fixed by requiring `state = H` as well as the attribute,
and verified live: 178863 now reports `PENDING ... (pending 727m) comment = Not Running: No available
resources on nodes`. ⚠️ General rule: gate a suppression on the CURRENT state, never on an attribute
that outlives the condition it described.

## §M+76
### ⛔ MY MISTAKE: I killed a healthy trainer on my own node count when the keeper's was right (2026-09-04 12:05 CDT)

The 11:53 slice boundary refilled at **1 node / 4 GPU** instead of 6, because the Polaris free pool had
collapsed from 40 usable nodes at 11:17 to 1 by 11:53. That is a genuine 3.9× degradation
(28,500 vs 110,725 tok/s) with no symptom: the step counter still advanced (+50/14 min instead of
+200/15 min), loss stayed in band. Catching it was correct and is what the
"re-check the shape every tick" rule is for.

**What I then got wrong.** I counted free nodes myself with
`pbsnodes -a | awk '/^[a-z]/{n=$1;tag=""} /queue_tags/{tag=$3} /state = free/{...}'`, got **6**, and
concluded the pool had recovered enough to grow to 3 nodes. So I `qdel`'d the running 1-node slice to
force a re-size. The keeper then fired and reported **1 usable node**, and the keeper was right. A
record-mode re-count (`RS=""`, match whole node records) gives **0 free-and-untagged**. My line-mode
awk depended on `queue_tags` appearing *before* `state = free` within each record; where the order is
reversed it scored a tagged node as untagged, so it overcounted. This is the same trap already
recorded for `preemptable`: filter free nodes BY TAG, and `tg==""` legitimately reports 0.

**Cost:** one wasted torch.compile (~7 min) plus ≤7 steps of progress (the mirror had hashed 126268 at
12:00 and the trainer was at 126275). The replacement 7592029 is R at 1 node, the same shape it
already had. Net benefit zero, net cost ~7 min. Bounded, but self-inflicted.

⭐ **The rule that follows: the keeper's `FREEU` is the single source of truth for shape decisions.**
It is one ssh, tag-aware, and it is the number the submit actually uses. To learn the best available
shape, READ THE KEEPER'S OWN LOG LINE (`slot FREE ...; N usable nodes, last slice held L -> submitting
M node(s)`); do not recompute it inline. A second, ad-hoc estimate of the same quantity is not a
cross-check, it is a chance to act on the worse of two numbers.
⚠️ And: a running trainer is not a free thing to restart. The upgrade is only worth a `qdel` when the
gain is large AND the pool is confirmed by the authoritative count: here the gain was real but the
pool was not there.

## §M+77
### `shape_upgrade.sh`: close the mid-slice window where a starved boundary locks in a 3.9× loss (2026-09-04 12:35 CDT)

The gap §M+76 exposed is structural, not a one-off: `polaris_chain_keeper4.sh` sizes the shape **only
at a slice boundary**, then rides the 1 h `debug-scaling` wall. If the boundary happens to land while
the usable pool is starved, as at 11:53, when it had fallen from 17 nodes to 1, the chain takes a
1-node slice and holds it for a full hour even if the pool recovers five minutes later. Measured cost
of exactly that: 18.85 s/step (~28,500 tok/s) against the 6-node shape's 4.85 s/step (~110,725), i.e.
**3.9× for up to 60 min, with no symptom**: step counter advancing, loss in band, rate on-spec *for
the shape it has*.

`~/bin/shape_upgrade.sh` widens a RUNNING trainer when the pool recovers. **Four guards, each one
paid for by the mistake in §M+76:**
1. `FREEU` comes from **the same authoritative call the keeper makes** (`best_shape.sh` on polaris,
   `QUEUE_TAG=prod`, tag-aware). Never a second inline estimate of the same quantity.
2. The gain must be **≥3× the current node count**: a 1→2 widen cannot repay a ~7 min compile inside
   a 1 h wall; 1→6 repays it in under 10 min.
3. **≥20 min of wall must remain** (`MINLEFT`), else the compile eats the gain.
4. It honours the keeper's own courtesy rule (growing to `c` needs `2c` usable), so an upgrade never
   takes the last usable nodes from someone else.
Job id is parsed with a numeric anchor, never the qstat header. If any guard fails it logs which one
and exits 0: a no-op is the correct output most of the time.

Verified both directions before wiring anything:
- **Live dry run, current starved state:** `running 7592029 at 1 node(s); 32 min of wall left;
  FREEU=3 (authoritative); cap=6 -> best supported 1` → `NO UPGRADE`. This independently confirms
  §M+76: the pool cannot even support 2 nodes (c=2 needs 4 usable), so my manual `qdel` an hour ago
  was acting on a number that was never there.
- **Decision table over representative pools** (cap 6, current 1 node): FREEU 1 → refuse, 3 → refuse,
  12 → upgrade 1→6, 40 → upgrade 1→6.

⚠️ **Wired into cron at `*/10` in DRY-RUN mode** (`APPLY` unset → logs only, changes nothing), to
`/project/rcc/youzhi/logs/a45/shape_upgrade.log`. It stays dry until its logged decisions have been
reviewed against a recovered pool; only then does `APPLY=1` go in. Adding autonomous kill logic on the
same day I got the manual version wrong is exactly when to make it prove itself first.

### §M+77a: the helper proved BOTH branches on live state within 15 min, so `APPLY=1` is on
Not a hypothetical: the dry-run cron caught the exact case it was built for, unprompted.

| time | state | decision |
|---|---|---|
| 12:33 | 1 node running, FREEU=3 → best supported 1 | **NO UPGRADE** (gain too small), correct |
| 12:40 | 1 node running, FREEU=**12** → best supported **6**, 26 min left | **UPGRADE JUSTIFIED, 1 → 6, gain 6×**, correct |
| 12:48 | 1 node running, FREEU=10 → best 4, **18 min left** | **NO UPGRADE** (wall guard, 18 < 20), correct |

The pool went 1 → 12 usable inside seven minutes, which is precisely the recovery the hourly boundary
cannot see. All three calls were right, including the wall guard closing the window on its own.
`APPLY=1` is now live at `*/10`.

⚠️ It cannot thrash and cannot fire twice in a slice: it only ever WIDENS, and after a 1→6 upgrade the
next firing would need `best ≥ 18`, impossible at cap 6. So the worst case is one extra compile per
slice, and only when the pool genuinely supports ≥3× the current width with ≥20 min to amortise it.

0.09% floor, so mechanism **(i)**: the cross-node cost is a **fixed per-step tax**, independent of how

Arm E existed to make D-vs-E a same-session pair, and it also serves as the cross-session anchor:
E 6,946 vs round 8's arm B 6,932 = **0.21% apart** across different jobs and placements. Cross-session
reproducibility is therefore ~0.2%, a touch above the 0.09% within-session floor and tight enough to
compare across rounds.

⭐ **This creates a new, sharper gap, which is the real value of the round.** The recorded 6-node
per-GPU penalty is **35.2%**, but a fixed ~11.3% comms tax can only account for a third of it. So
~24 points at 6 nodes come from **neither** known mechanism. And the arithmetic points straight at the
suspect: 6 nodes = 24 ranks = 528/24 = **22 micro-steps per rank**, an operating point round 8 never
tested: R8 compared 66 vs 132 and found the micro-step term *exactly zero*. Zero at 66-vs-132 does
not imply zero at 22, because per-micro-step fixed costs are amortised over 6× fewer micro-steps there.

**Round 10 submitted and RUNNING: job 7592395**, 2 nodes / 1 h, `nccl_ustep10.pbs`. Wire and rank
count held, only micro-step count varies: **G** 8 ranks / batch 540672 → 66 µsteps (same-session
control, and the cross-session anchor against R8 arm A's 10.990); **F** 8 ranks / batch 180224 → **22
µsteps**, the 6-node operating point. Pre-registered: F ≈ G means the micro-step term is zero at 22 too
and the 35.2% is explained by *nothing* we have measured, it should then be re-measured rather than
quoted. F ≪ G means the batch-shape term switches on below ~66 µsteps, the 35.2% is real and mostly
SHAPE not wire, and the fix is a larger global batch for wide shapes, not any NCCL setting.

## §M+80
### ⭐⭐ Round 11 CLOSED: there is NO knee. It is a FIXED 1.395 s per-step overhead, and the fit is exact. (2026-09-04 15:05 CDT)

Job 7592433, both arms complete at n=25. Adding R11's 44-µstep point to R10's 22 and 66 gives a
three-point ladder at 8 ranks / 2 nodes, all in the same rig:

| µsteps/rank | batch | min s/step | tok/s per GPU | deficit vs 66 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 22 | 180224 | 4.600 | 4,897 | −20.4% |
| **44** | **360448** | **7.800** | **5,776** | **−5.9%** |
| 66 | 540672 | 11.010 | 6,138 | n/a |

⭐ **The three points are EXACTLY linear in micro-step count:**
`s/step = 1.395 + 0.1457 × µsteps`, residuals **+0.000 / −0.005 / +0.000 s**.
So the pre-registered "knee" framing was wrong, and the third branch: *gradual, not a knee*, is what
happened. The mechanism is simply a **fixed 1.395 s of per-step cost** (optimizer step, the
un-overlappable head/tail of the collective, Python and launch overhead) that is amortised over
however many micro-steps the step contains: **12.7% of the step at 66 µsteps, 30.3% at 22.**

⭐ This is a better result than a threshold would have been, because it is a *model* rather than a
boundary: the deficit at any width is predictable from µsteps/rank = 528/ranks, and the batch
recommendation becomes a continuous trade with an explicit number to amortise, not a cliff to stay
above. R8's "66 vs 132 is flat" also stops being a separate fact, at 132 µsteps the fixed cost is
only 6.7% of the step, so the *difference* from 66 is small, exactly as the fit predicts.

⭐ **Fourth cross-session anchor:** R8 arm A and R10 arm G both min 10.990; R11 G2 min **11.010**, 
0.18% apart, just inside the 0.21% cross-session floor R9 established. Four independent measurements
of one shape agreeing to <0.2% is what makes the ladder above worth fitting.

⚠️ Still to be honest about: the fit is at **8 ranks**. The coefficient 0.1457 s/µstep is per-rank work
and should hold, but the 1.395 s intercept plausibly *grows* with rank count (a wider collective has a
longer un-overlappable head), and 6 nodes = 24 ranks was never measured directly. The composition in
§M+79 that reached 88% of the 6-node deficit used the 8-rank shape term, so the residual 5.8% is a
candidate for exactly that: a larger intercept at 24 ranks.

### §M+80a: the mirror's bottleneck is /eagle read contention, NOT the network (2026-09-04 15:20 CDT)
The 126793 copy was rate-aborted at 14:49 (rc=20, under the 3 MB/s MINRATE guard) and has been in the
30-minute backoff since. Measured the sophia→midway3 path directly with a 210 MB timed stream:
**1.36 s = 154 MB/s, 51× the guard's threshold.** The wire is fine.

So the slow copies are **reads of a 24.8 GB checkpoint off /eagle while the Sophia trainer is
saturating the same filesystem**, and the pattern across today supports it exactly: every mirror
completed in ~1.5 min while POLARIS was the trainer (125657, 126011, 126268, 126427), took 8 min once
Sophia took over (126604), and could not sustain rate at all after that. ⚠️ Do not chase the network
on this symptom again.

⚠️ Consequence for the standing backup task, stated plainly: while Sophia trains, the mirror is
competing with the trainer for /eagle and the guard will keep aborting until there is a quiet window.
Exposure stays bounded: 126604 is md5-verified on /project plus the 95055 anchor, and the retry is
automatic. ⚠️ Note the hash-first design reads the 24.8 GB file twice per attempt (hash, then copy),
which doubles the /eagle load; that is a deliberate trade to win the retention race (§the mirror's own
header) and is NOT to be "optimised" away without measuring what it protects against.

### §M+80b: the experiment allocation is queued behind ONE A100 node, not misconfigured
`exp-a5 57844963` reads `ReqNodeNotAvail, UnavailableNodes:midway3-0294`. Cause: **midway3-0294 is the
only a100 node in the `gpu` partition** (the rest are v100 / rtx6000), it has 4 GPUs, and it is
currently MIXED. `--constraint=a100` is not optional here: `cell_driver.sh` enforces a ≥40 GB card
("GPU capacity OK: smallest visible card 40960 MiB") and the h800 arms will not fit a 32 GB v100 or a
24 GB rtx6000. So this is ordinary contention for 4 GPUs on a single node, and the previous session
(57477255) ran on that same node for 33 h. Nothing to fix; it starts when a GPU frees.

## §M+81: the experiment card moved to Polaris `debug`, and THREE things that made that possible

The experiment line had been idle since `exp-a5` 57850040 went PENDING at 16:48 CDT: all 4 A100 GPUs
on **midway3-0294** are held by other users, and `sbatch --test-only` put our start at ~15:40 the next
day, i.e. ~17 h of dead experiment time. Polaris meanwhile had free nodes and nothing of ours running.
Moving the card there took resolving three separate things, each of which had a wrong prior.

**1. midway3's constraint is HARDWARE, not queue, so there is no lever there.** `gpu` has 11 nodes
all advertising `gpu:4`, and 10 of them had idle CPUs, which looks like an opportunity. It is not:
`AvailableFeatures` says midway3-0277…0286 are **v100** and **rtx6000** (cc 7.0 / 7.5, no bf16).
This arch trains in bf16, so 0294 (`a100`) is genuinely the only target in that partition and
`Features=a100` is not an over-constraint to relax. This closes the question: do not re-probe it.

**2. `preemptable` is dead RIGHT NOW, and a record-mode census is the only way to see it.** `exp4gpu.pbs`
carries `-q preemptable` and its own comment claims "2 h lands instantly". That was true once; it is
false now. Census (`pbsnodes -a`, RS="" record mode):

| state | tag | nodes |
|---|---|---|
| job-exclusive | prod,debug | 485 |
| job-exclusive | demand,**preemptable** | 55 |
| offline | prod,debug | 10 |
| **free** | **debug** | **8** |
| **free** | **prod,debug** | **1** |
| offline | demand,preemptable | 1 |

56 nodes carry the `preemptable` tag and **every one is job-exclusive or offline**, so a preemptable
job places on nothing. `prod` routes to `small` (≥10 nodes): barred by the never-take-more-nodes rule.
**`debug` is the only queue that can place a 1-node session**, and it did: submitted 22:12 CDT, `R`
within 45 s on x3005c0s7b1n0, zero pending time.
⚠️ **And I got the free-node count wrong AGAIN with a line-mode awk**, it reported 19 free nodes when
there were 9, because it depends on `queue_tags` appearing before `state = free` inside a record. This
is the *same* parsing fault that cost a healthy trainer on 2026-09-04 11:53. Record mode (`RS=""`,
`match()` per field) is the only form of this census to trust. `exp4gpu.pbs` is KEPT for when
preemptable nodes free; `exp4gpu_debug.pbs` is the new placeable variant.

**3. Polaris is FASTER than midway3 for probe arms: measured, against my assumption.** From 83
completed h400 arms in `/eagle/exp_results`: **4,117-5,363 tok/s**, and 5,354 at the tied-embedding
shape these cells use, versus midway3's **3,220** (cell 49's h800 arms). So per arm:

| horizon | midway3 A100 | Polaris A100-40G | fits `debug` 1 h wall? |
|---|---|---|---|
| h400 (8.192M tok) | n/a | **1,782-2,315 s (~30 min)** | ✅ ~30 min of margin |
| h800 (16.384M tok) | 5,354 s (89 min) | ~3,400-4,400 s (57-73 min) | ⛔ no |

That table is the whole placement rule: **h400 cells run on Polaris `debug`; h800 cells stay on the
midway3 A100.** It is why cell 51 (h400) is what got queued tonight and cell 50 (h800) did not.

### Two defects fixed on the way, both mechanism not instance

**`ARM_SECS` was hardcoded and its guarantee was therefore false.** `exp4gpu.pbs` states the contract
"a batch is only STARTED if enough walltime remains to finish it, so we never knowingly cut one off",
then pins `ARM_SECS=2100` (35 min), while the arms it was being fed declare `wall_guard_sec 7800` and
*measure* 5,354 s. A batch begun with 35 min left would be killed mid-arm by PBS, silently, and the
arms would come back as `wall_guard`/orphaned. The runner now **derives** the budget from the batch it
is about to start: `max(wall_guard_sec over the batch) + STARTUP_PAD`, with `STARTUP_PAD=420` (measured
startup+compile is 124-213 s, so 2× the worst). First live run printed `batch budget: need 3120s, have
3294s`: the guarantee is now computed from the arms rather than asserted about them.

**An explicit `kd_teacher` in an arm config overrides the runner's `A45_TEACHER` export.** Every arm
built on midway3 carries `kd_teacher = /project/rcc/youzhi/toxic-models/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base`, which
does not exist on /eagle. `exp4gpu*.pbs` exports `A45_TEACHER`, but that is only probe.py's *default*
: the config value wins. Un-rewritten, all 4 arms would have failed twice and parked in `failed/`.
Staging now rewrites the field, and both ends are **md5-verified** (checksum, not length: §the 2026-08-29
lesson). Anything staged midway3 → /eagle needs this rewrite; it is a property of the config, not of a
particular cell.

### Arm-level resume: the machinery is half-built, and finishing it would unlock `debug` for h800

`probe.py`'s `Mix.state()` / `Mix.load_state()` exist and are explicitly designed for cheap resume: 
"the sampler's ENTIRE state is 3 byte-offsets + the bit-generator state + counts … there is no shuffle
buffer, no worker state, nothing implicit". But **nothing ever calls them**: there is no `torch.save`
of arm state anywhere in the file (the only `ckpt` symbol is `torch.utils.checkpoint`). So an arm
cannot survive a session boundary, which is exactly why h800 is locked out of the one queue that can
reliably place. Wiring those two methods to a save/load at the wall_guard boundary would make arm
length independent of queue wall: the single highest-leverage change available to the experiment
line. Deliberately NOT done tonight: probe.py is the measurement instrument for the whole campaign,
and shipping an untested resume path and then reading a decision cell through it is how you get a
silent corruption instead of a result.

## §M+82: why h800 CANNOT be made to fit the 1 h wall: probe arms are already HBM-saturated

§M+81 left "run h800 on Polaris" resting on arm-level resume. Before building that, the cheap
alternative was checked: make the arm FASTER instead of resumable. `grad_checkpointing` is pure
recompute, so switching it off changes **no numerics at all**: every existing arm stays comparable, 
and typically buys ~1.35×. That would take h800 from ~60 min to ~44 min and fit `debug` outright.

**Refuted by the arms' own records.** Across all 83 completed h400 arms in `/eagle/exp_results`, on
`A100-SXM4-40GB`, with `grad_checkpointing=1` in every one:

| `hbm_frac` | min | median | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| | 0.8907 | **0.9188** | 0.9188 |

Arms are at **89-92% of 40 GiB with checkpointing already on**, and cell 51's live arms report
`hbm=95.9%`. There is no headroom to trade, so `grad_checkpointing=0` would OOM and the 1.35× is not
available. (Incidental, stated once: this also answers the standing "is HBM being left on the table"
check for the experiment card, it is not, arms sit at or above the ~90% target.)

⇒ **The placement rule in §M+81 is not a workaround, it is the only option:** h400 cells on Polaris
`debug`, h800 cells on the midway3 A100. The three ways to change that, ranked:
1. **Arm-level resume**: wire `probe.py`'s already-written `Mix.state()`/`load_state()` to a real
   save/load. Cost is the honest problem: model + Muon/AdamW state is ~12-16 GB per arm, so ~50-65 GB
   of **/eagle** writes per session boundary × 4 arms, on the filesystem whose read contention already
   measurably slows the checkpoint mirror and which the live trainer shares. Not obviously worth it.
2. **Shorten the arm** (the standing directive's answer), but h800 *is* the axis under test in cells
   46/48/49/50, so h600 would not answer their question.
3. **Wait for the midway3 A100**: currently ~17 h out.

⚠️ `hbm_frac` was already in every result record; a first pass looking for keys matching
`mem|gib|peak` reported "no memory fields recorded at all" and nearly bought a new instrumentation
change that was not needed. The field is `hbm_frac`, and `probe.py` also logs live `hbm=` per 25 steps.

### Reproducibility defect found and fixed: the tracked instrument was not the one running the arms

`/eagle/code/probe.py` (md5 `55d3532e`) and the repo's `exp/probe.py` (`54935508`) differed by exactly
**13 lines**: the `ddp_comm_hook = bf16` block, present ONLY on /eagle. So the ALCF copy that produced
407 arm results was a superset of the tracked file, and a routine sync out would have silently deleted
the block. The file's own `DATA` comment warns about precisely this ("a remote-only edit was silently
clobbered the next time this file was synced out"), which is how it was spotted. Block synced back into
the repo with a provenance comment; the two now differ only by that comment. **Diff the repo copy
against /eagle before editing either**: `exp/probe.py` is +292/−17 vs git HEAD, so neither git nor a
casual look tells you which version ran a given arm.

### ⛔ A `wall_guard` arm is marked INVALID but still lands in `done/`: it is never re-run

Found while watching cell 51, and it matters because that cell has only ~3.8 min of guard margin.
`probe.py` on a guard trip sets `status="wall_guard"`, `valid=False`, writes the record, and **exits 0**
(invariant I5: "a wall-guard trip still writes a record, marked invalid", deliberately, so a missing
result is distinguishable from a crash). But every `exp4gpu*.pbs` runner keys its bookkeeping on the
exit code alone:

    probe.py ... && mv inflight/$arm.json done/ || { ...retry/park... }

Exit 0 ⇒ the arm moves to `done/`. So a truncated, explicitly-invalid arm is recorded as completed and
is **never retried**, silently breaking the standing requirement that "any arm interrupted mid-batch
[is] re-run in the next session". Nothing ever reads `valid`. The two halves of the design disagree:
probe.py is careful to say "this result is not usable", and the runner throws that flag away.

Fix: the runner must read `valid` from the emitted result and return an invalid arm to `pending/`
rather than `done/`. Implemented in `exp4gpu_debug2.pbs` (a NEW file: `exp4gpu_debug.pbs` is running
cell 51 right now and a launcher must never be edited mid-run, since bash re-reads it from a byte
offset).

⚠️ And the cause of the thin margin itself: `wall_guard_sec=2700` for cell 51 was sized from 5,354
tok/s, the rate of the *fastest* h400 family on /eagle (`n726_tied`). Cell 51 inherits cell 37's config
and actually runs **3,564 tok/s**: 33% slower, so the real need is ~41 min against a 45 min guard.
**Size `wall_guard_sec` from a measured rate for the SAME config family, not the fleet best**, or set
it from the session budget minus startup rather than a guessed constant.

## §M+83: ⛔ MY OWN WATCHDOG KILLED CELL 51. `shape_upgrade.sh` read an experiment session as a trainer

**What happened.** Cell 51's session 7593041 died at 22:30:08 CDT, 17 min 47 s into a 1 h wall, with
`Exit_status = 143` (SIGTERM) and all four arms cut at **step 125/400**. No crash, no OOM, no
preemption: a clean wall-clock-aligned kill. The killer was `~/bin/shape_upgrade.sh`, which I set to
`APPLY=1` at 12:48 the same day. Its own log is unambiguous:

    22:20:04 running 7593041 at 1 node(s); 54 min of wall left; FREEU=1 (authoritative); cap=6 -> best supported 1
    22:20:04 NO UPGRADE: 1 is not >= 3x the current 1 node(s); too small to repay the compile
    22:30:07 running 7593041 at 1 node(s); 44 min of wall left; FREEU=23 (authoritative); cap=6 -> best supported 6
    22:30:07 UPGRADE JUSTIFIED: 1 -> 6 node(s), 44 min left, gain 6x
    22:30:08 released 7593041; the keeper polls every 20 s and will re-size from its own FREEU

The Polaris pool recovered between the two ticks (FREEU 1 → 23), every one of the script's four guards
passed *on its own terms*, and it correctly concluded that a 1-node trainer should be widened to 6.
The job it widened was not a trainer.

**Cause, and it is the SAME class of error for the FOURTH time.** The script resolved "the trainer" as
*any RUNNING Polaris job of ours*:

    ROW=$(qstat -u $USER | awk '$1 ~ /^[0-9]+\./ && $10=="R"{...}')

An experiment session drops `$R/.exp_job_<id>` under an EXIT trap for exactly this purpose, and
`trainer_status.sh`, `chain_watchdog.sh` and `best_shape.sh` all already consult it. `shape_upgrade.sh`
never did. Job existence cannot identify a trainer, and neither can job NAME: every ALCF job of ours
must be named `benchmarking` by owner directive, so the name carries zero information. `trainer_status.sh`
documents itself as "the third script to learn it"; this is the fourth.

Worse, the irony is on the record: `shape_upgrade.sh`'s own header says it was written *after* an
incident where I "counted free nodes with an ad-hoc line-mode awk, got 6 when the truth was 0-1, and
qdel'd a healthy trainer". A script created in response to a bad qdel went on to make a bad qdel of a
different kind. Fixing the node-counting did nothing about *what the id pointed at*.

**Fix.** A marker check immediately after id resolution, before any sizing arithmetic:

    EXPJ=$(ssh polaris "ls -1 $R/.exp_job_* 2>/dev/null" | sed 's#.*/\.exp_job_##')
    if echo "$EXPJ" | grep -qx "$JID"; then
      say "RUNNING polaris job $JID is an EXPERIMENT SESSION (.exp_job_$JID present), not a trainer -- never resize it; exiting"
      exit 0
    fi

**Verified by re-running the check** (not assumed): a dry run against the replacement session printed
`RUNNING polaris job 7593102 is an EXPERIMENT SESSION (.exp_job_7593102 present), not a trainer --
never resize it; exiting`.

**Audit of every other watchdog that can qdel on Polaris**, since one offender implies siblings:

| script | `.exp_job_` aware | can qdel | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shape_upgrade.sh` | ✗ → **✓ fixed** | yes | **was the offender** |
| `trainer_autopilot2.sh` | ✓ (line 83) | yes (10 sites) | safe: fails CLOSED for killing; an unrecognised script is never qdel'd, by its own design note |
| `polaris_chain_keeper4.sh` | ✓ (3 checks) | yes | safe |
| `best_shape.sh` | ✗ | **no** | advisory only, cannot act |

**Note on the widening logic itself, which is NOT wrong and stays.** Extra nodes are meaningless to an
experiment session in a way that is worth stating: its four arms are four INDEPENDENT single-GPU
worlds with no collective between them, so a 6-node allocation would run exactly the same four arms at
exactly the same speed while holding 24 GPUs for 4. That is the "never take more nodes than the work
needs" rule, and it is why the right response to this job is *never resize*, not *resize more carefully*.

**Recovery, all four steps.** (1) The SIGTERM meant the runner's own failure branch never ran, so the
arms were left in `queue/inflight/`: moved back to `pending/`. (2) Confirmed **no** `.fail_`/`.invalid_`
counters had been set, which is correct and matters: the session was killed, the arms did not fail, and
a strike against them would have parked them in `failed/` after one more such event. (3) Confirmed no
stale `.exp_job_7593041` (its EXIT trap does run on SIGTERM). (4) Resubmitted as **7593102** on the
`exp4gpu_debug2.pbs` runner (so cell 51 also picks up the §M+82 `valid`-flag fix): placed `R` within
50 s on x3005c0s31b0n0, all four arms restarted from step 0.

**Cost:** ~18 min of 4-GPU work, zero data (no arm had produced a record). **The arms restart from
step 0**: there is no arm-level resume, which is the §M+82 gap; had it existed, this kill would have
cost ~nothing. That raises the value of resume from "unlocks h800 on `debug`" to "also makes a session
kill cheap", though the /eagle write cost still argues against it.
